- AFTERWARD. 0 strange, 0 sad perplexity, Blind groping through the night; Faith faintly questions can there be In afterward of light? 0 heavy sorrow, grief and tears, That all our hopes destroy; Say, shall there dawn in coming years An afterward of joy? 0 hopes that turn to gall Mil rue, Sweet fruits that bitter prove ; Is there an afterward of true And eyerlasting love? 0 weariness, within, without, 'fain longings for release; 12 *ace to inward fear and doubt. MI afterward of peace? 0 restless wanderings to and fro, In vain and fruitless quest; Where shall we find above, below, An afterward of rest? 0 death, with whom we plead in vain To stay thy fatal knife; . Is there beyond the reach of pain An afterward of life? • Ah, ye.; we know this seeing ill, When rightly understood, In God's own time and way fulfil His afterward of good. —C7, ambers' s Journal.

div.p: Tarititto.

Oriental Wisdom.—Bef ore a Turk gets married he asks 311 good men to pray for him. A carpenter is seldom as handsome as his wife, because he is generally a deal plainer. Saw a sign in a barber's window the other day: "Boots blackened inside." Couldn't for the life of us think why anybody wants the inside of his boots blackened. Should think it would ruin a fellow's stockings. "Do you think piety to be a more important qualification for the ministry than learning?" once asked Mr. Wilber- force of an eminent prelate. "Certainly I do," he an- swered; "they can cheat me as to their piety, but they can't as to their learning." The humour of the Scotchman does not always seem to wear the most amiable complexion. Someone remarked to an Aberdonian "It's a fine day." " Fa's (who's) finding flat wP the day ?" was the not very civil reply. "Ye wad pick a quarrel we a steen (stone) wail" The French Ambassador to the English Court paid a neat compliment a little while back to a Peeress who had been talking to him for an hour. The lady said, "You must think lam very fond of the sound of my own voice." The Frenchman replied, "I knew you liked music." A young man living in Leadville forwarded to his little brother in St. Louis, as a present, a choice donkey of the diminutive species known as the Mexican burro. The agent, in making out his list, concluded that "burro" meant "bureau," and so reported to his euperior "one bureau missing, and one jackass over..' A good story is told of a boy at Eton who was alwayi reckoned a great dunce, and more disposed to cricket than to " Lempriere." One day in class he manifested intense anxiety to answer the question, "Name the three Graces," and on yielding to the young gentleman's pertinacity, the master was astonished to receive the following eager. an- swer :—" E. M. Grace, W. .G. Grace, and G. F. Grace!' (the famous cricketing brothers). A...minx-it OF Mr:am—The Rev. Mr. Imlack, of Merroes, Titall an able man, but a very absent-teinded one, and once, I in a public service of considerable importance, he spoke of all ranks and degrees of persons, "from the king on the dunghill to the beggar on the throne;" but, suspecting rather than perceiving the mistake, he proceeded instantly to amend his error by saying, "No, my friends, I mean from the beggar on the throne to the king on the dunghill." AN " HONEST WOMAN !"--The celebrated Dr. John Erskine, of Greyfriars, Edinburgh, was noted for the even- ness of his temper. His haedkerchief had disappeared every Sabbath dnring his descent from the pulpit, and suspicion could only fall on an elderly female, who, accord- ing to the practice of the times, sat on the pulpit stair. In order to discover the depredator, Mrs. Erskine sewed the corner of the handkerchief to the mmister's pocket. Re- turning from the pulpit, he felt a gentle pull, when, turn- ing round and tapping the old woman on the shoulder, be exclaimed, "No the day, honest woman •, no the day !" SLEEP FOR CRILDREN.—The old-fashioned doctrine that children should be rigorously roused from sleep at a set hour in the morning, and jump oat of bed the minute they wake, is exploded. If they go to bed early enough, healthy children will ordinarily wake betimes, and naturally. Bt they should have all the sleep they need, Some require more than others, and in some way nature's demands should be satisfied. But remember that early hours at night are to be chosen for sleep before late morning hours. If put to bed in season, little children are generally, like the birds, awake and singing in the early morning. A Yankee riding in a railway carriage was disposed to astonish the other passengers with tough stories. At last he mentioned that one of his neighbours owned an immense dairy, and made a million pounds of butter and a million pounds of cheese yearly. The Yankee perceiving that his veracity was in danger of being questioned, appealed to la friend, "True, isn't it, mister? I speak of Deacon Browne." " Y-e-s," replied the friend, " that is, I know Deacon Browne, though I don't know as ever I heard. precisely how many pounds of butter apd cheese he makes a year; but I know he has twelve saw mills that all go by buttermilk." Under the auspices of the late librarian, the reading-room of the British Museum was made, in its new shape, one of the finest places for students in the world. Before the pre- sent magnificent building was erected, a certain old lady— who still frequents the new room—had the privilege of sup- plying coffee to such of the readers as might require it. Just about the thus when the present edifice was out of the hands of the builders, our hitherto privileged:dame was invited to see the: grand architectural novelty. "Yea yes," she Bald, "it is very fine, very fine indeed. But where is the place for my fire and coffee pot ?"She could not see the improvement. "A GALLOWS AT BAITIL"—When the present fashionable spa of Bridge of, Allan was a small agricultural hamlet, it • was the abode of an old cobbler who was renowned for his witty sayings, and was never known to be put out. One -day, as he was walking in front of his little cottage, two young officers from Stirline. Castle came up. One had pre- viously betted with the other that he would overmatch the gobbler. "How far have we to go, Sawney ?" says the con- fident. "Just three miles," replied the cobbler. "How do you know ?" insisted the querist. "Because," answered the cobbler, "it's three miles to Stirling, an' it's three to Dun- blane, and there's a gallows at baith!" It is necessary to , explain that at the period of the incident there were public I executioners at both places. TAKING UP ONE'S CROSS means simply, writes Mr. Raskin, that you -are to go the road which you see to be the straight one carrying whatever you find is given you to carry as well and stoutly 23 you can, without making faces or calling people to come and look at you. Above all, you are neither to load nor unload yourself, nor cut your cross to your own liking. . Some people think it would be better for them to have it large, and many that they could carry it much faster if it were small; and even those who like it largest are usually particular about it being ornamental and made of the best ebony. But all that you have really to do is to keep your back as straight as you can, and not think - about what is upon it—above all, not to boast of what is upon it. The real and essential meaning of "virtue" is in that straightness of back. ANECDOTE OF THE rREMIER.—In Mr. Gladstone's house- hold at Hawarden was an old woman servant who had a son inclined to go wrong. The mother remonstrated, and ad- vised her boy, but all to no purpose; he seemed determined on a headlong course to ruin. At last the mother in her desperation caught the idea that if she could persuade the Premier to take him in hand, perhaps the prodigal mightbe reclaimed. "Screwing her courage to the sticking point" —for what will a mother not do for a child ?—she ap- proached her master, and in trembling tones preferred her request. Mr. Gladstone responded at once, and though the affairs of the greatest kingdom in the world pressed heavily upon him, with genuine simplicity of character he had the lid sent to his study, when he spoke tender words of advice and remonstrance, and eventually knelt down and prayed God to help in the work of redemption. This kindly action was effectual, and the lad became a reformed character. This anecdote is well authenticated. Lavß or TITLES.—An odd illustration of the indigenous love of titles in the Scotch occurs in an old newspaper. In the days of Bailie Nicol Jarvie's father the office of deacon (chairman of a corporation of tradesmen) was esteemed no mean distinction. Two worthy incumbents, who fretted their little hour upon a stage not far from the banks of the Ayr, happened to be invested with the above-named dignity on the same day. The more youthful of the two flew home to tell his young wife what an important prop of the civic edifice he had been allowed to become; and, searching the "but and ben" in vain, ran out to the byre, where, meeting the cow, he could no longer contain his 10y, but, in the ful- nem of his heart, clasped her round the neck, and it is even said kissed her, exclaiming, "Oh, crummie, crummie, ye're nae langer a common cow; ye'ra the deacon's cow r 7 The elder civic dignatory was a sedate, pious person, and felt rather " blate " in showing to his wife that he was uplifted above this world's hondurs. As he thought, however, it was too good a piece of news to allow her to remain any time ig- norant of, he lifted the latch of his own door, and stretching his head inwards, " Nelly," said he, in a voice that made Nally all ears and eyes, " gif ony body comes spierin for the deacon, I'm just owre the gate at John Tamson's!"

At Sciaeca the action of water and wear have laid, mosaic pavement of considerable archxological intereat. A Roman tomb has been accidentally oliscoverid Salerno. It contained bronze money, vases, lanterns oi coloured glass, and fragments of statues. Mr. Nugent Banks, who made a hit as a schoolboy with "A day of my Life at Eton," has just published a com- panion book on university life, under the title of "A Cam- badge Staircase." The papers originally appeared in the Cambridge Review. The satirist of John Bull is not going to have it all his own way, for it is stated that two writers are engaged upon I a work which will deal with each of the arguments put for- ward in "John Ball et Son Ile," and attempt a complete refutation of the charges brought against us as a nation. Lord Lytton's "Rienzi," Wilkie Collins's "Woman in White," and Sir Walter Scott's "Bride of Lammermoor," have lately been translated into Bengali by Damodar Mukerji, and published at Calcutta. Other novels are to follow, if the natives should show a taste for this new class of literature. At the meeting of the French Academy of Sciences, this week, M. Daubree announced the fall of a meteorite in the department of the Gironde. The phenomenon was well observed. Before the fall, five violent detonations, resem- bling the sound of artillery, followed by a noise similar to that of a rifle volley, were heard. A black cloud preceded the aerolite. The authorship of "The Bitter Cry of Outcast London" having been a matter of conjecture in many of our con- temporaries, it may be as well to state that the writer is the Rev. W. C. Preston, a xentleman connected with the London religious press, and author of "Mr. Manby's Mid- night Visitor," a short story relating to work among the outcast poor.—A thenteum, Herr Rubinstein has received from the well-known im- presario Pollini an invitation to undertake a tour in the United States and appear at 100 concerts in five months for a payment of £25,000 sterling. Of this sum £lO,OOO has already been deposited with a banker at Hamburg, but the great pianist has not yet accepted the offer. The origin of the word " agnostic " may some day be a matter of doubt and dispute. It is, therefore, satisfactory to have from Professor Huxley an authoritative statement concerning it. In a little publication just issued under the title of "The Agnostic Annual," he states that he invented the word about 20 years ago to denote his own position in regard to theological matters. The "Annual" contains also contributions by Professor Haeckel, Mr. P. A. Taylor, M.P., and Professor F. W. Newman. The last named, it is needless to say, disclaims the agnostic position. A remarkable meteor is said to have been observed at Fraserburgh a few nights ago. At first it appeared in mid- air nearly directly overhead, and flashed across the sky in a north-westerly direction in the middle of its course. The main body of it appeared about half the size of the moon, and visibly lighted up the country for many miles around, causing great alarm to the beholders. It was preceded by a luminous body of bluish colour, while the body tapered in a long series of balls of light, and disappeared from sight over the horizon. Madame Pauline Lucca is a remarkable example of the position to which singers of the first rank have attainedl under the present conditions. Herprospective engagements include four weeks at Moscow, for which she is to receive £4,000. In December she is to give representations in Ber- lin, after which she will return to the Imperial Opera at Vienna. Next year she will be in London during May and June, having been appointed £4AOO by the Messrs. Gye for her services, and she has an offer, which will probably be accepted, of £20,000 for a season of six months in the United States during the winter of 1884-5. MM. Mallard and Le Chatelier find that the temperature of explosion of mixtutes of hydrogen and air is between 560 and 600 degrees C.; and of mixtures containing car- bonic oxide 630 to 730 degrees. The explosive temperature of gaseous mixtures is little affected by the addition of other gases. From the experiments it appears that a tem- perature of 1,000 degrees can no longer be taken as the ex- plosive point of gases in coal mines. In the report of the French CommissionUn coal mine explosions 740 degrees is given as the temperature of explosion of mixtures of fire- damp and air, but it is added that the mixture must remain at this temperature for several seconds before ex- plosion takes place. The general result of the experiments of MM. Mallard and Le Chatelier is therefore a lowering of the temperature at which it _has been held that explosions , may take place. THE ROMAN ROAD OVER BLACKSTONE EDGE.—On Satur- day a party of twenty members of the Lancashire and Cheshire Antiquarian Society, including Mr. J. E. Bailey and Mr. J. P. Earwaker, paid a visit to the ,Roman Road ,over Blackstone Edge. The party traced the course of the road from the most westerly point on the Lancashire side of the hill to its connection with the turnpike road about a mile beyond the border line of the two connties. Down the eastern slope of the Edge, where workmen have dug up the roadway for about 40 yards, a very good section of the bed of theroadway and the pavement was obtained,and it was found that the shale of which the bed is made for the pavement was laid upon a substratum of peat, also that the face of the pavement was covered to a depth of nearly two feet with a tough vegetable growth which must have taken a long time to accumulate. It was the general opinion of the party that the face of the pavement had not been suffaciently exposed to admit of a conclusion being formed as to the object of the grooved line of centre blocks arld as to the formation of the ruts on each side of it. Mr. E. Kirk suggested that a good section should be cleared, and an impression made of the whole width in plaster of Paris, and that from this matrix an exact facsimile in Portland cement should be taken, to be placed endwise in some Institution in Man- chester for the use of students and others. As the road was not included in the Preservation of Ancient Monuments Act, and as it had evidently suffered very much from ruth- less hands, he thought several useful ends might thus be served. The suggestion was favourably received. There was a slight coating of snow on the Edge, but it did not interfere with the researches of the party.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

With Neg. and lldeg. of frost, one not acquainted with 1 gardening operations would naturally conclude that work comes to a stand, but such is by no means the case. Apart from the labour of attending to covered and uncovered ten- der subjects which frosty weather brings about, we find it most opportune for conducting several operations; the chief at present being conveying manure on the ground, as it can be performed much easier and the ground does not suffer from trampling and the action of the barrow wheels. The latter, when the ground is soft, converts it into paste, consequently we reserve as much as possible of this kind of work for this seasonable weather. Vacant spaces, which have been roughly forked, will be in a pulverised condition after a few nights frosts, and may be ridged, dug, or trenched according to its nature and requirements, but neither should be done whilst the ground is actually frozen, because it is obvious that if the frost be turned under it must tend to cool the other soil several degrees. This is not BO important in rigding as in deep digging or trenc'hinz,, because the ridges lay exposed to the action of the sun and are usually levelled down before the ground is used. When trenching has been carried on in frosty weather the congealed lumps have turned up some weeks after all traces of frost have disappeared. We are now subjecting a piece of ground to thorough trenching which lam been occupied by summer 1 cabbage and late c,auliflo vers, with an occasional row of 1 peas the two former being the most exhaustive crops in the garden. We found a frosty morning a fitting time to wheel the contents of the trench from one end to the other, which We take out 2ft. deep anti the same in width. When the ' subsoil is clayey the depth must be regulated by it, for it would not answer to bring the clay to the top beyond an inch or two at a time. As soon as the clay is reached it I should be forked up and covered over with manure, and the top of the next trench thrown on that. When it is Moved the next time it is trenched some portion of the clay will be altered in its nature by an admixture of the 4aanure and better soil and may be brought to the surface. It will , therefore be seen that the depth of cultivatable soil is in- 1 creased several inches in a few years. This is cultivation. 1 Digging the surface year after year is what a cynical friend i terms " something like an old hen scratching." The some- 1 what sadden severity of the frost if it continues will neces- sitate young cauliflower and lettuce being protected more effectually than they would if it had come more gradually. In the absence of an old light or two, a .frame should be made and covered with some textile non-conducting material and placed over them at night, and moved as soon as there are signs of thaw in the morning. Leaves and bracken or the common fern are plentiful in most country places; these, if placed amongst and over plants, afford good protection. THE FRONT GARDEN.—The Dahlias may now be taken, and if their colours are known, it should be written on a smooth piece of wood that has had a thin coat of white paint rubbed on with the finger. An ordinary lead pencil will make legible letters that will remain indelible for two or three years. These should be attached to the roots with thin pieces of wire. The advantage of knowing the colours will be apparent when planting time comes round. It will be as well to remark that it is not necessary to cut the stems of the Dahlia any shorter than ein. or Bin, from the root. The stems being hollow, they sometimes' contain a quantity of water, so we always invert them as we lift them, and place them in that position in their resting-place for a few days. It has occurred to us that the fronts of dwelling- houses Might be made more attractive than they are if adorned with suitable creepers, the greater portion of which are grown by nurserymen in pots, and can be moved at any time of the year. Some hundreds of valuable plants have , been planted against residences, and grow beautifully less , Year by year till the last vestige of them disappeared, and , their chagrined owner never thought of prying into the rea- ; Bon Why- He prefers to cherish a disgust towards these vic- tims of his own creation and other matters connected with ' horticulture, or he pronounces some anathema on the ven- dor, but not the planter. If we meet with non-success we always inquire for the latter individual, and, after some urns and ahs, we find he is as likely to execute the work as efficiently as a blacksmith would repair and clean a gold watch. THE WINDOW.—During frosty weather all plants should be removed as far away horn the glass as possible. The frost may not be sere enough to reach and injure the most tender plants, but we findethat when leaves of hardier plants are in contact with frozen glass they invariably perish. The Chinese Primrose is a favourite with everybody, but unfortunately it is beyond the capacity of the cottager to raise it from seed, or increase it by cutting. But it is always to be purchased for a few pence, and those who have sacceeded in growing them once are always eager for them . again. We saw some in a window a few days ago looking

There are aiew very charming half-hardy ,Prilmila.3 that ought to find a home in cottage windows. But no, it is the everlasting Fuchsia and Geranium. IN-BREEDING AND I NTERTILITY. —AS an illustration of the extent to which in-breeding can be carried without im- pairing fertility, it may be mentioned that in a long report of the Warlaby Shorthorns which appears in the Field of November 10,it is stated that two cows in that very clo3ely-- bred herd are now nursing twins, whilst a third has just produced three bull calves at a birth. MR. GLADSTONE AND THE IMPORTATION OF FOOT-AND- MOUTH DISEASE —The Secretary of the Central Chamber of Agriculture has received the following reply to the re- solution sent to the Prime Minister on the question of foot- and-month disease :—" 10, Downing-street, Whitehall, Nov. 9, 1883.—Dear sir,—l am directed by:Mr. Gladstone to acquaint you that he is in receipt of the resolution which you have transmitted to him from the Council of the Central and Associated Chamber of Agriculture, as well as of the report from the Cattle Diseases Committee, regarding the foot-and-mouth disease. In reply, he desires me to say that he makes no doubt that the Central Chamber have communicated their views to the Lord President of the Council, who will, Mr. Gladstone feels sure, see to the ful- filment of the engagements on this subject, into which her Majesty's Government entered in Parliament last session.— I am, dear sir, your faithful servant, E. W. HAMILTON.— To Major Craigie. WEEDS.—I feel something like a personal obligation to Sir J. B. Lewes for the sentence—" It appears to me quite impossible to maintain that weeds exhaust land. On the contrary, they operate as one of the great economics of Nature by filling up every vacant space with vegetation.' It is simply to prejudice the case to call All autumn and winter vegetation on land unoccupied by a set crop, "weeds." The green one sees, then and- there, is the evidence that Nature's own agencies are at work to prevent the resources of the soil from being " unnaturally " wasted. Lord Palmerston's dictum—that dirt is matter in the wrong place—applies mutatis mutandis to plant growth. Weeds are plants in the wrong place. The same species which, developing itself on land, not otherwise engaged, is "green manure," becomes a noxious " weed " when jostling for ex- istence another plant of greater value to the occupier. Wheat, from shed kernels, is a weed when it appears among flax grown for its fibre; and couch grass is not a weed, but a warming pan, when it arrests the vagrant juices of the soil in winter, and keeps them in place until the time comes to make a seed-bed for a more desirable tenant.— Greybeard. POLLUTED WATER FOR FARM Srocx.—The question is one of great interest to agriculturists, but the more it is treated the more perplexing it seems. Mr. Herman Biddell, of Pla.yford, Ipswich, writes :—" Forty years ago I was a regular visitor at ansild relative's, who farmed largely near Bury St. Edmunds. His premises, like most of his neigh- bours at that Unita, had very little of the modern covered- yard system about them. In the midst of his buildings were two small ponds. They were inside the yards; the rotted straw was stamped into the very edge of the water. The drainage of the whole yard filtered through the mass of manure the animals stood on, and the water was literally black—not tinged or treacle coloured, but black as printer's ink, from contamination. I was there at regular periods for nearly a quarter of century, and never once during that time were matters otherwise than as I have described. To my dear old relative disease as we have it among our cattle now was unknown. All the stock en the farm drank at these coepools. Many of his horses lived till they were gray with age; his cattle throve, and his cows gave plenty of milk. Ido not know that the milk was good, but the house was always full of his little nephews and nieces, and I never knew one ill while there." AN IMPROVED SlLo.—The increasing attention which the silo system is exciting makes it interesting to notice the recent advances which have been made towards perfecting the art of the manufacture of ensilage, the chief among these being undoubtedly the beautiful machine invented by M. Albaret, of Rantigny, Liancourt. A considerable im- pediment in the way of any wide dissemination of the silo system hitherto has been the difficulty of constructing underground silos, on account of the humidity of the soil, and in pVerground silos the unaatisfactory nature of any apparatus heretofore contrived for the purpose of filling. The latter difficulty_ has now, however, been to a great ex- tent overcome- by M. Albaret's machine, which was lately put to the test in France by M. Leconteux, one of the lead- ing agriculturists of that country. The machine in ques- tion performs a two-fold duty—first cutting up the fodder, which in this instance was maize, and then by the genera- tion of a strong current of air blowing it through a funnel into the silo to a height of five and a distance horizontally of from 14 to 15 metres; and this latter principle it is which is the chief characteristic of M. Albaret's inven- tion, enabling, as it does, the person filling the silo to dis- tribute the cut fodder as he may wish. The cutting is per- formed by knives fixed upon a large wheel, while the current is produced by a series of palettes attached to its circumfer- ence, the whole revolving within a drum similar to the venti- lator of a winnowing machine. M.lLecontenx's statistics are very instructive, both as showing the amount of work performed and the rola t Iva anzponsuto LA? worispoop/o, ea. rto cps, and fuel. On the occasion referred to, the machine, which is worked by a steam engine of 5-horse power, was left in motion for nine days, averaging six horses per day. During that time it cut 473,600 kilos. of maize and other green fodder, and 5,000 kilos. of straw and dry forage, thus averaging 53,177 kilos. per day, or 8,862 kilos. per hour, and completely filling two silos having a capacity of 296 cubic metres each, or in all 592 cubic metres. Nor was this all, for at times the machine cut and raised 10,000 kilos. per hour. As to the outlay, M. Leconteux paid for workpeople (16 in all, including women and young people) the sum of 241. per day; for the steam engine 20f., being at the rate of 4f. per horsa,power, the total of 441. being the daily ex- penditure for the cutting and elevation of the maize, or an average cost of 23f. 90c. per hectare. To this, however, must be added the expenses of cartage and clearing the field, which amounted to 401. per day, at the rate of 41. for each horse and 3f. per ox. This showed a total cost of 3601., or 36f. per hectare of 47,000 kilos., or 0765 per thousand kilos., while the expense of 16 men employed in loading and unloading the carts came to 32f. per day, being at the rate of 281. 80c. per hectare, the whole quantity being carried by 947 journeys between the field and theqsilo. THE NEW AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS ACT.—The following story is the first, I believe' yet made public, in which a notice to quit has been served on a farmer because he will not contract himself out of the new Agricultural Holdings Act. Twenty-five years ago Mr. X hired of the late Mr. Y about twelve acres of -grass land, about five miles from a market town, at the very respectable rent of £4B" per annum, the tenant paying all rates and taxes. There was no written agreement, the tenant being contented with the landlord's word that he might make the best he could of the land, and that so long as he did well he should not be disturbed. Some years ago Mr. Y flied, and his daughter became the owner of the farm, her brother, Mr. Y, acting for her. Last Michaelmas the tenant was requested by this gentleman to sign himself out of the Agricultural Holdings Act, and to agree not to sell any hay, and on his refusing to do so he , received six months' notice to quit. Now, the tenant. has only sold five tons of hay off the farm in twenty-five years, he has brought seventy tons of good manure on to it within the last five years alone, and the farm is said to be in capi- tal condition. Mr. Y admitted that he had nothing to say as to the management of the farm ; besides, it stands to 1 reason that a tenant who could pay £4 an acre through all the recent bard times must have done wed by the land. Of coarse an agreement to set the Act entirely aside would be illegal ; but a notice to quit is not. Probably, however, Mr. Y has found out by this time that, as there was no written agreement or notice setting aside the Agricultural, Holdings Act of 1875, his tenant was entitled to a year's notice from next April, the time of entry. At any rate the tenant has found this out, and will be able to stay in the farm till April, 1885, in defiance of Mr. Y. He will also be able to claim compensation for any improvements of the third class made during the past ten years. The names and places in connection with this case can be made known if necessary.—Mark Lane Express. THE MILK AND BUITER TRIALS AT THE ISLINGTON DAIRY Snow.—At a recent lecture at the Royal Agricul- tural College, Cirencester, Dr. Voelcker said: It is surpris- ing how rapidly oily matters introduced into f cod will find their way into the milk. I mention this to throw a little' light on the question whether morning or evening milk is the better. It is entirely a question of feeding. If you feed the cows well in the day the evening milk is rich, and if you leave off the feed at night the morning milk is poor. As a rule, therefore, the evening milk is somewhat richer than the morning, but it does not follow that it is invariably the case. I find, for instance, during the twelve months to which I have referred, that out of 32 samples of morning land evening milk, in eight cases the morning milk was purer !than the evening, on four days the morning milk was the richer, while on the remaining four days there was no ap- preciable difference between the quality of the morning and evening milk. From a table before me, I see I have found as much as 4 per cent. of pure butter fat, and I have found as little as 1± per cent. I have found similar difference in experiments which for the last four years I have carried on under my own personal supervision, seeing the cows milked, and so forth, at the Shows of the British Dairy Farming Association at Islington. In 1879 we had in the showyard an Ayrshire cow whose milk produced 5i per cent. of pure butter fat, whilst that of a Dutch cow gave as little as 2± per cent. In the succeeding years we had similar variations, but I cannot help giving you the results of the last year's milk trials, which have just passed through my hands, re- lating to the show held on the 24th October last, and I con- fine my quotations to prize winners. The first prize animal, a large Dutch cow, a very profitable animal to the milk dealers, gave in the morning 311bs. 40z., or about three gal- lons, and in the evening 291bs„total 601bs. 40z., roughly speaking, six gallons of milk in the day. But when we examined the milk I found that the produce of this Dutch cow gave only 2.86 of pure butter fat, total solids 12.12, leaving 88 per cent. of water;—evidently not a rich milk. The second prize cow, a very taking little Devon, gave in the morning 15,11b5., in the evening 111bs., total 26ilbs. of

milk in the day, or about 21- gallons, lesa than half the quantity of the Dutch cow. But the milk of the Devon cow gave 51 per cent. of pure butter fat, and would there- fore make llbs. of salable butter per day, while the six gal- lons of milk of the Dutch cow would only make I.llbs. of butter. There is an enormous difference between quantity and quality. If, then, you want to make and sell butter you will naturally select a cow which gives rich milk; but if you want to sell the milk you will keep Dutch cows. The Channel Islands cattle as a rule produce very much richer milk than the larger breeds. One of the richest samples of milk I ever analysed was that of a Kerry cow, and another equally rich was that of a little Brittany cow. These are very nice little animals, suited for a park, or where there is a limited extent of pasture land, but are not suited for the' milk selling purposes of the milk dealers. A little Jersey cow at the Dairy Show gave 181 be. Soz. of milk per day, which contained 554 per cent, of pure butter fat, 8.71 of solids not fat, or 14/ per cent, of total solids. That is a very rich milk. A little Jersey cow gave 261-lbs. of milk per day, containing 5 per cent, of pure butter fat, 9.07 of solids not fat, and 89 per cent, of water. That is a very good result. Guernsey and Jersey cows are very profitable to keep in towns, where you are limited in pasture, and have to feed your cows on dry food. You can also sell their milk at 2d. per quart more money as "nursery milk." Some enterpris- ing London milk dealers keep a herd of a dozen Alderney cows in nicely fitted up stable, and customers have to pay 21. a quart more for the milk, which is called nursery milk, than under ordinary circumstances. SALICYLIC ACID AND FOOT-AND-MOUrli DISEASE.—The following appears in a contemporary :—Some two years ago I wrote to the press giving the results of the use of salicylic acid to a friend's cows which were affected with foot-and- mouth disease. Until this autumn I have fortunately not had an opportunity of testing in my own stock the merits of salicylic acid as a care for foot-and-mouth disease. The introduction into this neighbourhood of two lots of Irish cattle also brought foot-and-mouth disease, which quickly spread from meadow to meadow, and showed itself on the 3rd inst. among twenty-six of my shorthorn cows and heifers; from these it soon spread to twenty-two other young heifers, bulls, kc., and to about forty-five of my breeding sows and yelte. As the cows were attacked I gave them about half a pound of salts, and twice thoroughly washed out their mouths and bathed their lips and hoofs with a strong solution of salicylic acid. The effect was astonishing, as in several cases cows which had previously refused the meadow hay began to eat as soon as their mouths were dressed. The acid appeared to dry up the vesicles on the feet and lips, and either hasten the formation or harden the new skin where the blisters which formed on the tongue had broken and the skin peeled off, so that, except in two cases where the tongue and lips completely peeled, the cows did not for more than two days refuse their food. The oldest and heaviest milking cows seemed to suffer most. With several of these the disease settled into the udder, the milk almost ceased, or was got from them with great difficulty, when it had more the appearance of pus than of milk; the teats and bag also became covered with little ulcers, which bled each time the cow was milked. I ordered the udders to be dressed with a solution of the acid, but this was not en- tirely successful, as it caused rather a hard scale to form, which peeled off each time (four or five per day) the bag was drawn. I then tried lard. This kept the teats soft, but the sores did not heal as quickly as I wished, so I made a solution of boro-glyceride and water, nine parts of water to one of boro. This very speedily effected a cure; it appeared to take out the soreness, and left the teats soft and pliable. Whether it was due to the use of the salicylic acid, the born-glyceride (which is a germicide), or sanitae, which I freely used, the disease did not extend beyond my neat stock and breeding sows; my growing pigs, boars, and yelts, numbering over two hundred and twenty, of various ages, escaped; a few of the youngest were in styes completely surrounded by stock suffering from foot-and-mouth disease, bat the majority of them were in other piggeries some dis- tance away. Six or eight of the sows were so lame that they refused to walk, but after two days' dressing with the acid and water, they were able to hobble about, and to seek as usual for their food on the meadows. I consider that my stock have come well out of the trial, as I did not lee° a single pig, and only one heifer slipped her calf. Of course, I cannot yet tell the damage sustained amongst the cows, but I am sadly afraid that I shall find that those cows which were in full profit will, when next they calve, have lost one or more quarters. Four of the cows, which were of course dry, have calved during the past week, and all have done well. The calves have scoured very much, but they have not shown any signs of foot-and-mouth disease, which our inspector says has taken its leave, so that my premises were to-day declared free, after being-an infected circle for nearly a month. The proportion of acid used was about four table- spoonfuls to a gallon of hot water.—SANDIRS SPENCER, Elolywell, St. Ives, Nov. 3.

div.head: WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF COMMERCE.
div.p: WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF COMMERCE.

On Monday at noon a •meeting of the Council of the Chamber of -Commerce was held at the Bowsey-ro.id offices. Piesent :—Messrs. C. Broadbent (in the chair), Joseph Har- rison, J. R. Pickmere, W. Long, Jolley, Pierpoint, J. Fair- dough, S. Rigby, Monks, and Joseph Davies. The business was "to consider a report and communication from the Board of Trade as to the proposed appiintrnent of local re- caiver in bankruptcy, and to receive the report of the Presi- dent and Vice-president as to the autumnal meeting at Derby."

THE MEETING AT DERBY. The PRESIDENT said perhaps most of the members pre- sent would have read the formal account that was given of the late proceedings at Derby, but he thought it was due to the Darby Chamber to say that the delegates from other towns were received ia the most cordial, he might almost say magnificent manner. The arrangements were admirable in every respsct, and the delegates were treated with the greatest hospitality. After business a lunch was provided for all the representatives ; on one evening a very , interesting soiree was held in the Art Gallery, where there was a beautiful collection of pictures and a museum which were thrown open to a large numbsr of guests by the Mayor, and the company was most pleas tntly entertained. Then a 17,1-and banquet was held in the Drill Hall, at which, of course, all the representatives of the different Chambers at- tended, and some distinguished guests, among whom was Mr. Kennedy, as representing the Foreign Office. Later on an excursion was arranged to the great breweries of Burton, they were taken over the whole works and tasted some of the
bitter b.3er and some of the finest five-year-old ale. (Laughter.) Other exeursilns were arranged .for varioni interesting
parts of the neighbourhood, the final one, but for which the Warrington delegates cauld not remain, bAng Matlock an
vicinity. All this was carried out and ai-ranxed by the Darby Chamber, hat both he and Mr. Long wore in- much

done, an that it would perhaps have been b4tter if each Chamber paid its own expenses than what was done there. As regarded the business of the meeting, the diseus-
sions were marked by plain good sense, and ere for the most part interesting. On the questions brought forward,

probably the most interesting was "The dev'elopment of the English trade with India." The English mercantile and manufacturing public were very likely more aware than they used to be, but not more than they ought to be, of the immense value of India to the trade of England in all matters, more especially to that of wheat. What was wanted, however, was better internal communication be- tween that great country and England. The telegraphic and telephonic communication with England had been con- trasted unfavourably with that of other countries, where

such modes of communication were much better and cheaper than in their own country. But they had a summary of the whole of the proceedings at the cenference, and could refer to any point which a member would like to hear more about. The wire and metal guage business was withdrawn owing to the issue ef a new standard wire guage by the Board of Trade, a copy of which had been sent to each Chamber. The di,cussion on the Land Laws, which many were looking forward to with great interest, was also withdrawn, as it was thought it would trench too closely on politicel and debateable matters. He should not omit to mention that the Foreign Office were ever ready to. receive any communications from the various Chambers of Com- merce with, at all events, the greete,st politeness and consi- deration. He had had some talk with Mr. Ken- , nedy, who expressed himself most anxious and willing ' ,to do all he could to forward any representations which might be made to the Foreign Office in matters re- lating to trade or commercial treaties with other countries. A new treaty of commerce was about to be introduced be- tween England and Turkey, and the British Consul from Constantinople had expressed himself anxious to hear any representations from Chambers with reference to trade be- tween England and Turkey, and what particular manufac- tures they wished to be iatroduced into Turkey. In answer to Mr. Pickmere, the PRESIDENT added that Mr. C. J. Monks, M.P., !presided very efficiently over the meetings, which were attended by a large number of members of Parliament.

Mr. RIGBY : In what Capacity? The PRESIDENT: They would be ex °Pio members of ' Chambers in thelr various districts. Mr. FA.IRCLOUGII: Is Mr. McMinnies ex-officio? The PRESIDENT: I think he is a real member. Mr. DAVIES: Only ex-officio. Mr. LONG, the vice-president, said he did not think he could add to ,the 'remarks of the President with regard to the meeting. There was of course a good deal ofun- necessary talk about c3rtain subjects, such as the decimal system, which occupied con- elderable . time. On thing tho. President had omitted to allude to, Wai that relatidg to the question of fires in towns. At their last meeting their was an interest- ing discussion on that subject, and the following resolution was proposed by tho Halifax delegates and carried : "That in consequence of the numerous fires that have oc- curred in recent years, involving enormous losses, and con- sequent onerous rates of insurance, this Association hereby records its opinion that it is desireabte that official inquiries should be made iato the Cause and extent of such fires and resolves that a memorial be presented to the President of the Board of trade requesting him to introduce a.Bill, mak- ing it imperative that an ioquiry be held by such official as Parliament may decide upon into the origin of every fire which may be brought under the notice of the police and which may be considered worthy of. investigation, or to which the attention of the authorities in ty be directed by any interested party." Mr. PICKMERE spoke in favour of such an inquiry not for the purpose of detecting incmlierisin or anything of the kind, hut from a p4blic point of view and as regarded the rte m of insurance.
_ Mr. RIGBY thought that the eximination or inquest should be taken up in each neighbourhood by the munici- pal authorities, who would lead and gaide Vim in the matter.
Mr. PICKMERE : It migbt be done by the Coroner for the district. _ _ __ _

Mr. RIGBY thought that a similar association should be formed for the prevention of fires as that having reference to boiler explosions, and means should be taken to secure preventitive modes, not only in the shape of appliances, bat in having ready a'plentiful supply of water immediately The fire at Cockhedge would never have grown to the ex- tent it did if there had been a plentiful water supply in the nehthhourhood. The plan he had proposed would be better than having a Government inspector, because it would be to the interests of the parties concerned. Mr..LowG asked Mr. Rigby how he proposed to bring that about, because he believed there were three boiler in- surance companies in Manchester? Mr. RIGBY said he did not refer to an insurance com- pany, but an associatioa for the persons interested in the use of boilers, and in preventing explosions. That was done mutually and by subscription. It was not insurance, but assuran-e. Mr. JOLLEY expressed his opinion that if the municipal authorities forme 1 a committee to inquire into the cause of fires it would be a much better and cheaper plan than em- ploying a Government Inspector or an insurancecompany. A committee might be easily formed from their own Cor- poration, and they would soon get the thing put right. The CHAIRMAN remarked that they seemed to be discus- sing the question what they should do for themselves and what the Government should do for them, bat he thought _

they were inclined to ask the Governmeet to do that which they could much better do for themselves. (Laughter.) , The suggestion thrown out by Mr. Rigby, and endorsed by Mr. Jolley, was, he considered, a very important one. , (Hear, hear.) The subject then dropped, and a hearty vote of thanks was then accorded the president, vice-president, and Mr. Bleckly for attending the Derby conference and represent- ing Warrington so satisfactorily. THE NATIONAL REFUGE HARBOURS SOCIETY. A memorial, similar to that before the Town Council a short time since and having reference to the want of im- proved harbour accommodation for Great Britain, was signed by the President, on the motion of Mr. RIGBY, seconded by Mr. LONG. THE APPOINTMENT OF LOCAL RECEIVER UNDER THE NEW BANKRUPTCY ACT : INTERESTING DISCUSSION. The following letter was read : Board of Trade. Whitehall Gardens, 1311 s Nov., 1883.—Sir, —I am directed by the Board of Trade to inform you that they propose to appoint Mr. T. J. Ridgway, solicitor, of Warrington. official receiver for the Warrington and Wigan district; and I am to request thet you will move your council to state whsther they are aware of any objection to the appointment. The favour of an answer within the next few days is specially requested.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, B. GIFFEN, the president, Chamber of Commerce, Warrington. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH supposed the district would be between Warringten and Wigan? Mr. DAVIES : Both boroughs. Mr. HARRISON said the area would extend about eight or nine miles around each town. Mr. PICKMERE: Not confined to the boroughs? Mr. HARRisoN: Oh dear, no. The Warrington district, he said, included Reincorn. Haydock, Frodsham, and such places, and Wigan would extend about the same distance, as that district was co-equel with Warrington. Mr. MONKS: It Will be settled by the Board of Trade. Mr. HARRISON: Yes, but the letter means the bankruptcy districts of the two courts. Mr. DAVIES said that as he had displayed some amount of interest in the bankruptcy laws, more particularly connected with that Chamber, he had been asked how it was that this matter was referred to the Chamber of Commerce at all. What he would say that morning would not be so much connected with the interests of the Chamber, but that the public might know what had been done by their Chamber in the matter of the bankruptcy laws. He I must go beck as early as the times when the Chamber was I instittetcd. Mr. Blackly he might call the father of their I Chamber, became he was more imraediately the promoter or founder of it. Of course there were other gentlemen taking an interest in it at the time, but be was their that president, and might be said to be the foremost man. That was in 1878, and one of the main elements passing in Mr. Bleckly's mind when he founded the Warrington Chamber was the vexed question of the then existing laws of bank- ruptcy. He found that at the very earliest point—in 1879 —there was the borough member, Mr. Artingstall, and Mr. Bleckly armed with resolutions of the Associated Chambers of Commerce. In September, 1879, the very reason why those two gentlemen representing the Warrington Chamber went to that conference was for the purpose of amending the laws of bankruptcy. In the month of December of the same year, when the Associated Chambers met at Belfast, Mr. Artingsteell and himself (Mr. Davies) went from that Chain-

Another monster trial is soon to begin in Hungary, the number of prisoners being 111. while 1,409 witnesses are to be called to prove their participation in the recent anti- Jewish riots throughout the west and south-west of the country. A number of iron mills in the vicinity of Pittsburg have closed, owing to the bad state ot the iron tr.dc. Over 8,000 people are thus thrown out of employment. The owners of a large mill atJohnston, Pennsylvania, employing 5,000 hands; have notified their workpeople of a reduction of 10 per cent. in their wages from December let. THE SALVATIONISTS IN CANADA.—The Salvation Arms- is making progress in Canada. A detachment has invade.d Ottawa on the invitation of Sir John Macdonald, who re- cently attended one of their meetings at Kinston. The- captain (Mrs. Abbo) has secured quarters, and hopes to re- form during the seosion many of the representativs of the country.

DARING ROBRERY r a Ilksir.—A daring robbery was committed on Wednesday evening at a banker's office in Stuttgart, by four men, two of whom seized and maltreated the proprietor and -a customer standing at the counter, while the two others completely emptied the cashb3x, and then made their escape in cabs. One of the band 1,a3 been ar- rested in an express train at Pforzheim, and on being taken into custody attempted to commit suicide. A MEXICAN RAILWAY TRAIN ATTACKED BY ROBBERS A gang of robbers on the Mexican National Railway, at the new boundary of New Leon, contrived to throw a passenger train from the track, killing the stoker and wounding the driver. They then attacked the train, and compelled the guard to try to open the express safe, which he was, h ,w- -ever, unable to do. They then robbed the train of $3,000 in bullion, and decamped. The Mexican troops afterwards arrived on the spot, but too late for the protection of the passengers.

ATTEMPT Tfi SHOOT THE FRENCH PREMTER.—A young man armed with a revolver, who was subsequently ascer- tained to be an anarchist, succeeded in entering the Ministry of Public Instruction on Friday, and, on being questioned, declared that he had intended to shoot M. Jules Ferry. He was immediately arrested. The vouth, whose name is Currieu, is an anarchist from Lille. He stole a revolver from his employer (a baker) and ran away to Paris. He can scarcely be classed as dangerous, and probably belongs to the same category as te Pole who recently aecused himself at Dantzic of intending to kill Prince Bismarck. THE SOCDAN : ANNIHILATION OF HICKS PASHA'S ARMY. —The worst fears as to the fate of Hicks Pasha and his army have been realised. The Egyptian Government re- ceived on Thursday full confirmation from Khartoum of the report that the army of the Soudan had been annihilated. The struggle between the forces of the Khedive and the overwhelming hordes in the service of the False Prophet took place between the 3rd and the sth instant. The Egyptian army held their ground for two days, but on the third the square which had been formed was broken by an irresistible onset, and from that moment the battle was lost. So complete was the destruction that it is said only one survivor," an artist," succeeded in making his escape. The Egyptian Govern- ment has resolved to concentrate the remaining forces in Upper Egypt at Khartoum. The English Government has, it is said, advised the Khedive to abandon his claims to sovereignty over the immense region known as the Soudan,' and to seek for and strengthen a defensive frontier. A STILANGSI MURDER TRIAL IN FRANCE.-A remarkable trial for murder has just ended in a verdict of guilty at the assizes held in the department of _ the Dordogne. A young peasant, named Camille Amblard, was betrothed to Lucie Fabre, tie daughter of another peasant in the same village. The father of Lucia Fabre refused for a long time to give his consent to the marriage, as he was anxious to marry his daughter Co one Fourneir, a suitor whowas much richer ' than Canaille Amblard. He was egged on to withhold it by his son-in-law, Amed6e Pinsat, married to Lucie's elder sister, as the latter had been promised an addition to his allowance by Fournier if the marriage took place. Lucie, however, having attained her majority, gave the necessary intimation, as required by French law, to her father that she intended to become the wife of Camille Amblard, and, as he still declined to sanction the match, she went to live with Camille's mother, pending the celebration of their marriage. Her father then relented, and it was mutually arranged that the wedding should be solemnised on the morning of February 11 this year. Upon the previous evening, Camille Amblard, who had gone to see a friend in a neighbouring village, left the latter's house to return home, but he never reached his destination. His mother and his betrothed, who were natu- rally much distressed at his non-appearance, had search made for him, but it was not until two days afterwards that his body was found in a pond, the appearance of the neck and face 'proving that he had been strangled. Two wedding rings were found in his pocket, and the examining magis- trate placed one of these rings upon the finger of the be- trothed as she knelt beside the corpse of her lover. The son-in-law, Am6doe. Pinsat, was arrested, and the charge was clearly brought home to him. The jury, however, gave him the benefit of extenuating circumstances, and he has . escaped with 2t; years' penal servitude.

her with various resolutions pressing on the Govert;rnent to bring in a Government Bill, and he believed they both con- siderably assisted the Associated Chambers at Belfast in arriving at the conclusions that they did. (Hear, hear.) The result was that when the' came back from the meeting. at Belfast it was on their suggestion that that Chamber ?e- -quested their then member, Sir Gilbert Greenall, to support the Government Bill on bankruptcy.. In January, 1880, Mr. Draper retired from the secretaryship, and he believed it was on the request of Mr. Dun and one or two others, who seeiag that their knowledge of bankruptcy proceedings should be assisted as much as possible, urged on his partner, Mr. Voisey, to take the secretaryship, and the latter did from time to time af- ford valuable informltion to the members of the Chamber on the question of bankruptcy'. That had been going on for the last four years, and they had n-) doubt observed that in their annual report of 1880 the subject -of bankruptcy formed the principal portion of the report. In January, 1580, Mr.. Artingstall, as representing their Chamber, again attended to support the bankruptcy resolutions of the As- sociated Chambers, and which eventually became law. (Hear, hear.) In February their secretary wrote to Mr. Whitwell, M.P. for Kendal—late president of the Associated Chambers, a very able man, and their mouthpiece in the House of Commons—framing resolutions which the War- rington Chamber had brought forward in 1879, and consi- dering they could not give better resolutions than they then suggested, Mr. Artingstall and himself attended in London to support those very resolutions promulgated by their own Chamber. On the sth March following the secretary wrote to Mr. Hole, still pressing forward the reso- lutions which Came from that Chamber. In May, 1880, Mr. Dun expressed a great desire to put an amendment to one of the clauses, and this was also pressed forward. In July, a new Government came into power, and it was considered by their Chamber and suggested by others, that the new Government should have some opportunity of obtaining a little information before a noir bill was brought in. In October, Mr. McMinnies supplied the Chamber with certain documents, and on October 6th a memorial was prepared on the suggestion of Mr. Bleckly, for the purpose of assisting the Government to bring in their new Bill on bankruptcy. In 1881, he (Mr. Davfas), being then president, the first item in the report of that year, specially referred to the bankruptcy laws, and in February of that year, Mr. Bleckly attended ik London, and the resolutions they framed, among others, were consolidated and submitted to the President of
the Board of Trade (Mr. Joseph Chamberlain). He was happy to state that the same were approved. In Jane he signed another memorial to the HOUS3

of Commons in support of the Government Bill, and it was presented by Mr. McMinnies on September 7th. It was still becoming a very pressierg question, and Mr. Bleckly, Mr. Artingstell and himself sub- sequently went to Plymouth, anl had an interesting meet- ing on that occasion, and where they still fought well in the interests of the Bankruptcy Bill, promoted by Mr. Chamberlain. in preference to that brought in by the Asso- ciated Chambers of Commerce. They supported that which they thought the best. (Hear, hear.) One clause they voted for, but which he did not see was carried, Was where the estates of intestates could be brought under bankruptcy without the necessity of a Chancery suit, and that kind of work; and he suggested likewise that the estates if lunatic intestates should be wrought out in the same fashion. Mr. Bleckly at the time -spoke very strongly on the Bill brought in by the Government. In January, 1882, he was re-elected president, and in that capacity he attended for three days in London with the view of pushing this matter forward more than any other. On the 29th January, 1883, he drew up a retort and suggested that they should give as much support as they possibly could to the Government Bill. In the month of July they had the satisfaction of recording on their minutes that the progress of the Bankruptcy Bill, which they in their humble and earnest fashion had sup- ported in Warrington, was very satisfactory. The Board of Trade, he thought, could not but think well of the Chamber of Commerce of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Their Cham- ber had been very active indeed, and made themselves well acquainted with matters connected with the Board of Trade, not only in bankruptcy, but in wire guage, foreign tariff., the Liverpool Water Bill, the Manchester Ship Canal, and the Railway Commission. As regarded the Railway Commis- sion, they afforded such information to the Board of Trade as to entitle them to the respect of the Board of Trade. (Hear, hear.) He did not take to himself credit for all this, bat he wished to show that their Chamber deserved well of the Board of Trade. (Hear, hear.) However, he took a little credit to himself for . the pains he had taken in maintaining that Chamber as a Chamber. That had been no little trouble, and it was not much reflection on the manufacturers ef Warrington that they did not support the Chamber ü they ought, because in Manchester and elsewhere it was the same, and there was frequently a diffieulty in keeping the associa- tions together. Coming to the subject of the letter from the Beard of Trade, Mr. Davies remarked that no one could think better of Mr. Ridgway than he did. It had appeared• in the papers that those appointments were confined to solicitors and accountants. He found that was so. There was a clause, the 162 ad he the Bankruptcy Act, which re- quired trustees to account for all monies. That was very' proper, and he. . might state that that clause was pushed forward by themselves. Believing it would be carried, his own firm worked day and night and prepared the whole of the returns and reports required by the Board of Trade before they were• applied to for them. He thought he was right in saying that they were the only firm Of accountants in England that did it. (Hear, hear.) The whole of the money had long since been paid. He brought these facts before the Chamber to show what had been done in the _mattereof the bankruptcy laws, both by the Chamber and his own firm. (Hear, hear.) The Pnearomcr said he thought they had all been very mach interested with what Mr. Davies had stated, and he thought it was due from him and themselves that those facts should be brought before them. They should be known not only by the Chamber—of course, the members were aware of them to a large extent—but also to the public, as showing the important position the Chamber had taken from the first, as Mr. Davies had so well stated, in the late alterations, and, as they believed, improvements in the bankruptcy laws of their country. With reference to the communication from the Board- of Trade, it was not only as -a icompliment that they should be referred to with re- gard to the new receiver under bankruptcy, but it might I happen that a Chamber of Commerce like themselves might be in the possession of some information with regard to the individual proposed, and it might be their duty to call the attention of the Government to something which would show that the person they had selected for the office was unsuitable. In the present instance they knew that Mr. Ridgway was highly respected, and he believed, was a fit and proper person to hold the office, but they would not go so far as to say that there was no other fit and proper person for the position. (Hear, hear.) He had no hesita- tion in seeing that some of Mr. Davies' firm, if called upon, would have performed the duties of the office as well as they were capable of being performed. (Hear, hear.) , Mr. JOLLEY, in the course of his remarks, said that both men—Mr. Ridgway and Mr. John E. Davies—were equally good for the office of Receiver, and seeing that Mr. Davies had been in the field for six months and had excAlent tes- timonials, would it not be in the province of the Chamber to state that Mr. Davies was equally fit for the position? The PRESIDENT drew attention to the words in the letter, "no objection." Mr. liertnisox did not think they would gain anything by the suggestion of Mr. Jolley. He differed with the lat- ter that the two candidates were equal, because on the one hand there was a candidate who had had a very great amount of experience in bankruptcy, whereas the other had had comparatively none. He did not for a moment meati to state that the one with intellectual capacity and attention to business would not in course of time be equal to deal with the bankruptcy laws, but at the commencement they would certainly not be equal. Mr. Momes observed that they could not well travel be- yond those words, "no objection. Mr. JOLLEY : My argument is that there is no objection to the other candidate. Mr. Moline said it might alter Mr. Chamberlain's views if in connection with the appointment he was made aware of the position the office of Messrs. Davies had taken with re- gard to bankruptcy matters. Mr. PICKAIERE did not see what the Chamber could do. The Board of Trade simply asked them if they had any ob- jection to the appointment of Mr. Ridgway. It was a plain question, and if they had an objection they must state it. He felt, however, it was hard on the firm of 'Messrs. Davies, who had taken such trouble in supplying information of very great importance to the Board of Trade, that Mr. John Davies was not selected. They all knew that Mr. John David would have been a gentleman eminently fitted for the office, and personally he regretted that that gentleman had not obtained it. But he did not see what the Chamber could do as regarded any objection to the appointment of Mr. Ridgway. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH observed that he would have been glad to support Mr. Davies in any way, but ho did not see what they could do in face of the letter from the Board of Trade. Mr. HARRISON: I don't think anything we could do would have effect at all. Mr. MONKS thought that whilst stating they had no objec- tion to Mr. Ridgway, the Board of Trade might, if they drew attention to the services rendered by Messrs. Davies's firm, reconsider the appointment. • Mr. LONG had no doubt the letter they had received was a stereotyped one sent to all Chambers of Commerce, and carefully worded to avoid disputes having reference to other candidates. Mr. DAVIRS remarked that from what he had seen of Mr. Joseph' Chamberlain, he knew the latter irrespective of politice would pay the utinost consideration to any repre- sentation that might be made to him regarding a particular appointment. Mr. LONG, in confirmation of this, said that in Mr. Cham- berlain's own town (Birmingham) a Conservative had been. appointed to the office, so desirous was he that the best man should be selected. The PRESIDENT heartily joined in all that had been said concerning Mr. John E. Davies, but he did not think the Chamber would add to its' dignity by re-opening the ques- tion. He should have been glad if the efforts of Messrs. Davies and the piit that Chamber had taken in improving and promoting the new Bill had been recognised in the present appointment, but if they had no objection to Mr. Ridgway, and he did not think they had, they had better reply to the communication to that effect in the most cordial way possible. Mr, DAMES; Bearing ia mind that what Mr. Monks and
others suggest would be of material usa to Mr.JDh Davies.

After some further discussion as to whether the eandida- ture of Mr. Davies should be referred to in any way in thelx answer to the Board of Trade, it was ultimately decided, 012 the motion of Mr. MONKS, seconded by Mr, Picxarlikli, "Twat in reply to the Board of Trade this Chamber has no object;on to the appointment of Mr. Ridgway as official re, ceiver under the new Bankruptcy Act for tha Warrington and Wigan district."

If was subsequently moved by the PRESIDENT, seconded by the VICE-PRESIDE:IT, and resolved unanimously. " That while forwarding the above resolinion the Council wishen to record Its appreciation of the valuable services rendeitd by Mr. John E. Davies during the many discussions that have taken place in this Chamber in promoting the accom- plishment of the Bankruptcy Law as it now stands, and be- lieves him to be well qualified to hold any each appointment as the above." This concluded the business.

It is stated that the Hon. Evelyn Ashley, member for the Isle of Wight, will contest the southern division of Hamp- shire at the next election, in competition with Mr. J. D. Lewis, who formerly represented Devonport. The acceptance of the Stewardship of the Chiltern Hun- dreds by Mr. M. F. Bisset, M.P., will cause a vacancy in the representation of West Somerset. Mr. Bisset has been in a failing state of health for some months. Viscount ICH- oonrsie (L.) and Mr; C. J. Elton (C.) are already in the field as candidates.

A PRESEXT FOR TRH Ranhtunt.—Mr. Gladstone has arranged to reoeine a depntetion of Liberal workingmen of Derby, at Hawarden, the third week in December, when a presentation will be made to the Premier of a costly des- sert service of crown Derby china, specially made and elaborately dealgned, which is now approaching completion, and was subscribed for by the Liberal workingmen of Derby. Tan SPRAICERSHIP.—The Daily Ireles has reason to be- lieve that although the Speaker at his conference with car- tain members of the Cabinet on the 10th inst. consented to hold in suspense his determination of immediately resign- ing, he is still desirous of retiring at the commencement of the coming session. The suggestion that he should con- tinue to occupy the chair until Easter has, we believe, no authority, and does not seem to be recommended by any consideration of expediency. The name of Sir Henry James is mentioned with considerable confidence as the probable successor of Sir Henry Brand. But of course nothing as yet can be considered as decided. The Dublin Freeman's Journal of Monday, after stating that the meeting of the Liberal Club in London, under the presidency of Mr. Forster, had decided the question that a Reform Bill extending household suffrage to the counties will be the first Government measure introduced next ses- sion, says): If the ,Government want the support of the Irish members for the Franchise Bill, Mr. Gladstone must give a distinct public pledge that the Government must stand or fall by the bill as a whole, and that he will not accept a compromise in the House of Lords based on the exclusion of Ireland. If the Government do not give that pledge the duty of the Irish members will be plain. It will be to resist the bill frOm the beginning to the end. The sooner this matter is perfectly understood the more likely it is to be satisfactorily arranged.

• THE UNITED THP,IPERANCE COMMITTEE.—The final meeting for the season of the United Temperance Com- mittee of Earlestown and Newton was held in the Good Temp!ars lodge-room, Bridge-street, on Friday evening last. A goodly number of the members were present, and, after a coffee supper had been partaken of, Mr. J. H. Graham oc- cupied the chair. Mr. J. Owen (secretary) presented the yearly balance sheet, showing a good balance in hand, al- though several works and movements had been carried on during the year. The officers for the ensuing season were afterwards chosen as follows :—Chairman, Mr. J. H. Gra- ham (re-elected); secretary, Mr. R. Higgins; assistant secretary, Mr. 0. Pickett -,and treasurer Mr. W. H. Adams. A HOLIDAY TOUR IN FRANCE AND ITALY.—On Monday evening last, in St. Mary's Catholic Hall, Newton, the Rev. Father Lennon read a paper entitled "Notes of a vacation tour in France and Italy." There was a comparatively large audience, who manifested considerable interest in the subject which had brought them together The Rev. Father Lennon gave an interesting account of a personal trip dur- ing the recent snmmer months, and in the coarse of his paper described the towns and cities through which he had ['lased, including Rome, Milan Venice, and Naples. The principal points of interest and the most beautiful scenery' were effectively shown on a large screen with the aid of lime-light apparatus, the views clearly illustrating the rev. gentleman's remarks. The address throughout was listened to with the greatest attention.
