11ISCELLANEi It is officially announced that the deanery oi Manchester has been accepted by the Dean of Carlisle. A Bath curate, whose father and brother are Church of England clergymen, has given up his position in order to join the Church of Rome. a Her Majesty the Queen, Prince:es Beatrice, Princess Irene of Hesse, and suite left Balmoral Castle on Tuescley after early luncheon for Windsor. THE NEW DEAN or EXETER.—The Lond'on Gazette an- nounces the appointment of Dr. Cowie to the Deanery of Exeter, void by the death of Dr. Archibald Boyd. The death is announced of Sir W. Siemens. A few days ago he accidentally fell in the street, and the injuries he then received appear to have ceased his death. HEAVY GALE IN SCOTLAND.—A severe gala from the west blew over the northern parts of Ecetland on Mondey. There was a heavy fall of snow. In Skye a thunderstorm was experienced, and a church on the Brae of Portree was struck and damaged by lightning. SUICIDE OF A TOWN COUNCILLOR.—Mr. Fredrick Leak, druggist and town councillor, of Walmeate, York, com- mitted suicide on Saturday morning by banging himself from one of the posts of his bedstead. He had occasionally laboured under fits of depression. An extraordinary escape of a child and the drowning of the mother has been reported. EIUM3. Wilcox was walking home from Atherstone to Orton, on Saturday, with her boy, aged seven, in her arms, when she encountered floods. She tried to get through, but was casried away. A man in a trap saw her hands upheld, and farther on found the boy speechless from exhaustion, but quite safe. The boy was taken home, and his mother's body was recovered. The position of the body showed that the mother had held the boy above water till she was lifeless. ExEcurtos AT DunEem.—A young man named Bray was executed on Mn day morning at Darhem_Gaol for the murder, eighteen months ego, of one Thomas Pyle ,who had ' incurred hostility by taking-work at Ushew Moor Colliery, where a strike existed. Bray, who was cue of the strike bands, beet his victim to death whilst ha was helpless from drink, with a hedge rail. Binns was the hangman, and pro- vided against the repetition of such a mishap as attended the last execution in Durham prison by adopting the pre- cautions then recommended by his predecessor. t VIOLENT HARANGUE BY MR. BIaGAR.-Mr. Biggar, M.P., speaking at a meeting in the Oldham Co-operative Hall, on Sunday, said the great body of Orangemen Were either knaves or dupes. He charted the Government with protecting rioters, whilst they prohibited meetings of well- disposed and well-conducted people; and spoke of Earl spencer as having, in his position of Lerd T•ientenent, superintended the packing of juries, and also as having Lad persons hanged who were either notoriously innocent or against whom evidence was not suthcient,on which to hang a dog. Mr. Stanley and_ Mr. Hopwood were described by the member for Cevan as the most obnoxious members in the House of Commons, the junior member for Oldham being a "wretch," who, "though honorable by courtesy, wasdishonourable by character, reputation and conduct." M. DE LESSEPS AT MANCHESTER : TliE SHIP CANAS Quisrmer.—M. de Lessepre arrived in Manchester from Liverpool on Friday night. Oa Saturday morning hd re- ceived addresses from the Corporation and the Chamber of commerce; he was entertained by.the Mayor at a public luncheon; in the afternoon he attended a great meeting in the Free Trade Hall of the subscribers to the Ship Cenral, and in the evening he received an address from the local Trades Council. Onßunday he was in the hands of the French community in the city, who gave him a dinner. The distinguished visitor was everywhere most cordielly re- ceived, and in particular at the Ship Canal ineetkig. He expressed regret that he was not acquainted with the details of our canal scheme, bat promised that, when ho returned to Paris, be wilt ask the opinion of competent engineers its re- gard to it, and let the promoters know the result. MR. lacceernmee., M.P., ON EDUCATION.-.-MY. M.P., presented prizes to the successful students in the local, aiebool of art at Peterborough, on Monday, and delivered an address on education. In the course of his remarks the right hon. gentleman expressed a hope that the time was not distant when the country would ask Parliament to lay down one uniform minimum standard below which no 'child of average intellect should be allowed to leave school. Pnblic opinien was se unripe on the question that he feared it wonld be many years before we could attain even to the fair average of education which was becoming for England as the first nation in the world. • Referring to art edanation, be said the Ration had made marvellons strides since the Exhibition of 1851, and what was wanted was that increased vertatility should he applied to the artisan and re- sources for the employment of the increasing -pepulation must be found in the fertile brains of the ,people. Art schools were giving them new resources, which he believed would be tuned to acconut for the benefit ef the whole country.

Errainsr nornerre.—The following patents amongst others, published in the Commissioners of Patents Journal were sealed during the week ending November 17th, 1883: —George Davies, of 4, t. Ann's Square, Manchester, con- sulting engineer and patent agent, improvements in the con- struction of apparatus employed for concentrating sugar cane juice and other similar purposes (a communication from Messrs. Lazarte and Laree, of Cuba); William Blackett Haigh and John Nuttall, Oldham, improvements in gas en- gines ; Thomas Bradford, improvements in the construc- tion of torso shoes; Joseph Millington, Spring Vale Fotlndry, Wolverhampton, improvements in negro-pots, Dutch stones, camp ovens, the.e John-Siddeley, Liverpool, an improved method of and apparatus forn-stracting paraf- fin and like solid bodies from mineral and other oils; Nicholas Bemetrues Spirtelli, Liverponl, improvements in the construction of propellers for navigable vessels ; Lud- wig Morel, Northwieh, improvements in gas generating fur- naces.—List supplied by Mr. George Davies, CE., Inst., Pot, patent solicitor. 4, St. Ann'setnuare, Manchester. THE RIGHT OF TENAWTS co Exximr Stows: IMPOR- TANT Deatsroto—At the Stonehouse County Court, the other day, Robert Trnte, Stum t-terrace, Stoke, stied Mr. James Taylor, builder, Pattery-street, to recover £lO for trespass committed by defendant or his workmen by fixing advertisements. of Colman's mustard against the front of a shop 8, Battery-street, Stonehouse, of which plaintiff is the owner. The tenant of the-shop in question is a grocer; and Mr. Taylor, as the agent of Messrs. Gelman, fastened the signs to 'the walls with iron.clamps. This was done, accord- ing to thooolaintiff's statement, without his consent.—Mr. Giles, barrister, urged that an action for teespass could only be brought by t e tenant, and not by the landlord of the property.—His Honour said the action-was not on the prin- . ciple of an action for treepaes at all, because there was no possession, but simply an insignificant damage done to the premises.--41r. Staubury, who represented Mr. Trute, said he thought damage had been-done to the property, and that on those grounds the landlord had a eight to sue—His Honour: Ent the tenant had a right to enhibit notices on the house. -Supposing be had suspended these boards out of the window, he would have been perfectly justified in doing so. There will be a verdict for thee.lefeedant. EXTRAERDIZARY STORY OF ROBBERY WITH VIOLENCE —The Criminal Investigation Department have been enga- ged in investigating an extraordinary case of robbery with violence. It seems that on Thersda.y maiming in last week a man was found lying in the road at Breshourne, Herts, helpless and bleeding. He was removed to Tottenham Train- ing Hospital; where bitinjuries were attended to, and from a statement afterwards made by him, the police authorities were communicated with. He cud hie name was Joseph Meier, that he was a porter at the Midland Grand Hotel, St. Pancras, and that on Wednesday evening he was pro- ceeding to a house: in Argyll-square, Enston-toad, when he was set upon by sere men. A sack eras ahrown over his head, his hands and feet were boned, and he was carried into a house in Liverpool-street, King's. Cross. 'There he was robbed of a gold catch and chain, and amine ef about £B5. He was detained irothe house all night, and on the following morning was placed in a cart and driven to Broxbourne, where he was thrown into the road, receiving rather severe :injuries through thetfo.ll. He was detained at the hospital until Friday manning, when he was reasoned to his home. ea is stated that Meier bad recently W. 341 erable sums oof money in connection with horse racing, and it istonjec- -tured that his assailants, becoming aware of this fact, and of his having the money aout him, laid their plans for his rabery accordingly. 'From later inquiriesit would seem as if Meier's original etaterneat is net confirseed. There is no doubt he was found lyinn,iu the road at Ilsddesdon with sets nose bleeding, but it has teen ascertained tttat he could not havo been thrown fro= the trap which was seen -near, and that -he had previouelor been drinking. Mr. Thomas Clement Cub&ld, C. 8., Conservative member for Ipswich, died on -Wednesday night. - The Horne Secretary has reprieved the unbappy woman who murdered her infant at Stalybridge. A LONG SNOOZE.—Mrs. MUunes, after sleeping for five months,awoke on Thursday morning in Glasgow Western Infirmary. Mr. James Anthony Froude, has consented to accept the presidency of the Social and Political Education League for the ensuing year. \VIFE DIMMER. IN lIIELAND.—A woman named Power was murdered on Thursday morning at Carrick-on-Suir by her husband stabbing her in several places. It was officially announced on Thursday that the Duke of Edinburgh- has been appointed to the command of the Channel Squadron, and that his Royal Highness has acclpted the command.

Oa Ttfeaday a builder and contractor, named Simpson. obtained L 2,00-0 damages against the North London Railway Company as compensation for injuries received in a collision between Shoreditch and Finchley a year ago. There was great excitement in Preston on Tuesday night, owing teethe suppression by the borough magistrates of an Anti-Popery meeting to be addressed by Edith O'Gorman, described as the Escaped Nun." A strong police force preserved order. " DESTRUCTIVE FlRE.—Damage to the amount of £20,000 was done on Tuesday by a lire which occurred at the ware- house of M6sSil. J. aud Walker, linseed merchants, Not- tinghem. The premises, which were completely destroyed, were fully insured. DEATH OF A WELL-BNOWN TURFITE —Count Frederick 43 Lagrange, well known on the tea ,as the breeder aud owner of race horses, die of gout on 'Thursday, at his resi- dence in Rue da Cirque, Paris. The Count had been an invalid for months past. THE NEWSPAPER LIBELS.—On Wednesday the Reeorder of .London refused the applic ttion of the "Central News" to add another count to the indictment against the Sportsman newspaper for libel. In the course of the day the Grand Jury Ignored the bill against the Sportsman but returned a "true bill" 'against Judy. STABBING HIS FATHER.—:A young man named Frederic Eli Hilton, boatmaker, was charged it Bolton on Thursday with stabbing his father. The two worked together, and the son, giviffg way to drinking, was remonstrated with by his father. The son packed up his foels with the intention of leaVing his employment: The father was again about to speakita.bim, when -he wae stabbed in the side by his son. The prisoner was committed to the sessions. ST. ANDREWS UNIVERSITY ELECTION.—The election of a Rector for the University. of St, Andrews, Edinburghetook place on Thursday forenoon, the two candidates being Mr. J. Russell Lowell, the American Minister, .and Mr. Edward Gitsson, M.P. for -Dublin University. The usual noisy demonstrations took place during the voting, and the keenest interest prevailed. At half-past eleven the result was an- nounced as follows:—Lowell, 100; Gibson, 82; majority for Mr. Lowell, S. DESTRUCTIVE. THUNDERSTORM U SEE.—On Wednes- day forenoon another severe storm of thunder and lightning passed over the islaiid of Skye. A house situated beside the Talisker Distillery was totally demolished by lightning, and one of the occupants, a woman, icas disabled in the arm and side ter the fluid. The damage done to the church at Braes ie estimated at £lOO. Since Sunday the storm has raged continuously, with heavy showers of hail and sleet.

MTWEIL BY A MOTHER.—MTs. Morgan, wife of Dr. Wm. Morgan, public analyst, Swansea, on Wednesday murdered her yhuneest child Alice, aged two years. She sent the seta vant out to make some purchase, and on the return of the servant came downstairs craving, saying she had drowned tittle Alice, and wanted to go at once to the magistrate, the 'child was found upstairs with its head in a bucket of water 'quite dead. The mother, who is supposed to- Ise insane, is kept under close restraint at her house. DISASTROUS, COLLISION AT SEA.: LOSS OF 88 LIVES.— Lloyd's agent at Fayal -states that on the Bth inst. the American ship Thomas Dana, from Liverpool to New F.crk, landed there 21. men, being the boatswain and part of the crew and passengers of the Rocaberg, a French brig, bound from St. Pierre Miquelon for St. Maio, which was suth by collision at five a.m. en October 30. The Rocaberg•foun- dered immediately after the collision. The remainder of the crew and passengers, numbering eighty-eight men perished. Lord Salisbury was the principal speaker on Thursday evening at a bangusa held in connection with the City Carl- ton Club, Landon. Alluding to the result of the 'fork elec- tion, his Lordship spoke, gi it as indicating what he hoped would be the path of safer,' through dangers of cacsiderable magnitude. He -dwelt on what he regarded as the danger attending political alliance with the Irish party, remarking that many Liberals were ready to sell anything, even the integrity of their country, to gain an election. Eeferring to the military catastrophe in the Soudan, Lord Salisbury said that while reluctant to go into the political considerations which it suggested, he could not avoid. conneeting it with the suggestions which had been made that the time had come for the evacuation of Egypt and for trusting British interests and British influence in Egypt to the native force. All such ideas, he imagined, would have disappeared by to- day. THE LITE/WOOL CANAL BANK THAHEDy.—The trial of Lewis Parry, a labourer, on the charge of murdering the girl Hutton. in Liverpool, on the night a the 13th October, was resumed at the Liverpool Assizes on Wednesday morn- ing. The defence was an alibi. The principal witnesses called to support it were the father and mother of the pri- soner; and at the close of the defence several detective officers were saaamined to show that on the morning of the Nth October, shortly after the arrest of Parry, his parents made statements contradictory of their present testimony, and that their account of his whereabouts was consistent with the theory of the prosecutin that it was he who com- mitted the murder. In summing up, Mr. Justice Delmar said the crucial point in the case was whether the prisoner was the man who crossed the flat in thescanal, and was found fast on the-spikes of the gates of the coal yard. The jury, after two hours' deliberation, returned a verdict of guilty, and the prisoner was sentenced to death. Dasvunerre7E Fans AT A WESLEYAN' CHAPEL.—At er.= o'clock on Wednesday evening a fire broke out in the Wes- leyan (hapel, Chorlton-cum-Hardv, a suburb of Manchester, and before it could he extinguished a considerable portion of the building was seriously damaged. The chapel, which is in the Radnor-street (Manchester) circuit, was a large one, and, cornaaratively speaking, new, having been built only a few years. The fire, which is believed to haste had its origin in a defect in the heating apparatus, appeared at the rezr of the building, near the organ and the pulpit. The Manchester.fre brigade was summoned, and took with them a steam: fire engine, but, although they made every effort, some four hours elapsed before the fire was subaued. By that time the organ was destroyed and about one-third of the chapel extensively damaged by fire and water. A large school which adjoined the chapel escaped without injury. The chapel La insured for ;£5,000 and the organ for £5OO. The building had been occupied during the day, and the heating apparatus had been in use. FLIGHT 07,A. BANE SECHETArty: HEAVY DEFALCATIONS. —The following circular has been addressed by Mr. R. I). Peebles, the managing director of the London and San Francisco Dank, to the shareholders, announcing that the secretary of the bank, Mr. Jtmes Davies, has absconded "Sir,—The directors regret to have to inform you that Mr. James Davies, who has been secretary to this bank for many years, has absconded, and it appears from the investi- gation which has been made that he has defrauded the bank of money and'securities to the value of about £50,000. The matter is. cf course, receiving tbe most earnest attention of the board, and a further communication will be addressed to you when the examination now in progress has been com- pleted." A award of £2OO has been offered by the bank for the arrest of the defaulter. This unpleasant intelligence (says a Leaden correspondent) was not known during busi- ness hours, and must tend to revive an uneasy feeling in the city. The paid-up capital of the bank amounts to £420,000 out a a norainal <capital of £.1,000,000, in £7 shares; an.' the reserve fund stood last year at £80,750.

A PIJBLIC-HOLW2 SACKED 4,7 THIEVES.—At the Bir- mingham Police Ceurt, on Thureday, two men, namekl Jones and Roger, were charged with tacking a public-house in Angelina-street, tbe property of Messrs. Bates, the well- known local rewers. The priseners broke into the house, and, telling the neighbours they bad been sent by the land- lord to take the s,xtneas, they were allowed to be there a fortnight unmolested. During this time they took away everything that was moveable, even to the doors, chimney piece. the flooring, gas pipes, and every bit of iron there was in the place. At le.st the police got wind of the affair, and forced an entrance whilst the prisoners were is the house. They inineediately made their escape through the skylight, and as one of the policemen e-eas following they dashed the skylight on •his head. Sub:equently, after an eseiting chase on the roe, Jones fell off the three-litoryed building, and, though seriously injured, he crawled into a •breerhonse and drew himr,eif into the chimney. The other man.bid in the raftere, andevas only indieeed to surrender by the police threatening to throw bricks nt him. , It is , stated that it will cott .fl'so to repair the ,premises. The ' ,prisoners were committed fotetrial. Yonie ELLCTIO/C—The ,polling for the ekes-ion of a Par- liamentary representative of the city of Y.:l.k, rendered necessary by the death of MT. J. J. Leeman, M.P., took place on Thursday. The candidates ware Sir F. Milner (C) And Mr. F. tacker-it:ld, Q.C. (L). There were 113 voters on the register, but as will be esen from the Egures below only 7,875 burgesses recorded an elanion on the isenes sub- mitted to them. Mr.. T. F. Weed, sheriff and ree:erning officer, bed divided the city into 1-3 polling districts, with 213 stations. Dut-Leg the day there was little publit deseon- stration. At four o'clock, ‘vhen the poll closed, the LCIC9S were taken to the Mansion &use 'thee a large staff of enu- merators were in reediness. Shortly before eix o'clock an immense crowd assetelled in front of the Mansion House, •from the steps of which the declaration was to be made. The 'wildest excitement pree-ailed, as it was nearly eight before: the numbers were declared by the Sherriff. As the numbers .ran so exceedingly closeetke ballot vapersfeed lee be recounted, and it unfortunately turneidut that about one hundred vot- ing papers were informal, as they had been etemped on the ,ceunterfoil instead of on the portion banded to the voter. This was an error on the part of the presiding ofßcer. A considerable time was occupied in discussing this point by the candidates and their agents, and at length the matter YCZ3 arranged. EMIGRATION AMONG TICE Ittort.—An argument in sup- port of emigration as a means of relieving Irish distress would appear to be furnished by a scene witness.id at Tip- perary, on, Tuesday. ",4 number of unemployed, Ctnecily clad, and eniaciaieci-looking'h.;l,ourers" attended at a meeting of the Board of Guardians to ask to. „riploY; mentor out-door. relief. Toe Chairman said the Boar,. could give nei her, and in answer to the pretest of the spokesman of the deputation that they "could not live without food," the -Clerk said that the Government auditor had threatened a surcharge in case the Guardians spent i money on the relief works in the way they did last winter. 1 To this the labourer without labour rejoined, "I wish to mercy you'd send us out of the country entirely, and not be in a state of starvation here, without employment, and without food for ourselves and our families. Sure we can't , stand it. What are we to do ? The Chairman could only offer the men admission into the workhouse. He added— what suggests the existence of some apathy in taking ad- vantage of beneficial legislation—that the Gtiardians had expected that the erection of laboarers' cottages would by this time have found ethployment for them, but he feared that a commencement could not be nude forleur months. • THE FENIAN MURDER TRIAL IN DUBLIN : EXTRAOR- DINARY SPEECIL—The trial of Joseph Poole for the murder of John Kenny, in Seville-place, was resumed on Tuesday in Dublin Commission Court. Lamle, the approver, repeated his former evidence respecting the division in the Fenian party, and said; he belieVed at the time of the murder Kenny was an informer. ,At their meeting the removal of Detec- tive Mallon and Judge Lawson was decided on. Francis lieoghatran heard Poole say on the night of the murder that Kenny would tell no more. Dr. Webb, for the defence, urged the insufficiency of the evidence against the accused. The Attorney-General replied for the Crown, urging that the evidence was totally inconsistent with the innocence of the Prisoner, who undoubtedly was present at the niurder. The judge summed up and reviewed the facts. The jury retired at twenty minutes to six, and returned at seventeen minutes" past with a verdict of guilty Poole, when asked if he had anything to say why sentence (if death should not be passed, spoke at considerable length in earnest and excited tones. He emphatically denied hav- ing murdered Kenny, but admitted being a member of the Irish Republican Brotherhoo4 saying he wont!' be proud to go to the scaffold for being a member of that organisation. Their object, he said, was not to murder, bet to free Ireland from the tyrannical rule of England, and be expressed his belief that it was on account of his being an enemy of the Government under which he bad the misfortune to live, that he had been prosecuted. He acknowledged being with Kennyon the night of the murder, but had no hand in strik- ing him down. He had been a menber of the Irish Re- p-übikan Brotherhood since he was 143, but he had never be. longed to the Vigilance. His object was to wait until such time as his countrymen were prepared to strike a blow for independence, when he intended taking part with them. - He concluded by saying :—" I am not afraid to die. Farewell to all. Farewell to Ireland. Three cheers for the Irish re- public, and hell with English tyranny."—The prisoner was sentenced to death. ,

INTERFERENCE BETWEEN MAN AND WIFE
"111;-. EIGHT OF PRIVATE JUDGMENT."

earliest days of the Church, immediately effect Pentecost, the apostles themselves bad h. ass rt and contend for it. Wiem the rulets of Jeruselein laid hands on Peter and John, and forbade their preaching any more the gospel of their Master, so endeavoerin.g by the force of civil authority to interfere with their duty to their Lord,—the apostles had no hes;tancy as to their answer,—no uncertainty as to the conduct they should I adopt. If it had been some matter of purely civil and worldly kind, concerning which the rulers laid their injunc- tions upon the apostles, obedience would aieve b--en full and prompt. But when they sought to coerce the apostles upon nutters of religious faith and practice, then the reply wee inevitable from men loyal to consc;ence and Christ,— " Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto von more than unto God, judge ye." " We onght to obey God rather than men." And from that time onward, wherever religious faith has been attempted to be in any way coerced, whether by the force or threat of human ' authority and power,—and men have resisted the authority rather than sacrifice conscience,—there the conflict for this sacred right has been witnessed. The " noble army of martyrs" has been enrolled from loyalty to this principle. Ile "rights of conscience" and "loyalty to Christ" have been the mottoes on their blood-stained .banners. The martyr ecenes in the coliseum at Rome On the dungeons of the Reruish yilaidon ; the tires ort our own Bmitirfield rue massacres in the villages of Switzerland and Italy ; in Madagascar 40 years ago: and all over the world, have been essentially cursed by fidelity to this principle. Conscience' before everything ! No human power can rightly coerce it. Nor can it be rightly .conquered by any human power. It is wrong to attempt the coercion; it is equally wrong to allow it to succeed ! " My conscience binds me,"—that is a man's only lawful word unit' a matter of faith hefore God. And when a man feels that and acts that, be is stand- ing upon his most sacred and inalienable right, and is assert- ing, in sublimest fashion, his manhood in the sieht of God. It will be one worthy result of our present study of Luther, and of the noble army which has fought for conscience throughout the world, if conscience should with ua hence- , forth be ever held supreme. What a grand motto for a man's life, "My conscience binds me !" Conscience, says one, is God's vice-gerent in the soul. The saving is true, it it be a conscience enlightened and regulated by the Word of God. There is such a thing as an evil eonscience, an ig- norant conscience, a prejudiced conscience, a warped and injured conscience. But the conscience that has been il- luminated by the divine Spirit,—taught by the Word of the living (10,a-that is man's truest dignity, and obedience to its behest's, a man's truest life. Place ypurself, my friend, under the influence of God's Spirit, bathe, your spirit in the light of Scripture and of truth wherever you find it, and then let nothing prevail against your conscience. To all corners, who would cajole you by temptation, or coerce you by semblance of authority, or threat of what may befal you if you do not yield, have this one answer, "My con- science binds me." That bondage will ever keep you free. I trust in what has thus 'far been said, it has been made sufficiently clear what is meant by the Protestant principle of the "Right of Private Judgment." It is the right that is tersely stated in 'this text: The right of proving all things. "It is the right in matters spiritual for each man to take them to the test of the law and the • testimony," and to conclude that if they "speak not ace: cording to the word, it is because there is no light in them." It is the right of "trying the spirits" that clamour for our attention and our faith, in order to see" whether they be of God." It is the right of every man to do as did the Bereans of old, to " search the scriptures daily, whether these things are so." It is the right of obeying Christ's word, Who bids us "beware of false prophets " and "false Christs," which He said would surely arise and clamour for our obedience. It is the carrying out of that power which Paul declared to be the possession of the Christian, "be that is spiritual judgeth all things." But now, having thus endeavoured to state and explain this right, it becomes necessary to define the limits within which this "right of private judgment" exists. I think that what has already occupied us must have suggestel, at least to some, the truth upon this point. We have been reminded that the right of private judgment was asserted as a principle of Protestantism by the Lutheran Reformers, and that, as laid down by them, it meant the right of the individual independently of all outside author- ity to form a judgment upon matters of belief according to the teaching of the Bible. It was a declaration of personal liberty to read and judge the scriptures, in opposition to, and revolt from, the tyrannical authority of the Papal Church. Well, there you have the limits of this right. It is necessary to state these limits, because we find a readiness in some quarters to run away with this principle; and to make it the foundation of a perfectly lawless licence in matters of religion and conscience. For example: How popular it is in these days to say "a man has perfect right to think just as ale pleases aboet religion."• We hear that claim very often etude, especially by young men who do not always weigh words with accuracy or precision. Indeed it has becomequite the proper thing to say, in some circle!. It savours of advanced thought, of being abreast of the age, of having escaped from leading strings, of having shaken off theedusty creeds of the past, and of having taken up with the new philosophy and the latest science of the day New, it is worth while enquiring how far this popular idea is sen- sible; how far indeed it is founded upon truth. "A man has perfect right to think just as he likes about religion." Let me say, that if this perfect "freedom to think as he likes," simply meant civil freedom, social freedom, we should not need to criticise the statement. Happily in these days that freedom is arrived at, or, at any, rate, very nearly so. Thera are instances in which it is yet denied, or at least hampered with restrictions, respecting which I have a word to say presently. But at least a man exposes himself to no legal pains and penalties, to no fine or imprisonment, simply for what he may think and believe, even though his thought and his belief should be very foolish and erroneous indeed. The days of martyrdom (physical at least), for an idea are gone by. But when men talk about having right to think as they like about religion, it is not the civil right that they mean. They mean the moral right. They con- strue the ‘Right of Private Judgment" to imply and convey freedom to doubt, freedom to deny, freedom to discard re- ligion altogether. Now, all such lawless freedom as that, I believe to be as sinful as it is lawless. And so lam prepared to deny the "Right of Private Judgment" implies any such freedom whatsoever. "A man has perfect right to think just as he likes about religion." To that statement I reply, to begin with, that a man has not a perfect right to think as he may choose to like about anything. A inan's thoughts about a thing must be guided or governed by the facts about a thing. Those facts limit the freedom of his thought. You would not consider a man wise or clever, if he should deliberately refuse to think according to the facts. A scientific man, who should ignore facia, would be a sorry sham. A professor of law, who should argue and theorise about law, in perfect ignorance or oblivion of the statute book, would be something like a lunatic. A man can only I reasonably tkink as the facts of the matter allow him. And , hence it is vain to say that a man can thidk just as he likes ' about anything. The curious and striking point is this, however, that no one ever talks in this way in relation fo anything else except religion! Religion is the only subject in the whole domain of thought about which some men claim unlimited liberty to think, or not think, as they like! And they seem to fancy that the Protestant principle of the right of private judgment cenfers upon them this absurd and lawless license ! Very ably does Dr. Dale, in a little book upon "The Ultimate Principle et Protestantism," ad- dress such men, "Exercise your right of private judgment in matters of religion, and I will honour you from my heart whatever may be the conclusions at which you may arrive; but if on those great and awful questions involved in the relation of God to the universe, and the duty and destiny of man, you exercise, not yanr private judgment, but your private fancy, you are guilty of the most frivolous trifling, where trifling is not only a folly but a crime." My friends, it cannot but be too plainly stated that this great principle ofeProtestantism does not contemplate any shelter or suc- c3ur or justification of scepticism. Its great design is, not to enable men to doubt, het the better to enable them to be- lieve. It was asserted and contended for in the interests of a pure faith, to enable every man to come near and better know his God ; to break down the barriers raised by a cor- rupt and tyrannical church, and to leave the way of access to God free and open to every individual. Therefore, men make a strange use of this Protestant principle, if they use it to bolster them up in sceptical and cynical indifference about religion. There can be no question that a large and increasing number of men are doing this. Numbers of young men lay hold of the difficulties of religion, and without taking any great pains to grapple with them, they practically ignore religion because of its theoretical dAculties. Then they defend their conduct by pleading the fundamental right of a men to freedom of thought. At the same time they wou'd ridi- cule a men acting in this way about anything else. They would say that it is a man's duty to grapple with difficulty, to make himself master of his science, or his art, or his pro- fession, and that if he would do so he would probably find his difficulties and uncertainties largely disappear. Yet in this highest and most solemn of all matters they claim freedom to discard what they do not take the trouble to in- vestigate, a right to doubt what they do not care even to try to disprove. I am here to express my fear that there is in these days, among young men of some modicum of intelligence, a great deal of very solemn trifling. If half the effort expended in picking holes in religion and in Scripture were devoted to investigation of their truth and of the validity of their claims upon faith and obedience, believe we should meet with far fewer sceptics, and far fewer of that latest school which calls itself " Agnostic." Of course, there are accasionally to be met with men who are honestly and seriously perplexed upon matters of reli- gion. But such persons as these are saddened by their doubt. It is a trouble to them; a continual anxiety. Their cry day after day is "More light, more light !" They feel that the matter is of unspeakable moment, that nothing can be compared to it, and that it preases for some satisfac- tory and tranquilizing conclusion. But your fashionable agnostic states his difficulties with ill-concealed gratifica- tion; in style which betrays his belief in the keenness of his critical faculty, and which , shows how proud he is to rise superior to those who are yet held in the delusion and bondage of , religieus faith. All such "agnosticism" is unworthy trifling with the profoundest themes. Such men should un- derstand that no Protestant right of private judgment, nor any right of that nature whatsoever can justify them an conduct so unintelligent and untrue. In the language once more of Dr. Dale, in the book already quoted—" The Refor- mers never intended to maintain the right to doubt. To doubt is to be ignorant, and ignorance is to be deplored as e. calamity, not (defended as a right * * * We have no right to remain ignorant of duties which we might discever by a strenuous and laborious effort to discover them, and therefore we have no right to remain in doubt about great facts by which our duty is determined, when it is possible

to discover whether the facts are sustained by adequate evi- dence. The right of private judgment is not the right to form no judgment at all on matters of transcendent practical impertance. If it were it would be an apology for intel- lectual indolence, and for moral cowardice." Let us nn- derstand,—the right of private judgment is 'limited to tbe definition already assigned; it asserts the right of each man to believe and act for himself in matters of religion agree- ably to the teachings of the Word of God, and it defends him in all such matters from any intervention whether of a church or of the civil power. We must now say a word or ,two upon the religious toleration, which is the logical outcome of this principle. Putting this point shortly,—we most yield what we claim. We claim the right as Protes- tants to take the Word of God, read it for ourselves, and in dependence upon the teaching of the Holy Ghost, form our own judgment about IL 'Enlarging somewhat, bat quite naturally, upon 'this principle, we claim a right to worship God in that special way which commends itself to our judgment as most right and fitting. We gather our creed, we arrange our ritual as appears to us most true, most bean-, tiful, and most consistent with scripture: Now, what we thus do ourselves we must, in loyalty to our own principle, allow others to-do also. We must not hinder others in their I exercise of this right. Neither may we denounca them for exercisicg it, ;',,g.ot may we persecute them ler doing so. We have no right whatever for any such course. We sin against the essence of oar own principle, foi instance, when we inflict any social or political disability upon a man on account of his opinions.. So long as those opinions are not injurious to social and civil order, we, who claim the right of private judgment, can have no justification for socially or politi- cally persecuting—well, let it be frankly said, Mr. Brad- laugh, or anybody else. Ido not hesitate to say that his ' political martyrdom has been a violation of Protestant prin eiple, and is to be deeply deplored in consequence. We equally violate our principle when we call a man a heretic, jut because he does not agree with us. As Dr. Parker well asked last Sunday at the City Temple, " .11 Protestants will not allow a woman who is a Roman Catholic to hold a situation ,in their houses; if Churchmen sneer at Dissenters; if, Dis- senters expel one another because of differences founded upOn honest grammatical interpretation of scripture, where the right of private judgment? There is an infallibility of Protestantism as well as of Popery." The fact of the ra ltter is this—the right of private judgment gathers us all, Nvhattver our church or creed, around the Book of God; it bids us honestly and in devoiat spirit, "read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest it," and then. each . one believe .and each one act as we may understand , it to teach. Meanwhile, we are to exerciseslarge and genial charity. We are to remem- her that the Truth of God is larger than the most accu- rate and ,comprehensive creed. It is greater than all the many creeds ef Christendom put together. All theologies all confessions, all articles of religion, all creeds came out o, the Bible; and yet they have neither absorbed nor approxi- mated the 'solids of its truth. This wondrous Book, at which some carp and *evil, and some despise and reject, is alike unfathomable aed infinite. It is the transcript of the Diiine mind ; the outcome of the infieite heart. And our individual aim should be cherishing as large and cordial a -unity with our fellow-men as is possible, to arrive with them at its meaning, and to enter with then) on a sacred rivalry to embody and display its spirit. This leads me to my last word. It is this. Every right which men possess implies a corresponding duty. We have been speaking of the right of privaie judgment. ' That right is Valueless to us, unless we properly exercise it. So I say to everyone here to-night, that his duty is to use this sacred right which 'belongs to hire. Your duty is to come to God, as lie has revealed Himself in Christ, for yourself. It is your 'duty to pursue a persolfal and devout study of theeßible.. It is your duty to arrive at an intelligent faith, , founded upon honest con- viction of thetruth. . It is your duty to live from day to day as Christ teaches in His Word. These are the duties attaching to your right. Discharge them, and ditty will transfigure into privilege. Neglect them, sod duty will avenge its violation by-inevitable penalty. Most earnestly would I seek to call yciu to this sacred duty: " This is the duty of life: "Fear Clod, and keep His Commandments, for this is the whole duty of man."

div.head: ROBBERY Al WARRINGTON.-THE "CAT."
div.p: ROBBERY Al WARRINGTON.-THE "CAT."

John Hines, aged 23, labourer, and Thomas M‘Hugh, aged -3C, hodcarrier, were charged with having, at Warring- ton, on the 29th of last month, stolen with violence from the person of Frances Farrell a purse containing 4s. .d. and two pawntickets.—On the evening in question, about nine o'clock, theprosecutrix met a militiaman, named Col- lins, who, having received his bounty that lay, gave her ss. They had a drink together, and were subsequently walking along Sankey-street, when they were met by the prisoners, one of wtom demanded from the woman her purse, which they had seen her put into her pocket. She refused, and Collins told them that he had given her all the money she had. Hines thereupon struck Collins, and a fight ensued. Collins was knocked down and rendered insensible, and the prisoners then robbed the woman, and, after abusing her, threw her into a pool of water, from which she was taken by some persona who came up. Information was given to the police, and the prisoners, who had made on, were sub- sequently apprehended. The jury found them guilty, and previous convictions were proved against each of them.— His Lordship said it was one of the most cruel, brutal, and savage robb,ries he had ever heard of, and he was going to give both of the prisoners a punishment to which he rarely resorted. This was one of those cases in which the Legis- ture had given the judges power to add corporal punish- ment to the sentence. Algiugh was the older man, and he had been often convicted, and the sentence of the court upon him was that lie be kept in penal servitude far seven years, and that within a week from that date, and again within six weeks, he receive on each occasion 25 lashes with the cat-o'-nine-tails. WHugh pleaded for mercy and for another chance, but his lordship ordered the warders to remove him below. Then, addressing Hines, his lordship cad he had not been so frequently convicted, and he was also younger, but he was a bad fellow, and the sentence upon him was that he be kept in penal servitude for five years, and that at the end of one month he receive 30 lashes with the ."cat."

Emmanuel Hennessey, 17 years of age; Thomas Garrity, 16 years of age; and Jane Flynn, 18 years of age, were charge 4 with having, at Warrington, on the 12th November, stolen 12s 9i, with violence, from the person of Michael Garrity. The prosecutor took lodgings at the house where the prisoners lived, and on the night in question they all went out together, and were drinking in a public-house in the neighbourhood. After leaving the public-house, Flynn took the mnney from the prosecutor's pocket, and the other prisoners knocked him down and kicked him.—Sentenced the first and last-named to twelve months' imprisonment each, and Garrity to fifteen months' imprisonment.

All the witnesses seemed to be or the opinion that Whatever may be the merits or derwrits of the Davy lamps in otter respects, it cannot be safely use() in mines wherein the air current is so strong as it is in tie Ma'am collieriee, After about ten minutes' deliberation the Jury round that the explosion was caused by a sudden outburst of gas, but that there was not sudicient evldtriee to show Low the ges was ignited.

div.head: SEWION BY THE REV. JOHN YONGE, OF WAR-
div.p: SEWION BY THE REV. JOHN YONGE, OF WAR-
RINGTON.

I On Sunday evening the Rev. John Yonge, pastor of the Wyctiffe Congregational Church. preached to a large con- gregation on ‘• The right of private jadgment." The rev. gentlemais took for his text let Thessaloniane, v. 21, " Preve all things, hold fast that which is poi." The preacher said: This text very happily sets forth the first great principie of Protestantism, namely, the right of private judgusent. Now it seems quite likely that, to any who are unfamiliar with the formal phraseology of the great Protestant controversy with Rome the announcement of the !abject of this discourse would hardly prove attrac- tive. I shall hope to make it plain, however, that this sub- ject is one of considerable historic interest, and still more, is - one of great personal importance to us all. At the outset let us „?.nclaayour to define and explain this great principle. We shall pronibly do that best by recalling the nature of the circuinsizin`:•6s which gave rise to its assertion in the days of , Luther. In these days a;;;;Z:',..%)in was 1d aUct held in 1 subjection by a powerful CoUrch, Which claimed the sole and supreme right to govern the human conscience. Men' were to accept the faith as that church declared it. On no account and in no measure were they to differ 91: dissent , from such doctrine and belief. The Church and the Church alone was the spiritual teacher of men. Its voice was to be alone listened to; its precepts were to be a'oae trustul and obeyed. Men were thus taught, and came, ia the vast majority Of cases, to imagine that they were entirely incom- petent to -form any trustworthy judgment in - matters of religious belief. The Bible was declared to be a book for the learmd alone, which. meant in the' days not very long before Luther, that it was only a book for the priests and doctors of the Church. Learning was then largely monopo- lized by the so-called sacred orders, For the common people, therefore, the Bible was -a sealed book, and, was, moreover, hidden away in the impenetrable recesses of uni- versity and monkish libraries; where it was yet further ob- scured from the vulgar eye by being entombed in the ancient langnages. All spirit of enquiry was sternly die- countenanced, and, indeal, absolutely prohibited. Men were to believe as, they. were told, and so be : saved; or, if they refaced such obedient belief, they should "without doubt perish everlastingly" in the next world, while they subjected themselKes to serious pains land penalties in this. Every individual, therefore, in the matter of his religious faith was virtually waited upon by the United powers of the Church and the world. 13efore him they placed a creed,authenticated,_as they alleged, by the , lemming and influence of a saintly hierarchy, stretching from the days of the apostles; and made necessary to salva- tion by order of the direct successor of St. Peter himself— ' and then the maxi:: wee told he must believe that or be damned. Thus a man was to be saved not by believing in Christ, but by believing in the Church • not by trusting his Saviour, as a direct Act between himself and Jesus, bat by submitting intellect; heart, and life to the dogma and autho- rity of Rome. Such was the condition of things which, in the days of Luther, gave rise to the assertion of the right private judgment. Now with that condition before us, it is easier to define this principle. We see at once that it is a principle the very opposite of that which then obtained. Its meaning is this, that, no far from a man being bound to be- lieve as he is told by any human authority, his duty is to believe only what God tells hint. So far from any human aathority being competent to decide for him what he is to believe, he is himself*the only authority competent to deter- mine that matter. Instead of acting on the authority of a Church, which says "accept all things wt-rich the Church commands you; bold fast them all, for they are all good," be is t) act upon the Apostolic precept, and "prove all things," no matter who gives them, and only "hold fast that which is good." Mr. Froude, in the 6th vol. of his History of England, pithily puts the whole 'controversy between Luther and Rome on this point:—" Liberty, as opposed toi submission; the natural intelligence of the living man, as opposed to the corporate sovereignity of the outward and, visible Church; these were the sharp antitheses which were dividing Christian Europe." The right of private judg- ment," therefore, is the right of 'each man to judge for himself in matters of faith and conscience. Such matters are supremely, indeed solely, matters between him and his Maker. "To his own Master, he standeth or, falleth." No man, consequently, and no body -of men, however wise, or saintly, or orthodox they may be, can have any true right to come between the individual 'and his God. Personal access to God'is the natural right df -every Man. It is the right arising,trom his very creation. The child has an indefeasible right to enter his father's presence and listen 'to his father's voice, and consider his father's Words. Man is God's child, and all a child's rights and liberties are His. That is the truth of the Bible, and on that lies securely founded, and plainly established, the "Right of Private Judgment." Now, the Church of Rome has ever been shrewd in its refusing the Bible tolhe people. The doctrines and pretensions of that Church always find rapid dissolution before the clear light of the open Bible. There can be no question, at any rate, that the Bible is a book which addresses itself to the individual conscience and heart. There is a Voice in the Book which makes per- sonal appeal to every reader. It calls for, and it claims, and it must in some sort receive a verdict, a Judgment, an opinion, a belief (call it what you will), 'from every man to whom it comes. It professes to be it claims to be, a communication from God to man; and inasmuch as it bears its Own sufficiently obvious and uetnistakable creden- tials, credentials which are to be discerned by whomsoever will regard it in the true spirit, the Bible demands , individual attention, and decision, and action. The Bible not alone teaches the "Bight of Private Judgment," it calls upon men to exercise it. Jesus Christ always appeals to the heart and conscience of the individual. You cannot study Christ's teachings, with- out seeing that he regarded men as 6mi:in a tribunal in his own soul—a tribunal to which the truth can make its appeal, direct, dear, without any intervention 'whatsoever. There is all the difference in the world between man as Christ regarded him, and man as the Church of Rome regarded him in Luther's day, and continues to regard him still. Accord- ing to Rome, man is a poor, helpless, incapable creature, lost iu the slough of sin so utterly that god can only suffer his approach through many mediators; and so sunken in spiritual ignorance and imbecility that he cannot think aright, or understand aright, or beiieve aright, unless he be led and even driven to the needed faith. Christ knows man's sin, but comes personally near him in his leprosy, and puts His saving, sanctifying hand upon him; Christ speaks straight to his heart, and reading rightly iiiB need, says to him individually, "Will thou be made whole? Come unto Mel you shall find rest, you shall be forgiven, you shall have everlasting life." And thus does God in Christ re- cognise man's power to listen to, and discern, and judge truth. As Dr. Dale has well said in his lecture on this sub- jecte—" The appeal which God makes is to me, directly to me, and if priests, or bishops, or synods, or councils, or popes, are guilty of thrusting themselves between me and my God, I revolt against their blasphemous pretensions! In Christ God speaks'to me; for myself I must listen to Him. To listen to them instead of to. Him is a crime—a crime which His .Majesty must avenge, and which may change His very love into lery indignation. If I stind alone, with all Christendom against me, I will receivett first hand the glorious revelation of the infinite love of God." Now, / say, my friends, that there can be no doubt of the shrewdness of the Church of Rome in hiding and withhold- ing the Bible. That Church has involved itself bra most profound responsibility in so doing; but it has, at least been guided therein by much worldly wisdom. Directly a man receives the Bible, and stands bathed in its light, he is dis- illusioned ,concerning both the authority and doctrines of 1 the Church of Rome. He holds in his hand the only re- ! vested and competent authority on matters of spiritual belief. . He has poseession of that from which Rome heraelf has de- I rived all that is true and good in her dogma or ritual. And ' he has that which enables hint to test the truth of her teach- 4 ing, and the validity of her claims. The Cburch of Rome, ,1 the Church of England, any and every Church is on its trial ' before a man who holds the Bible in his hand and reads with 1 a spiritual mind. That book alone proves or disproves the ' truth or genuinenes of any so-called church. Having the ; Bible, a man is qualified to judge in all essential spiritual ' matters, provided that, he place his mind in docile submis- sion to the spirit which animates the book. Now, it was 1 Luther's discovery of the Bible, hidden away in the library of Erfurt University, that led him out into light and liberty. ' Before that he had been bound band and foot in mental ' and spiritual bondage. And but for that it is likely he would I have remained the spiritual prisoner of Rome' and would ,I have died at last in gloom, and unconquerable doubt and ' sorrow. That unearthed Bible, however, became to him the I means of spiritual awakening and illumination. By its 1 help be passed in review the doctrines of his church, with ' its pretensions and its practices. He found bow untrue the whole thing had become. He found that so far from being inspired with the spirit of Christ, thespirit of Anti- Christ, the spirit of the world and of evil reigned supreme. It was light from the Bible which made him vehement in his protest against the Papal indulgences. It was light from the Bible which made him clear and emphatic upon the doctrine of justification by faith. It was the truth, as it bad appealed to his own con- science from the Book of God, which made him draw out his celebrated theses and nail them on the door of Witten- berg Church. Andiwhen he did that he was making his first open claim for the right of private judgment. He was then and there setting his opinion and belief, drawn from Holy Scripture, against the dogmas and the practices autho- rised by the Church of Rome. He was declaring himself a 1 judge of Holy Scripture; and, therefore, a competent critic of Romish doctrine. And he followed up this claim to pri- , vete judgment by his subsequent conduct before the august papal and imperial assembly at Worms. There—at risk of liberty and life—he resolutely clung to his opinions; refus- ing to retract them until they were proved contrary to the Word of God. These splendid words, in which all his titan- hood spoke, "Provo to me out of Scripture I am wrong, and I submit. Till then my conscience binds me! Here I stand! I can do no more. God help ma 1" Those words were a claim of "the right of private judgment," the echoes of which can never die so long as the world stands. Luther was then saving, in face of all the combined powers of church and world, that he, the humble monk, the man of peasant origin, was greater than they all. He could neither bend his spirit nor bind his conscience at their bid- ding. The courage of his act is sublime. But there is something yet sublimer than the courage, and that is the truth which inspired it, namely this, that a man's faith is due to God alone' and that no power on earth, or under' the earth, can ,properly interfere with it. It must not be sup- posed that Luther was by any means the irst to discern, or to contend for, this most sacred right. The Book of the Asses of the Apostles tells us that in the very

APPLETON.

INQUEST.—Mr. Ridgway, coroner, held an inquest at the Thorn Inn, Appleton, Cheshire, on Saturday, on the body of Thomas Tomlinson apparently about 45 years of age, who died on Friday.—Peter Street, a farm labourer, living at Lower Peover, said the deceased had no settled residence. Witness and Tomlinson had worked together with one of Barker and Brookes's threshing machines for about two months. On Thursday last they were employed by Mr. William Darlington. at Appleton. After working until about a quarter to six in the evening, they rested for about a quarter of an hour and then walked to Mrs. Barber's shop. As they had about a mile to go, and it being raining at the time, they went quickly. When they got to the shop de- ceased asked for some provisions and immediately fell down dead.—Dr. T. S. Smith, of Warrington, said he had that morning made a post-mortem examination of the body of the deceased. Externally there were no marks of violence. The body was well nourished and the brain was quite natural. The lungs were congested and the heart was full of blood on both sides. The kidneys were congested and the liver enlarged. The cause of death was disease of the heart.—A verdict of "Death from natural causes" was re- turned. ASHTON. RECRABITES MERINO AT Asia-rm.—A public meeting in connection with the Onward Tent (Ashten-in-Makerfield) of the Independent Order of Rechabites was held in the Con- gregational School, Ashton, on Monday evening. There was a goodly number of persons present. The chair was occupied by the Rev. H. Wilson, who was supported by Mr. Tunstall (Ashton), and Messrs. John Green, 'Wm. Hudson, Thomas Hall and J.,S. Green (all of Warrington.) Inter- esting addressees on the Rechabite Order in particular and temperance movement in general were delivered by the gentlemen named ; and at (ho close a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to them. The meeting concluded with a similar vote of thanks to the chairman. A6IITON RECREATION SOCIETY ANNUAL TEA PARTY AND BALL.—The annual tea party and ball in connection with the Ashton Recreation Society took place on Monday even- ing at the Public Hall, Bryn-street. The gathering was a most successful one. About 60 members and friends sat down to an excellent tea, the following ladies presiding at the tables :—Mrs. Painter, Mrs. Latimer, Mrs. Boardman, Mrs. Mitchell, Mrs. George Hill, Mrs. W. Hill, Mrs. Middle- burst, Mrs. Holbrook, Mrs. Williams, Miss Livesley, Mrs France, Miss Scully, and Mrs. Talbot. Mr. Lythgoe's string band from Wigan capitally discoursed a .choice selection of popular dance music, and the party, increased to about 100 persons, thoroughly enjoyed themselves during the evening. The masters of ceremonies were Messrs. Marsh, Vernon, and Middlehurst, and to them and the committee thanks are due for the pleasant manner in which everything passed off. CADISHE AD.

The Cadishead Brass Band held its animal ccncert in the Wesleyar Day School on Tuesday evening. There was a large attendance. The selection of music was good, and its execution highly appreciated by the audience. A theological class for young people in connection with the Wesleyan Chapel has been commenced by the Rev. R. Dillon. It meets in one, of the vestrys every Wednesday evening. The attendance so far is encouraging. CULCHETH.

RISLEY PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH, CULCHETH.—The an- nual sermons in aid of the Sunday School were preached in the above church on Sunday afternoon and evening, by the Rev. J. Gordon, M.A., or Wharton. There were good con- gregations 4 each service, and the collections amounted to £s3s ad.

At the Knuteford Quarter Sessions, this week, Martha Didsbury, 53, charwoman' was sentenced to two months' hard labour for stealing afowl, value 55., the property of Mr. Samuel Peacock, at Frodsham, on the 10th November. LECTURE.—On Monday evening Mr. John Simpson, of. Dunsdale, delivered a lecture in the Girls' School. Fred- sham,in connection with the Frodsbam Literary and Debat- ing Society, when Mr. Henry Linaker presided There was a good attendance. The subject of the lecture was "Eng- land past .nd present," being a contrast of the mode of travelling, dress, &c., at the present time and a hniadred years ago. Several ancient articles were produced to illus- trate the lecture, amongst which was a " Bradshaw's rail- way guide" for 1842, which presented a striking contrast when compared with the modern railway guide to every. where. Ai the 'dote of the meeting A coA,Zi vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Simpson for his excellent lecture, on the motion of the vicar (the Rev. H. D. B. Blogg, M.A.), seconded by Mr. E. A. Wright, J.P. Mr. Simpson, in responding, proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman for presiding.

Both morning and evening the pulpit was oc:upied by the Rev. J. M. VValtasley, of St. Helens, who preached to large congregations. The annual public nits- -siOnary meeting was held in the same building last evening (Thursday), when there was again a good attendance. In- teresting addresses on the mission Cause were ...I 6 ven and a collection was made at the close in aid of the Mission funds.

MORE POLICE WANTED AT GOLBORNE: PETITION TO TIIE COUNTY AUTHORITIES —The movement for obtaining two additional police officers for the parish of Golborne is a very wise and judicious one, for there can be no doubt that they are wanted. The local Parochial Committee are be- stirring themselves in this matter, and the following petition has been drawn up :--"Golbarne.—To the Justic,s of the Peace for the county of Lancaster in Quarter Sessions assembled,—The memorial of the ratepayers of the town- ship of Golborne, in the said county, respectfully sboweth, that the said township of Golborne, which contains an area of 1,679 acres, eight miles of streets and roads, and a popu- lation of 4,502, and having a rateable value ot 22.238, is insufficiently provided with police officers, there being two only residing in the township at the pr.( sent tiro.- ; such number being totelly mad,quate for the preservati..o of law and order and the protection of 'property in a district embracing so large an area, and so many miles of streets and roads, and containing such a population as does the

- - I said township. We memorialists therefore respectfully ask that two additional officers May be appointed for the better preservation of peace and outtr and protection of property in the said townsbip."—At a recent meeting of the corn- mittee their Surveyor (Mr. C. S. Bennie) was instructed to Obtain signatures to the memorial and forward it to the pro- per uthorities: For the information. of .these ratepayers who desire to sign it—and no doubt there will be many will- ing to do sir—we may add that it lies at th.a office of the surveyor, High-street._

ST. JAMES'S SCHOOI,, HAYDOCE.—On Monday evening a magic lanterrientertainment was given in this school. The subject is of special interest at the present day, " China and the Chinese." The sixty beautifully coloured viewe. illustrative of the subject, were much admired; and we understand that by request they will be again shown in the course of next month. The second part of the entertain- ment consisted of several liaydoCk picturcs and portraits. The Vicar sang " The village blacksmith "and read "Jane Conquest;" the connective readings in relation to China being given by Mr; .Arthur Evans, who also preeided at the pianoforte and harmonium. Mr. Charles ForsLaw played several popular airs on the cornet. HORNS' SUITE/Y. An entertainment in aid of the Horns' Smithy Band of Hope fund, toot plaoe in the Mission Room ou Wednesday evening. Mr. E. T. Eccles presided-,, There was a crowded audience, and the following took prt in an attractive pro- gramme :—Miss Espley, Messrs. D..:rooby' W. E. Roberts, J. SERVICE OF SONG. On Monday eventrg last a service of song entitled "The Giver and His Gifts," waa rendered in the Methodist Free Church. Kingsley, by the choir of Efiesmere•street Chapel, Runcorn. The chapel was filled RI: - its utmost capacity and large numbers were nimble to gain • admission. The Rev. R. Trotjer, of Frodsham, ,read the connective readings in an elcriptent and inipressiVe manner, the choral numbers being ably rendered by the their, who sang several anthems in addition to the service. Mr. John -Holford acted as conthictor aid Miss Clough accompanied. The object of the service- WILS to aid the funds of the "church, and we are pleased to see that it has been so suc- cessful.

LEIGH. DRATII_ OF MB. T. T. RAYES.—Yeaterday week; Mr... Thomas Travers Hayes, of Fairfield, Leigh, cotton spinner,. died in the sixtieth year of his age. Mr. Hayes was created a county magistrate in ISCD. He was a consistent Liberal, and associated with the cause in South-West Lancashire. He had been ailing for some time. OUGHTRINGTON.

The Rev. Forbes Winslow, who conducted special mission services at St. Peter's Church, early in the year, again visited the village on Monday and Tuesday, when two mons were preached. • RAINHILL. CONSiRVATIVE ASSOCIATIOI4.—On Thursday evening the members of the abov‘e association held their third annual meting in the Club-house, J. Sirenll, Esq., in the chair. There was a good attendance. From the reports read by the treasurer and s-cretary, the-association is evidently in a flourishing condition both financially and in regard to the number of members on the roll.

MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN—Oa Sunday last sermons were preached and collections made in Rainhill Parish Church, on behalf of the above rvis9ion. The preacher in the morning was the Vicar of Rainbill. In the 'evening the Rev. T. Patrick, M A., chaplain to the mission, de- livered an address, showing by statistics and perronal ex- perience that the mission was doing a good work among the seamen frequenting the ports of Liverpool, Birkenhead, Garston, Ellesmere Port, and Runcorn. The cAlections amounted to £ll.

NATIOVALIoots.—A concert in aid of the funds of the Rainhill National Schools was given in the bo7s' school room on Wednesday evening last. The whole of the arrange- ments were made and admirably carried out by Mr. and Mrs. ThOmson. The following were the artistes :—Miss Ella Herriman (pupil of Madam Sainton Dolby), Mrs. Thomson, of Rainhill; Mr. H. Broadley (member of Mr. Lea's Hope Hall Concert Quartette), and the Cambrian Quartette, con- sisting of Messrs. D. J. Davies, D. Williams, J. T. Jonee, and 0 J. Rowlands. The subjoined programme was ad- mirably performed, and where all so ab!y rendered their parts it would be invidious to mention any person in par- ticular. Part I.: Pianoforte solo, "Gavotte Chloris," Mr. C. Collins; quartette, "Meet me by moonlight alone," the Cambrian Quartette; song (encored), "Waiting," Miss E. Herriman; song, "The harbour lights," Mr. H. Broadley; song, "Madoline," Mr. D. Williams; deett," Huntingtower." Mrs. Thomson and Mr. Broadley; song (encored), "Going to market," Miss Her„riman ; quartettes, "Absence," and "When evening twilight," the Cambrian Quartette. Part II.: Pianoforte solo, "GavoLte Selriich," Mr. C. Col- lins; song, The minstrel boy," Mr. H. Broadley; song (encored), Let me dream again," Miss Herriman ; quar- tette (encored), "By Celia's Arbour," the Cambrian Quar- tette; song, "A summer shower," Mrs. Thomson; song, . "Norah, the pride of Kildare," Mr. J. T. Jones; song, "The wolf," Mr. 0. J. Rowlands; duett, "The manly heart," Mrs. Thomson and Mr. 0. J. Rowlands. The attendance was good, and doubtless the concert will be a financial as well as- musical success.

A. VIOLENT Yourm—A respectable looking youth n.,med John Taylor was on Tuesday charged at the Prescut Petty Sessions with having been drunk and disorderly on the 4th instant at Roby.—A. police officer stated that he had been called to the Stanley Arms, Roby, on the day named, and when he arrived there he saw the defendant making a dis— turbance and refusing to quit at the request of the landlordr who had refused to serve him withtlrink.—A fine of 5s and - costs was imposed. .

ASSAULTING A FEMALE.—At the—Prescot Petty Sessiode, on Tuesday, Nathaniel Dingsdale was charged with having assaulted Mary,Barron at Tarbuck. An altercation, it seemed, had taken place in a public-house between the two parties, and the defendant, it was alleged, struck the complainant. —A, fine of is and costs was inflicted.

SOUTHWORTH-WITH-CROFT. RATEPAYERS MEETING AT CROPT.—A special meeting of the ratepayers of the township of Southworth-with-Croft was held at the Board School, Croft, on Friday evening List, to consider the new basis or standard for the county rate and to pass resolutions thereon. Present—the Rev. T. P. Kirk- man, M.A.,F.R.5., rector- and Messrs. James Hatton and Lewis Birchall (overseer:), Reginald Owen, jun. (guardian and waywarden), Charles Wild, James Hunt, E. W.Sankey, and George Briraelow (assistant overseer). The Rector having taken the chair, the Assistant Overseer read the notice convening the meeting, and afterwards a copy of the new basis or standard for the county rate assessment, which showed that the county basis for the year 1878 MS £5,050. and for the year 1883 £5,246, being an increase of £196 over the basis for the last six Tears, and £326 more than the rateable value of the township. A letter on the subject from Mr. Sutton, the clerk to the Warrineton Board of Guardians, having been read, Mr. Birchall moved, and Mr.' Hatton seconded, that Mr. Sutton be authorised to appeal against the increase on the following grounds, namely :- Ist. That the township is already very highly assessed. 2nd. That there is no railway passing through it. 3rd. That there is very little or no building operations going on. 4th. That the trade is entirely of an agricultural character, and sth. That they could not look forward to any increase of value in any direction. The resolution having been put to the meeting and carried unanimously, the proceedinpler- minated.

SOUTHWORTH-WITH-CROFT SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting of the abnve Board was held at the Board school on Tuesday evening, when there were present the Rev. T. I*. Kirkman (chairman and clerk), and lliessre. James Hatton, Lewis, Birchall, Richard Turner, James Gooden, and Alfred Dixon (school attendance officer). The Attendance Officer submitted his report, which stated that he had visited the various schools in the district during the past month, when he found that 44 children had been away from school Dick during the month; but be was glad to say that most of them wore now ifimroving, and would 800/1 be able to attend school again. The average attendance at the Board school for the past month bad been 119 8. He also Stated he bad warned nine parents during the month that unless their children attended school more regularly they woad be summoned to appear before the Board to show a reasonable excuse for such children's absence. He further ' reported that be had served one notice to a parent for child to attend school, and summoned another parent to appear before the Board that night. He also presented a list of the names of several chihiren who still kept very irregular in their attendauce at school, and the names of tboae chlidren who had been away from school sink. The report having been adopted, summonses were ordered to be issued in two cases against parents for the continued -neglect 0 their children to attend school in conformity with Abe bye-laws of the Beard. Several accounts having been passed, the proceedings terminated. WINSFORD. LIBERAL CLUB.—The establishment of a Literal Club for this imp°, tant salt town has evidently supplied a desideratum, if one may judge by the numerous admissions and the great accession to the list of members. It is a , source of gratification to its promoters, that so many readers are found gathering information respecting political and other matters, that so many works have been given bearing on such topics, and that the funds have so freely flowed ir as to enable the committee to open:and furnish, and at t' same time to aid to such furnishing every comfort desir and recreations needful to most of its members. div.head: EXAMINER
div.p: THE EXAMINER
SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 24, 1683.

Notwithstanoing all that Tory orators may say to the contrary, the condition of Ireland at the present time is very satisfactory. There were indications of unrest a week or two ago, during the visit of Sir STAFFORD NORTHCoTE, but with the departure of the right hon baronet these disquieting signs passed away, and neither In the north, the south, the east, or the west are there any appearances of dis- content, of agitation, or of a recurrence of the horrible outrages which have so disgraced the pages of Irish history. Our Tory friends ad- mit, though very reluctantly, the tranquility of the Emerald Isle, but they are very fond of ascribing it to the coercive policy of the Go- vernment rather than to the measures of relief which the present Ministry have been instru- mental in passing. We are disposed to think Ireland's peaceful condition is due to a little of both phases of the Government policy. From whatever cause it arises there is reason for thankfulness and gratitude. That the re- pressive or coercive legislation has not been without good results let recent statistics prove Under the Prevention of Crimes Act there has been altogether about 700 cases, intimi- dating and boycotting constituting the half of these; but recently very few complaints have arisen under the Act. In the year ending the 31st October last there were only two agrarian murders in Ireland, certainly more than enough; in the previous year there were no less than 32. Again, in the year endinz the 3i St October last there were 911 agrarian out- rages reported, or an average of very nearly 76 'Da month; but in the previous year there were 4 365 such outrages, or an average of about 364 a month. In the last month of this year there were 53 agrarian outrages only. There has, therefore, been a steady decrease in crime within a very short time, and there is, we think, reasonable hope that the decrease will he still more marked. Now, what the remedial le,islation of the Government has done may also be proved by statistics. It is estimated that the total number of holders of agricultural land in Ireland is from soo,ooo to 600,000. Of these, 154,344 had up to the end of last month either applied to the Land Courts or had their agreement as to rent fixed out of court. Of the 154,344, the cases dis- posed of had been 125,098, leaving 29 24.6 undealt with. At the present rate of speed the whole of the cases will soon be overtaken by the Commissioners. Of the total number of holders of land, that is the 500,000 or 600,000, a deduction must be made for house- holders who do not come under the scope of the Act; and after m-iking that deduction, and setting aside the 150,000 tenants already referred to who have applied to the Land Courts to have fair rents fixed, it will be at once apparent that there are in Ireland a very great number of tenants getting voluntarily from their landlords as good terms as the Land Court would be likely to give. This is a circumstance that is exceedingly gratifying. Then, with respect to the operation of the Arrears Act, passed with the object of wiping out the arrears of rent, we find that under that Act there has been about 136,000 appli- cations, all of which have been disposed of With the exception of about 6,000. The total amount of money supplied for the seztlement is £BOO,OOO ; but let it be remembered that the settlement of arrears is as advantageous to the landlords as it is to the tenants. These facts, in our opinion, point to but one con- clusion, and that is—as Mr. W. H. SMITH has very candidly put it—that "the Govern - Ment has now found out how to govern the People of Ireland properly." The secret clearly lies in conferring upon Ireland and the Irish people the benefits of the same laws and the same rights and privileges which we in England enjoy. By this means alone can agitators be silenced; by this means alone can the connection between England and Ireland be maintained; and by this means alone can the memory of the injustice Which Ireland has been made to suffer at the hands of England in the past be wiped out. This, however, does not seem to be the opinion-entertained by some of our Conser- vative friends, and a remarkable instance of this is furnished by the speech of the late Home Secretary, Mr. CROSS, on Wednesday evening. The extension of the franchise to the counties of England, Scotland and Wales cannot, we all know, be long delayed. We see no reason whatever why Ireland should be exempted from this extension, and we have confidence that Ireland will be included in any future Reform Bill; but we find Sir RICHARD CROSS urging with all the elo- quence he can command that it would be folly to include *lreland in the Bill. We suppose that what would Please Sir RICHARD would be to see the People of Ireland altogether excluded from representation except, of course, those of known Tory proclivities, —and the country subjected to something like martial law. Ire- land did not, indeed, experience much better treatment from Sir RICHARD and his friends during the reign of the BEACONSFIELD Ad- Ministration, and they have nothing more to

div.head: EXAMINER. ,J6'IITRPAY, NOVEMBER 24 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. ,J6'IITRPAY, NOVEMBER 24 1883.

'hope for from a SALISBURY-NORTHCOTE Cabinet. The Irish people are now, how ever, beginning to look upon the Conserva- tives as their sworn enemies, and the enthu- siasm with which they have supported the Liberal candidate at York is a proof that they recognise who are their friends, that their feelings of bitterness and animosity against England are being buried with the past, and that they are not wanting in gratitude for what the Government have done for them and are prepared to do. We notice that this week Mr. W. H. SMITH has been complaining—and with some decree of reason—about the in- temperate language indulged in by Mr. HEALY and the extreme wing of the PARNELL- rfE party, and he calls upon the Government to suppress it. The language is, we confess, of such a character that it cannot be de- fended, but we think Mr. SMITH should be equally ready to condemn the utterances of some of his intimate associates. Is he, for instance, blind to the unwarranted and dis- graceful licence of speech indulged in by Mr. LOWTHER, the once Chief Secretary for Ire- land, who has surely some idea of the cares and responsibilities of office, and ought to be guarded in the choice of his words. Speaking at Bristol the other day, that irrepressible foe of Ireland delared that her MAJESTY'S loyal subjects in Ireland were " first of all deli- berately robbed by her MAJESTY'S Govern- ment, and then handed over to the knife and bullet of the assassin." Language of this description is simply scandalous, and aperson resorting to such slander only discloses his weakness and shows that he has a very bad cause to defend.
