THEFT OF BEEF AT RONCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Ses- sions, on Monday, Emma Carter was charged with having on the previous Saturday stolen 31bs. of beef, the property of Ahab Sayle, butcher, Bridge-strdet.—About a quarter past eleven on Saturday night Mr. Robert Wright was walking along Bridge-street on his way home, when his attention was directed to Sayle's shop by a youog man named Sin- clair Armstrong, saying " Look at that thief." Mr. Wright, looking through the window, saw the prisoner take up a piece of beef from off the board and conceal it about her person. As there was no one in the shop, he went and in- formed Mr. Hurst, the complainant's father-in-law, and to- gether they watched the prisoner purloin another piece of beef of about 4lbs. weight. She then left the shop, but was captured by Mr. Hurst. The pieses of beef were after- wards feund on the ground near where she was standing. by the complainant, who gave her into the custody of P.S. Walley. She denied the theft.—The Bench committed her to Inutsford Quarter Sessions for trial. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES.—The an- nail sermons in aid of the Trust Fund of the Zion United Methodist Free Church, Widnes, were preached on Sunday, morning and evening, by the Rev. W. Valise, the pastor. There were large congregations at both services. Under the conductorship of Mr. John Betney the choir sang special hymns and anthems in effective style. On Monday even- ing the annual tea meeting and entertainment were held in the some building. A good company sat down to tea, the following ladies presiding at the tables :—Mrs. Savage, Mrs. Turton, Mrs. Atherton, Mrs. Williamson, Mrs. Ogden, Miss E. Betney, Miss F. Cavraey, aid Miss E. Ritnmer. The sub- sequent proceedings were presided over by the Rev. W. Vann, and there was a large audience. Addresses were de- livered by the Chairman and Mr. Bray.; Mr. E. Bate and Mr. C.l Hart gi,ve recitations; while Mr. Robert Yates favoured the audience with a reading. Dnring the evening the Church choir sang in their usual accomplished manner the anthems, "I was glad," " Kedron," and " I will extol thee." Mr. John Betney wielded the baton. MAINTENANCE or PARENTS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, John Hood was summoned to show cause why he should not contribute towards the ' support of his aged and infirm mother, who is an inmate of Prescot Union Workhouse. Mr. S. H. Hartley, appeared to prosecute, and Mr. Seamell, the relieving officer, having given evidence that the defendant was a married man with a wife and four children, and earning 30s to 35s per week, the Bench ordered the defendant to pay 2s per week.— Nicholas Gillon was summoned to show cause why he should not be committed to gaol for neglecting to contribute. towards his mother's support. Mr. Seamell stated that several months ago the Bench ordered the defendant to pay 123 ed per week towards the support of his mother, who was an inmate of Whieton Workhouse, but he had not paid a single penny, and the arrears amounted to £2 lie. For- merly he worked at Widnes, but he was now employed else- where, and witness had been unable to God his whereabouts. He came home every NI eek end and kept his wife and family in respectable condition. The Me was withdrawn. ST. —at all events in the Gaiety. Arthur Cecil also watched a play in which he had himself so lately taken so leading a part, and Corney Grain loemed extretn4y large in the door ways. Miss Bromley's ;Acting was a eurprise. All it wanted of heine excellent was " go." Maoy parts of it were admirable. People c ark: nt 11,Ip remembering Mrs. Stirling an:l Mal i - Wilton ; but Miss Bromley had a dignity and a beauty which did not belong to those Peg Woffiagtons. bba looked like a por- trait by Reynolds, and her dresses were one lovelier than another, and she became them all. The scene where she in- troduces herself and her friends, the crities an! actors, to the young country wife, who is her unconscious rival, was excellent, as was the famous scene where she dances the jig with the starving poet and his children. Herman Vein got a warmer reception than any of the artists. It was a most pathetic impersonation, and a very many-sided one,—putu- lant, digniried, subtle, all the irritability of a poet, and with that a kind heart and an honest nature. It was a pleasure to see an actor known for heroic parts succeed so well and win his way into the affections of his audience so grad:rally and yet so surely as he did, in a play of which the interest is entirely domestic Miss Sophie Eyre put great feeling into the part of the young country wife, ani Mr. Kemble, as Snarl, gave the little character great importance. I hear that the last nights of lolanthe are not indeed an- nounced, but anticipated. They will not take it off so long as it draws, but tleey will take it off soon. In the meantime the new piece will be rehearsed. Miss Lilian Russell has been engaged for it. She acted some time ago at the Gaiety during the dull season, and if she did not draw great houses, at least she created a favourable impression with critics and managers.

Great things are expected of the Ameriedn actress who is to open the (Thera Comique. She is represented as the queen of soubrtttes. They are a commodity which we chiefly import. I think Lottie Venn is the only soubrette on the English stage. The French have many of them, from Mdlle. Samary downwards. Lottis, who is the coming attraction, is described as being a superior Minnie Palmer. If she proves to be what she is represented to be, she will certainly be a success. Mr. Gladstone's enamels continue to be a great attraction et the South Kensington Museum. They occupy several cases, and are of extraordinary beauty. I hear that the set of Crown Derby which has just been made expressly for the Prime Minister, and will be presented in the course of next month, is the finest work which the new factory has yet turned out. The Premier's collection of china is not large, bat is extremely select. The drawing-room at Hawarden is a little museum in itself.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

CABINET COUNCILS - SIR CHARLES DILKE'S "WALKS ABROAD"-GREAT FEES IN GREAT CASES - COMFORT FOR 'LAWYERS, JURORS, AND JUDGES-MR. BENCE JONES-THE ELEC- TRIC LIGHT-CONGERS AND TURTLES-THE CHILTERN HUNDREDS - MISS BROMLEY'S MATINEE AT THE GAIE rY - lOLANTIIE - A NEW SOUBRETTE-MR. GLADSTONE'S CHINA.
LONDON, TIITRADAY.

The season of Cabinet Councils has commenced, and the series will be continued pretty regularly. The subject of these deliberations is no secret. The Government has to decide upon a course which must be all settled before Par- liament meets, and there is a general opinion that Parlia- meat will meet some ten days or a fortnight before its normal time for assembling. There are the two great measures, and which have to be brought in and passed, and there is a well known difference of opinion amongst Ministers as to which of these should have priority. nere is no split in the Cabinet, or anything approaching to a split. Ministers are agreed as to the importance of both measures. It is a question of precedence, and Sir William Harcourt would give the precedence to the County Govern- ment Bill, and Mr. Chamberlain to the franchise question. If Parliament were younger it would not make much matter, but at its present age there are difficulties in settling the question. Of course the Franchise is the more important and should naturally come first, but its weakness lies in its importance. There is a ve7 general belief that the Lords will throw out the measure, and, as the present Parliament is not in its pronairejeunesse, will, insist on an appeal to the country. But an appeal to the country might not give the Government so strong a hand. The Parnellites would certainly improve their position, and it is doubtful whether Mr. Gladstone would still care to be at the helm. He is not so young as he was when the last general election called him to power. These are all arguments for putting the Franchise Bill second. But, then, second may mean nowhere. The reform of London Government is no doubt a big undertaking, but still it is scarcely sufficiently large to be put in the front. If both bills were safe to be carried before Parliament was prorogaed, it would not make much matter which were to come first. On the whole, even assuming the meet perfect concord during the Ministerial deliberations, there is good cause why the Cabinet should sit often and sit long in oonsultation.

In the meantime, while the fate of municipal London is thus being settled, Sir Charles Dilke, returned from his summer wanderings, is going on a strange winter tour. The whole London Press has taken up the subject of London poverty, and the intelligent foreigner if he were to read his Telegraph or his Daily Noes would be qnite horror- struck as to what we think of our capital. A judicious selecticn has been made of the very worst and poorest quar- ters which London misery, poverty, and overcrowding can supply; and with his accomplished cicerone to lead him about Sir Charles tales his useful notes. London seems to be full of these rookeries which Charles Dickens described in Bleak House, and which at the time were said to be highly coloured and exaggerated. Nut already people are asking what the outcome of these visits will be. One thing is certain, that Sir Charles will be both deliberate and thorough in his reforms, and it is no less certain that what he has seen makes him have little doubt that an immediate dealing with the subject is imperatively necessary. In the great case now before Vice Chancellor Bacon em- ployment has been given to quite a mob of big wigs. Eigh- teen Queen's Counsel are briefed and the amount of money at stake in the suit may be guessed from the amount which the lawyers are taking out of it. Mr. Horace Davey has 800 guineas marked on his brief, and his junior, Mr. Buckley, has £450. As to Mr. Charles Russell, he must be a sort of universal provider of opinions, arguments, cross-examina- tions, and stirring addresses. He seems te be everywhere and in everything. In strange contrast with the fees in the Kelle and Lucas else are those in the Date Coffee Company. I hear Mr. Russell only got 50 guineas. t

I hear that in the Christmas recess great changes will be carried out in the New Law Courts. They will not be structural imprsvernents, and indeed will have more to do with upholstery than brick and mortar. The judges have nearly all got colds, an several successive juries have fallen victims to draughts, independently of the one gentle- man who s) narrowly escaped being harpooned in the head by an umbrella, and having his organ Of veneration per- forated against his will. Curtains are to be put up, and jury boxes are to he made a little less intolerably un- comfortable than they have been for the last half century. The judges are all to feed together at luncheon time, instead of enjoying as heretofore a dignified and solitary but dyspeptic meal. A large room will be necessary for the suitable entertainment of these giants refreshing, and it will have to be found somewhere in the building—or to be built. Ii the meantime the head of the bench makes a concession. The Lord Chancellor's rosin will be used as a feeding place for his brethren.

I think everyone who knew him will be sorry for Mr. Bence Jones. He was a well-known figure in London ball- rooms and in the park during the season. His enormous height made him remarkable wherever he went. I saw him at Lisselane this summer, and know Low much he was liked by the tenantry, who certainly treated his father so badly. I think I never saw a .man whose appearance in country differed so much from his appearance in town. At Clona- kilty he generally wore knicker-bockers, in which costume his figure looked almost portentous. He was very fond of shooting, and used to bring over Oxonian frienas to enjoy the not very abundant sport which the place yielded.

At Brighton there has been a row about the proposed lighting by electricity. The new illuminant is not popular there, and the price which has to be paid for it adds to its unpopularity. Here we have had a new experiment which may lead to important results. One reason why people don't care for electric lighting is that they object to the dynamo- machine at work so close to their houses. You may see the ugly shed.which holds it outside the Savoy Theatre, and you may hear it thudding and thumping, and pulsating for many yards off. It seems agreed that if the machine could be kept at a distance the light in private dwellings would be much more general. And this .is what has been accomplished on the Metropolitan line. Between Notting Hill Gate, Edgeware-road, Gower-street, and King's Cross, a new system has been adopted which at this mo- ment is working with success. The engine is at Edgeware- road, and the electric current can be transmitted from this centre along the wires a distance of fifteen miles. If this achievement can be improved upon we shall soon have the electric light not only at our doors but inside them. The engine used at Edgeware:road is a thirty-horse power machine, and the current operates as far east as Aldgate. It is curious to see that at most of the stations on the Dito. trict Line the electric light has been abandoned.

The conger eel discussion this week has been exceedingly unpalatable. Sir Henry Thompson is a notable man in London Society. He is the friend of many artists and of many men of letters. Thus, what he says has a kind of fic- titious value. 1 think if anyone else bad written that letter about turtle soup and conger eels we should have heard no more about it. The effect of it has been not so.mnch to make conger eel appreciated as te make turtle soup rather dreaded. The truth is, we never know what we are eating. Sir Henry has done for the favourite Aldermanie mess what Charles Dickens did for the humbler mutton pie. By sug- gesting a disagreeable ingredient he has given it a bad name. It is some consolation to know that turtle are imported into England annual!y to the value of some f. 25,000. If the Thompson recipe for the soup be both good and true, if it really is as largely adopted as he say i it is, it is clear that there must be an enormous consumplion of congers. And yet one does not see many of them in the market.

I see it announced in many papers that Mr. Metge, M.P. for County Meath, has accepted the Chiltern Hundreds. Now, this is absolutely untrue, though no great harm is done by the announcement. He has not accepted them; because he could not accept them. He has applied for them, but he cannot accept them till he gets them, and he cannot get them till Parliament meets.

Miss Nelly Bromley's matinee at the Gaiety was a com- plete success. The house was very full, and the audience was very friendly. There were certainly many more actors before the eurtain than behind. Mrs. Bernard Beere was there, having hurried away from the Haymarket, where the rehearsal of Mr. Pinero's "Lords and Commons" has been going on every morning these many days. Nelly Farren, accompanied by a daughter who looked like a twin sister— the mother was so young looking and the daughter so old— seemed in the stalls to be at the wrong side of the footlights

div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BIARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Board-room, Vic- toria-road, on Thursday afternoon. Mr. T. Sutton Timm's presided, and there were present the Revs. Father Clark and Father Finegan, Messrs. Bradshaw, Brock, Deacon, R. Shaw, P. Glover, and G. H. Danby (clerk).
DISTRICT EDUCATION.

The minutes ef the committee on this subject, which were passed on the motion of Mr. DEACON, stated that du- ring the month of October (five weeks) there had been 15(3 applications for fees, and 304 persons had appsared before the committee for contravention of the Education Act. Fees were recommended to be paid in 131 cases, and 46 persons were convicted by the magistrates. One scholar was sent to an industrial school, two to truant schools, and one to the training ship Clio.

div.head: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE.

This committee recommended that Miss Callis be ap• pointed head mistress of the infants' department of the War- rington-road School (vice Miss Hay), at a salary of LSO per annum ; that Miss E. M. Callis be appointed assistant mistress in the infants' department of the Warrington-road School, at a salary of £35 per annum ; that Elizabeth Leach be engaged as a candidate pupil teacher, at a salary of £l3 per annum ; and that the tender of the Garwood Coal and Iron Company (Limited), dated November 7th, 1883, be accepted for the supply of slack and best Orrell coal. The committee reported that they had opened a fourth department (junior mixed) at the Warrington-road schools, and placed the school under the charge of Miss Hay, head mistress of the infants' department.—The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Rev. Father FINEGAN.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Finance Committee recommended for payment ac- counts amounting to £609 2s 61; and reported that the school fees for October were: Siinms' Cross School, £46 lie 101 ; Warrington-road School, £21183 10J; IVest Bank School, £4O 4s 7d. The Government grant for Warrington- road School amounted to £283 lie. The committee recam mended that the seal of the Board be affixed to the mort- gages to secure the amount of the fourth loan from the Public Works Loan Board to this Board for £3,000, and to the receipt and order for the Public Works Loan Board's certificate for the same. div.head: PRESCOT RURAL SANITARY AU rHORITY.
div.p: PRESCOT RURAL SANITARY AU rHORITY.

An ordinary meeting of this Au:hority wis held ia the Workhoulse.Whiston, on Thursday, Mr. Meadows presiding. There were also present Messrs. Newsome, Hall, Gilbody, L.atherbarr.,w,Eatock, Svder, Leigh, Kenwright, the Rev. T. Chambers; and Mr. H trtley (clerk).
THE SMALLPDX AT WIDNES.-STRICTURES ON WIDNES GUARDIANS. • _ _

The Rev. T. CHAM—B—E-R—S---ked if it were within tbe province of that Authority to recommend re- vaccination at Widnes. It had been proposed that such should be done at the last meeting of the Guardians, but he mast say it had been unceremoniously rejected. Since the previous Thursday, however, he had read an article in a newspaper which certainly very much startled him. They had been told by the Widnes Guardians that no new case of small-pox had arisen, but the article referrel to went so far as to say that it was an indivutable fact that there were new cases, and that an intimate friend of one cf the Guardians had himself a case in his own ; house which must have been known to that Guardian. He was sure, at the same time, they all believed that the Widnes Guardians were gentlemen who came there to dis- charge their duties, and had only said what they thought to be true. They also gathered, he said, from the article that in no case in which revaccination had been resorted to had there been a death, but only in cases in which re-vaccination had not been resorted to had fatalities ensued. He thought the Widnes Guardians ought to have accepted the recommen- dation for re-vaccination made at tlie last meeting of Guar- dians, and he suggested if that Authority had any power with regard to the matter they should exercise ir.—Mr. HARTLEY said the law with regard to vaccination was to be carried into effect by the Guardians, and not by the Sanitary Authorities.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS: How is it that Widnes is associated with us P—Mr. HARTLEY : Widnes is not with us as a Rural Sanitary Authority.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said he had been under a misapprehension, but he did not withdraw a single word that he hal said. He thought Widnes ought to be placarded far and wide; small-pox had not been stamped out, and there ought to be re-vaccination.—Mr. LEATHERBARROW suggested that a recommendation go from that Authority.— The CHAIRMAN quite agreed in what had been said by Mr. Chambers. It was a great pity that the recommendation by the clerk was not adopted by the Guardians. He thought a recommendation ought to go from that Authority to the Guardians in favour of notices being posted.—Mr. HALL said he bad been told by a Guardian for Widnes that there was a great deal of truth in the article in the Courier. He believed it was Father Finegan who said that no case had broken out for ten days. Mr. NEWSOME: It was stated by three Guardians. The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said it was only charitable to suppose that those Guardians believed what they had said. He did not believe that Father Finegan or any of the Guardians for Widnes would come and deliberately state there were no new cases of small-pox in Widnes when there was. He then proposed that thae Authority recommend the Guardians to put out the notices with respect to re-vaccination, and sug- gested that this be done not only for Widnes, but for the whole district.—Mr. NEwsoma seconded this proposal.—On the advice of the CLERK, however, this motion WAS with- drawn, and Mr, CHAMBERS undertook to bring the matter before the Board of Guardians as a member of that Board. The meeting then terminated. eeseaneweseeemet•

- - PRESCOT 1.0.G.T.—0n MOndav evening the first public tea and temperance meeting of the Watchman Lodge was held in the Gospel Tent, when upwards of 100 sat and enjoyed an excellent tea, provided by Mr. George Eaton, Present. After tea a public meeting was held in the same place, , Brother G. Whitehead, Esq., of Liverpool, G.W.Co , presi- ding. The chairman addressed the meeting in a lengthy and interesting speech,in which he detailed his experience as a member of the Order since its first introduction into England, and congratulated the Order in most praiseworthy terms on the progress it had made since its establishment in Present. After the conclusion of the chairman's address, a very interesting programme was gone through. A most pleasant and attractive feature was the presence of coloured brethren. Votes of thanks to the chairman and visitors ter- minated a very successful meeting.
TEHPERANCE DE&IONST RATION AT
RUNCORN.

Under the auspices of the United Kingdom Alliance, a public meeting was held in Runcorn Public Hall on Tues- day evening. There was a good audience, and Mr. James Handley, J.P., presiled. There were 4190 on the platform the Revs. C. H. Murray (Preston), J. D. Thomas, S. Mees, E. Williams, J. Pickwei I, Messrs. John Simpson, T. Norman, J. H. Frith, J. Humphreys, A. Randle, G. Bellanny, and J. 1). Jones. The proceedings were commenced by the Rev. S. Mees offering pp prayer.

_ . The Cllitumsx, who was enthusiast'cally greeted, ad- dressed the meeting as follows :—lt would have been a very great satisfaction to me if some one much more worthy and bettel qualified than myself had been chosen to preside over this meeting. I say this in all sincerity, for I look upon the temperance cause as one deserving of the greatest ability obtainable for the advocacy of its claims. I ant glad, however, to tell you that we have on this platform several gentlemen to speak to us who will amply make up for any deiiciency of your chairman. We are delighted to welcome in our midst once again Mr. Raper, whose life has been spent in advocating the claims of temperance, and whose heart, I am sure, must rejoice at the present position to which the temperance cause has attained amongst all classes of his countrymen. If we reflect that it is only just 50 years ago since the seven men signed the teetotal pledges drawn up by Mr. Joseph Livosey, at Preston, that the United King- dom Alliance, of which Mr. Raper is so distinguished a mem- ber, has only been in being for 30 years, and that it is only little more than 10 years since the Christian churches called inte existence definite organisations to assist and help for-
ward the long cortinned—and persistent efforts of the early
temperance —reformers, we must all. feel some measure Of
satisfaction at the prominence which questions connected with the sobriety of the people now occupy in the public _ _ _ .
nand. Our dairy papers just now are filled -With the 'utter-

. . ances of our public men in different places throughout the country, and in some part or other of their speeches we in- variably find allusions to the need of improved legislation for regulating the liquor traffic. I feel that we owe a deep debt of gratitude to those zealous temperance friends who laboured on for so many years with very little encourage-

ment andthel.p from With-out, and the -best atonement we can make for past neglect is to determine to work the harder now; and I am sure they will willingly share with us the glory to which they, and they alone, are entitled, for their self - denying efforts. The time has gone hy for it to be necessary to explain the effect of drinking as being detrimental to the moral well-being of the nation, for public officials all concur in confirming the opinion always held by temperance refor- mers, that the greater part of the crime of the country can be traced to drink. The medical profession, too, now speak out more plainly than formerly, that those who abstain from intoxicating beverages are less liable to several kinds of disease. Sufficient interest has perhaps not been as yet taken with regard to the economical aspect of the temper- ance question. Mr. William Hoyle, of Manchester, has again brought all his great talent to bear on this side of the subject, and has given the result of his investigations in a pamphlet recently issued. I should like to call your attention to a diagram founded on Mr. Hoyle's figures, and which shows in a striking manner the enormous waste of wealth through the drinking customs. What does this diagram tell us? That one million and ifty thousand pounds is the average amount annually raised in the United Kingdom during the last ten years for Christian missions, that for household coals fifteen millions is spent annually, for milk thirty millions, for butter and cheese thirty-five millions, for woollen goods forty-six millions, for the rent of farms sixty millions, for , bread seventy millions, for tea and coffee twenty millions, but for strong drinks of all sorts the amount _ directly spent (besides all spent indirectly), the figures reach the large sum of £136,000,000. These figures represent a sum so enormous that we cannot realize it; but to make it plainer to us Mr. Hoyle supposes that a certain number of men spend £3,000 in drink in the coarse of a year. Some people might say, well, the £3,000 is not lost, it is circu- lated throughout the country and what does it matter how it is spent? But Mr. Hoyle puts it in this way. He sup- poses that these workmen had put their money in a Build- ing Club and built 20 houses. The money would be circu- lated in the country just the same as if spe.at in drink, only in the one case £3,000 would be circulated plus nothing, and in the other C3Se it would be circulated plus 20 houses added to the wealth of the nation. And then look in the ease of the money spent in drink, at the drunkenness, loss of work, misery at home, and all sorts of evils, and in the other case, work found for labourers to build the houses, happiness in families, and comfort in lieu of misery. Mr. Hugh Mason, M.P. for Ashton-under-Lyne, also tells us that if only half the amount were expended in intoxicants, say 70 millions instead of 136 millions, that probably every shuttle and loom and spindle in Lancashire would be work- ing away at their utmost speed for the benefit of the employer and the employed. You will doubtless bays seen references in the daily papers to a pamphlet which has been recently published by the Congregational Union entitle 1, " The bitter cry of outcast London." It is setiefactory to s..e that the issuing of that pamphlet has led enuiriee on all h ands into the condition of the very poor, especially in our large centres of population. I feel sure that the result of these enquiries will lead to the finding out Chet indulgence in drink has had more to d) with the bitter cry then anything &se. In view of the improved legislation regarding the liquor traffic, that we are all so anxiously expecting to be brought before Parliament when it next assemeles, the fact of this bitter cry coming to the front Set.M3 most opportune. Well, to bring these few remarks to a conclusion I should like to urge on all present the adoption of total abstinence, and that we all do what we can in our various spheres to forward the cause of temperance, and thereby to have no part and responsitiility in Satan's most potent fector for evil. If we all engage in this work in the strength of God as Christian men and women, striving by example and by preclit to do His will on the earth, we shall help to hasten on that future sunshine so ex- quisitely described by the prophet, when he says, Gladness shall fill the wildermss and the solitary place, the desert shall rejoice and blossom as the rose. It shall be covered with flowers, and shall leap for joy with songs of mirth and with shouts of triumph. The glory of Lob-anon shall be given to it, the splendoer of Carmel, end of Sharon." (Loud aplause.) The hey. J. 1). Titoetes moved the following resolution: " That recognising the enormous evils inevitably resulting from the traffic in intoxicating liquours, this meeting depre- cates the policy of leealising and supporting such an evil system, and protests against the injustice and cruelty of thrusting it into, or maintaining it within, any parish or district, contrary to the will of the inhabitants of the locality, who are the most deeply affected thereby, and who ought to have an effectual vote for the protection of their homes and families from such a grievous injury and ter- rible wrong." He remarked that he need not say that he heartily sym pethise I with the resolution, and there was ne paint to which he would briefly call their attention ; and that was the traffic in intoxicating liquers. The liquor business stood alone both in its gig antic proportions and in the enormous moral, social, and physical evils which hid resulted from it. Out of 6 600,000 houses in the United 'Kingdom, 180,000 were houses where intrexic sting liquors were sold, being 1 in 36 throughout the entire country. If these licensed houses were Concentrated in one town, they would make a city twice tire size of Manchester; and if they were placed in ono street, they wou'd extend over a dietance of 600 miles,l which would more than reach from Land's End in Cornwall to John O'Groets in North Scotland. Then look at the vast arriay of men and women engaged in this traffic. Reckoning only three persons for each licensed house, which he thought was a moderate calculation, there WAS a total of 330,000 persons engaged in the business, being an army almost three times as large as that which was annu ally voted by the British Parliament for the defence of the British Empire. They were told that in America there were few grog shops to every church, and six barmen to every minister. He thought the proportion was very much the same in the United Kingdom. The capital in- vested in the drink trade in Great Britain alone amounted to £200,000,000. and the amount which was annually spent in the purchase of drink was £127,000,000 or thereabouts. According to one authority there had during the past seven years Ueen spent in Great Britain £937,000,000 for strong drink, and £100,000,000 had been paid for the mischief caused by the drink It had been °lmputed that the sum spent in four years for alcoholic drinks in Great Britain would purchase all the railways in the country, and the sum spent in six years would pay off all the National debt. It was a fact of con- siderable importance that the licensed victualler contributed snore than one half of the annual revenue of the English Government. The sum which was daily rec ived from the aecuried drink traffic by our Government was no less than £lOO,OOO. Was it any wonder, seeing the fabelous wealth expended in the manufacture of drink and the vast army engaged in the sale of it, that the evils resulting therefrom should be sr, enormous. People had gone into the trade with zeal and enthusiasm as if the drink which they supplied were a cure for every evil and woe, whereas they knew that the drink they applied were the occasion and source of more than ohe half of the crime, the poverty, the sickness, the lunacy, the wretched- ness, and the irreligion of the country. Referring to the pamphlets, The bitter cry of outcast London" and "Squalid Liverpool," the seeaker said he had seen a good deal of the wretchedness that existed in some parts of Run- corn, and he did not hesitate to say that it was occasioned chiefly by strong drink. In a museum in the city of Copen- hagen there was a painting which illustrated the evils of strong drink. Over the head of a drunken man there was an owl with candles and spectacles. Owl-like the inebriate was blind, and could use neither candles nor spectacles. Give man the light of education, if he was drunken it would not save him from dishonour and shame; give him the light of the glorious gospel of the Blessed God, if he was drunken it would not show been the way to our Father's house above. (Applause.) The Rev. S. Mans said if there was one thing in our national life about which all right thinking and right feel- ing peonle ought to be united, he thought it was the matter of giving the people of any town or district the power of saying whether there should be any of those places of evil to which that resolution referred. (Hear, hear.) It seemed to him a must appalling thing that public-houses should be forced upon people whether they would or not, and though he had not taken so active and prominent apart in the good work of temperance advocacy as many ministers did it was rather for lack of ability than for want of sympathy. It was a re liter which needed to be alters I by the Legislature, and he hoped that the time was not far distant when the

power be establish or take away drink shops should be put into the bands of the people. (Hear, bear, and applause.) The Rev. C. H. MURRAY, in supporting the resolution said it was affirmed on behalf of the publicans that the; were as respectable as any ether class of tradesmen, but tke question was not as to the character of the publican, but as to the sort of work they did. (Applause.) It did not matter where they made the inquiries, whether of the judges, magistrates, or missionaries of the country, they would find the same testimony, that the effects of the driak traffic were evil, and that continually. Mr. Murray, referring to the , difficult position of magistrates in regard to the liceneing question, said Mr. Handley was honoured by presiding over such a meeting. He concluded by rem irkeag that the national Parlianaent which had swept away great evils which had afilicted the nation in days past, hid tne virtue and the power to fight down the evil of the drink traffic, and now was the time to do it. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN observed that he had heard Mr. Clarke .Sspinall, the coroner for the city of Liverpool, say, some time ago, that he,. as a magistrate, would be clad if the power of issuing licenses was taken out of his halide for they were the most unsatisfactory laws hell id to adminieter. He (Mr. Handley) fancied that that was the feeling of most magistrates. He had not had much experience himself on the magisterial bmch—in fact, none in connection with liceneing—but he was sure that the m teietrates in many in- stances would like to consult the wishes of the residents of the localities, and that was all the Alliance wanted to bring into law. The motion was then carried unanimously. Mr. J. R. Fiarra said however much they might desire to assist their London friends in obtaining for themselves proper government, they. as temperance advocates, con- sidered that the law which would kenetit their fellow-man morally and spiritually should take precedence of every other measure. (Hear, hear.) A gen leman had recently taken exception to teetotal magistrates sitting on the licens- ing bench. He hoped their chairman would some day sit on the licensing bench—(applause)—ind that he may use his influence in assisting those who desired to set the work. ing men and everybody else removed front the thraldom of the drink traffic and assisted to that which was honourable and right. (Hear, bear, and applause.) He begged to move "That this meeting congratulates the friends of temper. ance, and of social, moral, and religioue pr•igress, on the acceptance by Government of the • Loci!. Option resolution' of Sir Wilfrid Lawson, as a basis for esirly and efficient legislation, so urgently required in the best interests of the nation. The meeting, however, deplored the subsequent in- action of the Government, and records its conviction that whatever may be the future constiertion of the licensing authority, any legislation to be satisfacLory must include clauses empowering the inhabitants of parishes and dietricts to exercise a direct popular veto upon the issue or renewal of licenses for the sale of intoxicating liqaors within their boundaries, and hereby calla upon the Cabinet no longer to delay, but at the earliest moment in the next session to in- troduce a measure including such clauses." The Rev. E. Wtemaats formally seconded the resolution. Mr. H. RAPER, vice-president of the Alliance. was loudly applauded on rising to support the motion. After a few humourous sentences, he remarked that the meeting was not a teetotallers' meeting but a citizsne meeting, for that resolution appealed for the support of cities's of every de.. scription. The whole thing turned upon the question whether intoxicating liquors were I.a2neficial or injurious, .and he quoted the evidence of such eminent men as Dr. Gull, Dr. Richardson. Sir Henry Theinson, Dr. W. B. Car- penter, and others to show that the injurious effects alco- holic liquors had upon the physical frame. Dr. Richardson had stated that it the English people were sober their longevity would be increased by one-third, and this opinion was unmistakably confirmed by the statistics issued by as- surance societies. The question of giving the people a direct popular veto over the granting of licenses was a very serious one, and a great man hart tried to deal with it. He referred to Mr. John Bright. (Loud applause.) He (the speaker) had not one word to sty a.;aiust his proposals, which he had taken from Hansard, they having originated from Lord John Russell, who embodied them in a bill which successfully passed the Rouse of Commons, but which was rejected in the House or Lords. Temperance reformers, without putting themselves in direct opposition to any plan Government might have in hand for establishing a licensing authority, could only express the opinion that they would not be satisfied until alongside that licensing autherity whatever it might be, there should be direct popular veto given into the hands of the people. The speaker pointed out that the people already had this control in other matters. A town council, a board of commissioners, ot a local board conld not undertake any scheme involving an expenditure of a certain amount of money without first consulting the ratepayers in public meeting, and if there was one dissentient, who demanded a poll of the whole of the inhabitants of a town or district, a poll must be taken. The Manchester Corporation formula- ted a scheme to purchase Thirlinere lake with which to sup- ply the city with water. It was submitted to the ratepayers, and 62 thousand voted in favour of the water scheme. He suggested that Parliament should take that machinery as it stood—they did not ask for any alteration. If it answered for the purpose of finding out whether the people wanted water it would act equ illy well in finding out whether the people wanted whiskey. (Loud laughter and applause.) At considerable length Mr. Raper described the provisions of the licensing bill which had recently been passed by the Canadian Legislature, and which will come into force on the first of January next. The Act placed licensing matters in the hands of commis- sioners. There were three commissioners for each licensing district. One of thes.e men was to be county court judge for the district, another the mayor of the city, or the head of the governing body, and the third elected by local go- vernment. The Act provided that there should be four licensed houses for the irst 1,000 inhabitants, and one for each 500 afterwards, so that a town of 11,000 inhabitants would have 24 public-houses. But this was the maximum number, which the commissioners could reduce, but not in- crease. A man who had not obtained the signature of at least one-third of the ratepayers in his neighbourhood had no locus standi before the licensing commission—he could not apply forts license. One clause provided that if one- fifth of' the electors demanded a poll it must be taken, and if three-fifths voted that they did not want a licensed house, henceforth that district would be clear from tine sale of in- intoxicating liquors. Her Majesty had given her consefit to this—it was constitutional—and they in Runcorn that night were attempting to alter the British Constitution with regard to the liquor traffic. Speaking of the difficulties of the Government, Mr. Raper said they could not force

this question. They could not have a row in Hyde Park, or shoot landlords—(laughter)—public or ether land- lords; but they could cry aloud and spare not. The assizes were going on now. How eloquent they were. Could they read the newspapers day by day without feeling that they had the favour of the Almighty on the temperance question In gaol there lay a man to be executed in Manchester, on Monday next, for the Preston murder. The men committed the crime when he was drunk—one more victim to a system in which they and he (Mr. Raper) were partners ; and when he heard the Chancellor of the Exchequer give his statement in April next, and state how much he had re- ceived from the drink traffic, he should not forget how many murders were involved in that terrrible list. They had much to answer for. Let them try to do their duty, and unite with one another to secure the parishes of the country from the dreadful traffic which was so baneful in its effects. (Applause.) The motion was carried. Mr. HUMPHREYS moved, and Mr. J. D. JONES seconded, the following resolution, speaking in complimentary terms of the Chairman :—" That the best thanks of the meeting be given to the Chairman for his services in the chair ; and that he be requested t. send written copies of the foregoing resolutions, on behalf of the meeting, to the Prime Minister and the Home Secretary, and also to each of the members of Parliament for the borough and county." The motion was carried with acclamation, and the Chair- man having replied the meeting concluded.

div.head: "Letter to the editor.
div.p: "Letter to the editor.
" ANGLO SCOTUS " IGA,IN.

roe the Newtonians have been coursing the hare on the land near thaf,Lunatic Asylum from which one of the inmates eecoe el the last time I visited Newton, and did his level best to wake me out of a sound sleep, until he was tackled by a `Tenant police constable and as tenderly and hu- manely as possible conveyed back to his quarters. Can you spare me, for the sake of the young people, space for a little literary coursing of "the timid animal ?.' The domains I hunt are Persia, and the new and complete edition of " Krilof and his fables," by Mr. W. R. S. Ralston, and my chief bag er quarry is the story of "The Hare at the Chase." Having united in full fore..., the beasts captured a War. They strangled it in the open, and then .began to settle among themselves what part each of them should get as his or her share. But at .this po:nt the hare, forsooth, suddenly appears and clutches the tear's ear. " Hallo, you squinter there !" they shout at puss. " Where on earth have you ceme from ? No one Lae seen you during the chaee." "Really, now," answered the hare, "and who WAS it, if you please, who drove the bear out of the wood? Didn't I frighten him entirely, and drive-him, this dear friend of ours, right afield to you ?" Such brag- ging was somewhat too palpable, it is true; but it had such an amusing air about it,that the hare was presented with a morsel of the bear's ear. Omar Khayyam, the Persian pact, who died in the year 517 lat., in his Clst quatrain, Ups : Men's lusts, like house-dogs, still the house distress With elarzeur, barking for mere wantonness; ' Foxes are they, and sleep the sleep of hares; Crafty as -wolves, as t!.,/,ers pitiless." I wonder how many Londoners even are aware of the fact that the district of Soho derives its name from the cry "So hoe !" used in olden times in hunting the hare. The site of the densely populated district was at one time the "fickle where my Lord Mayor and hit friends used to corns and hunt the hare afore dinner," and al-co where, if time and inclina- tion permitted, "after dinner they went a hunting the fox." The Duke of Monmouth (theelt:iag's son by Lucy Walton, who lived in Moninoeeth House-.-built on the south side of Soho Square by Wren) also chose " So hoe !" as his watch- word or war cry on the battle feld of Sedgemoor. The last- named event occurred in 16235, and resulted in defeat, flight, hunger, the shelter of a ditch, and death at the hands of the headsman, for the " natural " who rose in rebellion against his king. Who can say what will happen in or before 1685 to the fortunes of a certain scheme or speculation established and conducted against the rules of nature or the dictates of humanity? As people just now are having a hearty laugh at the es- capade of the jokists who so cleverly managed to smuggle the waggon-load of mutton into the Lord Mayor's procession, and as pantomime time is again coming on, it may interest elder Newtonians to harn that in my Lreeide wanderings I recently came across a record of the person who dug out from antiquity Noah's rabbit hutch and its peculiarly ?shaped in .mate, an account of both of which my jocular friend "Newtonian" published in the Examiner. He belonged to an aesociation formally constituted by Charles II on the 22nd April, 1662, under the title of "The President, Council, and Fellows of the Royal Society of London for the Inaprovement of Fatural Knowledge." Quaint and creduloue were many of the inquiries of these old philosophers. On one occasion they wrote to aek one of their fere'gn correspondents "if it were true that dia- monds grew again where they were digged out; "again, as "to what river in Java tartar; wood into stone ? " 1 hey pre- served in their museum "a .one taken out of a merm iid'e, head," and issued reports of "a mountain cabbage three hula, dred feet high." Charles II was amused by their vagaries, and Butler thus bits off the attempts of the society : To mseinre wind and weigh the air, To tn,n a circ'e 'o a square, And in the braying of an ass Ft • d out the treble and the buss, It mates nelp,h alto, and a cow In doub'e diapas n low: Butler especially satirises Wilkins, afterwards Bishop of Chester, who believed that not only was a new world to be discovered in the moon, but that it amuld or could be reached by flying machines. In this last connection a witty lady—(the ladies will be in it, you see)—once asked him hew "he would contrive to bait upon the road." The society for a time hang out at Gresham College, which then stood on the site of the present Royal Fxchange. To such men a " short-eared and long-tailed rabbit" would be no novelty. Leaving the quadrupedal for the bipedal connec- tion, what will readers of the Examiner sty to the follow- ing, taken from the Army and Navy GFette:—Among the cases of wounds received in Egypt and recorded in the late report of the Army Medical Department, one of the most re- markable is that of Private Robert Gaw, of the Scots Guards. This marvellously hard-headed man was shot in the side of the head -t Tel-el-Kehir. He fell stunned, but soon recovered euffieSently to double after his regiment. The bullet fractured his skull, but the edge of the broken bone Cut the bullet almost in two. In March last, the firmly- imbedded mass of lead was extracted with some difficulty. The use of chloroform WAS offered, but declined, with thanks we presume. Grew bore the operation well, "and was greatly pleased with the result." After this we should hear no more about gimlets in connection with jokes and the heads of Scotchmen. What does it matter if you do now and again fail to see or catch the point of a far-fetched or forced attempt at " wut," if you are possessed of a cranium not cnly thick enough to resist the impact or penetrating force of a modern rifle bullet, but capable of repelling the would-be deadly missile flattened or bisected? There is, indeed, much virtue in oatmeal.—l remain, sir, ice. ANGLO-SCOTUS. Newington, London, November 17,183.

THE TRADE INTERESTS OF ENGLAND. Sir,—Many unfair laws have from time to time been repealed in our country, and doubtless posterity will alter much which is at present allowed. One of the laws likely to be altered will be that respecting unfair trade. The steady decline of our industries pro rata with the increase of population, the constant loss of home orders by our manufacturers, and consequent loss of employment and wages by our workmen, will demand in the near future an inquiry into our present Free Trade policy. Already there appears to be a desire in certain directions to avoid the Free Trade question, and this of itself is a sign of weakness; cir- cumstances will, however, at length force the question upon our legislators. Let us hope it may not then be too late. Is it not already a most startling fact that England, with her boasted Free Trade policy, is compelled to say to her people, Clear out, emigrate, the land of your birth can no longer find you with employment; whereas protected Americi, a country directly opposed to our Free Trade ideas, should be, not only able to support her own people, but positively be able to find remunerative employment for thousands upon thousands of our countrymen who are no longer able to find it at home? We had every advantage to begin with; how then can we account for the dlference, seeing that America is now crowded with manufacturing as well as agricultural industry ?i Simply because America protects or defends itself, whereas England lays herself open to the manufac- turing attack of all nations. British energy and ingenuity have striven hard to uphold our position, and England's best thanks are due to the discoverer of steam power, an agency which has so wonderfully assisted her manufacturers and. promoted her interests even in the face of an adverse policy. What really do we gain by our Free Trade policy? Can it be shown that we gain anything ? Our Govern- ment appear to require nearly ninety millions sterling annually from us, and they at present collect this partly by a duty upon fool imports, such as tea, coffee, cocoa, &c. (manufactured articles being allowed to come into our country duty free), the balance being made up by internal taxation upon beer, incomes, and a whole bast. of other things. We pay the money now, and we could only pay the same required amount if foreign manufactured articles con- tributed to the revenue; whereas there would be a great benefit in giving home orders to our own manufacturers and employment to our workmen, thereby securing the labaue, which is the principal value in a;1 manufactured articles, to our own country.—The rnanufac'uring success of other countries during the past ten years ought to prove a lesson to us. We never really encountered opposition before; therefore our Free Trade policy had never been subjected to a practical test. Manufacturers can ilow tell how miser- ably this policy has failed in upholding onr position. The one misfortune of our country is that we have too many persons who are mere t'leorists, yet who have the audacity to place their theoretical ideas against the practical experience of iron and other manufactur, rs. A few manufacturers in each manufacturing town supply weekly almost all the money circulated in the town—they are as it were anchored to the soil ; have they not then a prior right to consideration? One thing, however, is cer- tain: if bricks and machinery could be turned back again into sovereigns, manufacturers would soon be few, and leave the country as a huniing ground to the foreign manufac- turer. Very much has lately been said and written respect- the cornlawn . of the poor, but it is because our working population have so little employment and indifferent pay that the majority are poor, and the principal cause for this is foreign competition. Whilst poverty lasts crime will sever cease— " For Satan finds some m'schief still For idle hands to do."

; There are, howevel., always a certain number of persons I preaching universal philanthropy, and willing to lay claim to some uegro or Indian brotherhood -because these happen to be in a distant land.; but these same individuals appear \to forget that they have many fellow-countrymen dragging on a miserable existence within a mile from their own doors; , and to whom constant employment would prove the very I greatest blessing. This blessing •crtn, however, only be ob- tained by patronisin; our own industries and minufactured articles, and this Would be more effectually done by en- couragement given from our own Government in favour of I our own manufacturers. Failing this; British workmen have the power to demand a true representation of their interests. Let them ask each Parliamentary candidate, Will you pledge yourself to inquire into the• Free Trade policy of the country, which is at present robbing the British workmen of employment, and is really the true cause of so much poverty? —Yours faithfully, S. LAWRENSON. Warrington, Nov. /6th.

Sir,—Under the above heading Mr. Lawrenson is :seeking once more to revivify that dead and gone fallacy, protection. In your own paper it was that I first noticed one of his effusions. Since then the gentleman has dealt with the question at greater length-in one of the evening papers. Now, I am not going to inflice upon your readers any long des- sertetion of my own. Free Trade versus Fair Trade litera- ture has during the past two or three years been spread broadcast over the country, and I should think it has been extensively read, judging from the incliCerence shown by the people towards this particular question. Mr. Lawrenson says that "British m inefectures cannot compete at the price foreigners sell at," for the following amon4st other reasons:—" Owing to the natural increase of population house rents have advanced ; nearly all farm Produce are dearer than they were twenty years ago. We tax tea, coffee, cocoa, and fruit." Now, woulc) anyone believe it ? The above are given as reasons viby we cannot compete with the foreigner, and we are ceolly requested to remit these very neceesary duties, and place the tax upon manufactured articles coming into this country. Sir, I should like our friend to be a little mere precise. What would he tax ? And when he has accemplished this difficult feat, how will it benefit the working men? Our fair trading friende are so much in the habit of bandying about the words "import and export" that I fear they must have mistaken their real meaning. If not, for political purposes they must be thrown as dust in the eyes of the ignorant. Now, Mr. Lawrenson is engaged by a firm who roll their own rods, rods differing very much in (quality from German rods. His- iirm fails to secure orders for drawn wire; the cause for this is because German wire is allowed to come here untaxed. Mind, I argue this from the tone of Mr. Lawrenson'b letters. Will he kindly say, in as plain words as possible, how much nearer we should be in securing foreign orders supposing we were to tax all German iron coming into this country. Believe me, as a British workman, I am much interested in this question as a Radical politician I wish to get at the root of the evil, but I cannot understand fair traders. One calls for protection against the German iron manufacturers, another would lay 103. per quarter on imported corn, keep out foreign cattle cries another; sethat if these gentry could pick and choose just as they liked we should have taxes levied on all our importations just to suit their separate in- terests. I grant that protection may be needed at times, but it can only be in the eases where individuals wish to injure -the public at large. We must protect even protectionists against themselves. Out of every four loaves eaten in this ccuntry three come from abroad; would it be better for the people that the three fshesild be taxed in order that the grower of the fourth should he enabled to pay an increased rent to a grasping landlord? Mr. Hermon would impose a tax on imparted cotton, thereby increasing the price of the manu- factured article. In the .event of him being successful in his elcerts to impose this tax, how would oar manufacturers succeee, in obtaining orderc, seeing that their goods would be increased in price to the extent of the tax imposed? "Oh," Mr. Lawrenson may zay, "I am not interested in these various branches of leteeiness." Perhaps' be may trot out the import and export question; or, what is more likely, he may insist upon keeping to the iron wire question. Well, by all meln-:, let us settle this. Is protection right in prin- ciple? Would it be good for ;es, as a people, all round? Suppose we lcok at the patent steel wire trade; here is an article produced that is hemmed in on every side by protec- tion, The concequence is that the eeensumer has to pay a fancy price for his goods; hence it follows that the con- sumption is very limited, and during the last twenty years the workmen engaged in that trade must have walked about the streets ten years of the time. Now, suppose no monopoly had existed, the public would have had the benefit of a cheaper and superior article, and to that extent would have benefited. This country has had a monopoly in the markets of the world. This has ceased to exist, and we have made no preparation for such a atate of things. Hampered by a Conservative King Log, we are prevented from making the best uses of our natural resources. First, as Mr. Lawrenson says the population question has something to do with this point, I ask him to circulate the pamph'et on "The Population Question ;" second, make the land yield to the nation's requirements its full tribute; third, deprive the railway and canal companies of their re- atrictive monopolies, and what goes to individual prosperity deeote to a nation's welfare. How can we have trade when it costs £2 a ton for goods from Sheffield to London, the same being sent from London to Melbourne for 15s. per ton. Allow me, in conclusion, to put my question as clear as possible to Mr. Lawrenson. Suppose we tax German im- ports, how will that enable British manufacturers to obtain foreign orders? keeping in mind that tkousands of pounds worth of drawn wire is yearly imported into Warrington, then worked up, and exported with a profit to Warrington manufacturers. H. WHITHAM. Warrington, Oct. 1383.
