div.head: EXAMTNEP, SATTTPTYkY, NOVEMBER 94, 1883
div.p: THE EXAMTNEP, SATTTPTYkY, NOVEMBER 94, 1883

The Comtesse, an Irishwoman, having first apologised for the Comte's indifferent English, and his desire she should speak for him, then in warm, almost impassioned language, welcomed Major Etheredge and his followers. She then, inviting the former and the officers into the hall, again spoke with emotion of the great relief their coming was to them, adding in calmer language an explanation. The peasantry had turned against them, through quarrels with their agents about payment of rent; laad driven their horses and many of their servants away, and had not only refused to bring food or other necessaries, but had actually threatened the servants of their tradesmen, so that for sotse days they had been in all but actual want. To complete their troubles a band of men, supposed to be Fenians, had come, only two days ago, forced their way into the castle, and though they were respectful in manner, had taken away all the arms and provisions in store they could find.
In sympathetic response, Major Etheredge told briefly his recent experience ' - which, no doubt, was with the same body of men who had mile this in-road on the castle.

What was to be done with so little rood in the place, and so many half-starved, chilled, and wounded men waiting and hoping for meat, drink, and shelter? Thc Comte and Comtesse took counsel together, and at the end the latter said, with a sad but sweet smile, to the Major— 'l think we can manage for yourself and a score of others some bread and cheese, and what you please to drink or smoke, here in the hall. As to those outside, whom we cannot b2tter entertain, they shall have a little whiskey and tobacco for each man, It is humiliating to confess it, but this is all we can do for these brave men, for it is all we have for ourselves."

Of course, the Major was touched and grateful. "You can use the stable," she continued, "to put your borses and men in—these and the outhouses are all at your service. Perhaps the thy ma v come when this unhappy country, myown dear Ireland, shall be at re,st, and then we should covet the opportunity to treat you all in a manner more wormy of you and ourselves." And so matttrs were arranged. The Major and other officers, the non-commissioned officers, and the wounded men, were entertained in the halt; the rest Lad to shift as they could in the pieces designated, where they soon made themselves comfortable, many of them affirming that to- bacco and whiskey were not after all each bad meat and drink, when nothing else was to be got. The hall was very large, and contained some fine suits of armour, which caused 6tephen to amuse himself with a comparison between the warriors of the day represented by this armour, and the warriors who were now face to face with them, but thinking: only how cold it was, and wondering how long the bread and cheese would be in coming. The domestics lighted great thee la Lie magnificent fire- places; and brought chairs and seats of all kinds, some of which the soldiers used to dry their'damp clothing. • The Comtesse arranged for the Major and the officers to be seated at a table apart, where she anti her husband waited upon them with all the stately and graceful courtesy of the land in which she had married and spent a great part of her life—France. The pleasant and hospitable things she said were made more sweet by the accent—surely one the most charming to be found in the whole world, when issuing from the lips of a refined lady, a sweet-voiced and comely woman—and all these were combined in the hostess.

Then she left them to the care of her husband, who managed to keep up a broken sort of conversation, while :she addressed herself to see if the wounded wasted any- thing that was possible to give them under present cir- cumstances. They were all, however, glad to leave things alone till they should get where proper help could be ren- dered, being in the meantime not badly daetered by a couple of old sergeants who had gained a little reputation in that way, and rather liked to be called on. While these things were in progress, Stephen, who . . . . .
was busily drying his clothes by one a the haff-lit. fires, noticed among the attendants a grey-haired, keen vis- aged man bustling about with a bundle of faggots for the Ares.

Something in his face and air suggested to Stephen he was not an ordinary servant, and then from his dress and bearing he judged him to be an old soldier, who had turned gardener or something of that sort, possibly with his former master.

Still the man was of no particular interest to him; and it was only from the fact that the scene gave the smallest incident a value and importance, that his eyes followed hide in preference to any of the other figures moving about when once the Comtesse had withdrawn to send in the promised. food. 'The person in question came up to the fire where Stephen was—looked at him, and then gave a second and peculiarly scrutinizing look before putting. his wood in the fire, stoop- ing onlis knees to make a blow pipe of his hands, and then gradually kindling the fresh wood, which began to blaze and brighten all around and near. "That's nice!" remarked Stephen to him, as he drew eloser, holding out his palms to enjoy the cosy warmth. "It makes one forget the outside we came from, and must soon go back to !" "Like a bit of tobacco, young fellow, while the grab comes ?" asked the man, with a humorous smile, as if con- scious of a soldier's weak points. "Well, old fellow, I really think I should," answered Stephen, with a lauel, as the supposed gardener took out a goodly roll and handed it to Stephen. "There, smoke away! The Corntesse won't mind. The others be at it as soon as they have settled their stomachs with sometbiug more substantial." The attendant now came in with the bread and cheese, and the whiskey, both in sufficient supply, while smething extra had been managed for the officers' table, which they ate with great relish. "Shall I fetch you something to go on with '1" asked Stephen's new acquaintance, "and so save time in waiting for your turn ?" "Well, upon my word, you are the )Inest old fellow I ever did rneet with—nnder such circumstances—and I don't mind confessing I am horribly hungry." "I thought so. You look so." Off he went to the far end of the hall where the bread and cheese was being put up into rations, and the whiskey poured out into tumblers so that water might be put to it or not as the drinkers pleased. Taking one of the rations, a tumbler with whiskey, and a bottle of water he came back, gave them to Stephen, and squatted down on the hearth in the absence of a convenient ehair, and seemed to take pleasure in watching Stephen's enjoyment of the food." "A Corporal, I see," was his next remark during a pause between the eating and drinking. "Expecting to be Ser- geant ?" "Of course; then sergeant-major, then quarter-master then a commission as ensign, and then right slick away, as the American's remark, to be a general, and so to the top of the tree as commander-in-chief. .If I make any mistake as to the sequence of the steps in advance, doubtless you can set me right. The quarter-master step, for instave, does, I believe, precede the general step, and certainly the final resting place as commander-in-chief ?" Was Stephen amusing himself with satirising the curiosity of his entertainer, or simply indulging himself with a bit of fun which might draw the latter out? That question might almost have been read in the face of the " old fellow "as he again closely sertetinised the face of the "young fellow.' But the only comment he made was that as far as he knew the quarter-master step did pre- cede that to the generalship. But the tone was so like Stephen's own,., one so com- pounded of latent humour, and a pretence of simple igno- rance and ingenuous deeire to learn that Stephen began to suspect he was making an ass of himself, in the presence of one quite capable of seeing that truth. He looked at the old fellow for a moment with feigned seriousness, as if to convince him he had meant all he said ; but presently bursting out into loud laughter, as he added "Old fellow, I'm no such fool. I mind what Shakespeare says about vaulting ambition o'erleaping its sell, that means its saddle, you know, or don't know, and so I shall be content to take the good the gods provide." "Are you a gentleman ?" "As a soldier I should be sorry to be thought other- wise." "Are you a gentleman ?" again asked the old fellow. " Are you ?" demanded Stephen, thinking simply to throw back a question that it was inconvenient to answer, and which might be tio replied to as to help him to put an end to the query. "Well, I'm somewhat of your faith. I'm but a sort of helper here at present, but I don't know that that should prevent me from playing the gentleman." "Exactly my case, so let's say no more about it. Humble fellows as we are, we'll both stand up for the right to be esteemed gentlemen if insolently challenged." The old fellow's eyes sparkled as he heard this, but he made no remark on it. Would you like to stretch your legs for a bit ?" "Very much, in your society." "Come, then." They wen': out into the courtyard, crossed it, and stopped at the only deor that had not been opened to the soldiers. This the old fellow unlocked, and they entered. Stephen could not guess for what all the place had been destined. It was empty, dirty, and strewed with brorren bottles, broken boxes, empty cans, torn paper covers, and a heterogeneous mass of rubbish. Seeing his wonder, the old fellow said to him— "This is where we kept a large supply of stores for the winter, which the Fenians broke up and cleared out for us; but they, too, played the gentleman, and robbed us with admirable grace. Follow me !' He opened a door, and they ascended a staircase to an upper storey, where the long room was filled with bins and cases, the former for wines and reams, the latter for to- bacco and cigars of all kinds, as he at once explained to Stephen. "All empty now ?" said Stephen. "All nearly full !" was the reply. " What! the Fenians left all this ?" "Ay, d—n them, they were much too clever to be caught that way. I left the door below open especially for their accommodation. But when I bad occasion to come in, for they ordered me about in right royal style, and it suited my humour to obey fresh ma:ters for the time, I found a couple of men standing just vhere you and I are now standing, with nvolvers in their hands, rr•nated to shoot down any of their own kidney who shot:, • Awe up in hope of a. grand haul. . . . .
" Really !" ejaculated Stephen, at this new trait of the enemy.
"Well, now, you shall have what you like."
" I say, old fellow, you must have a pretty goodiplace here, to be trusted with the key of these treasures, and to be entitled to offer them to a new comer like me."

" Oh, the place is well enough. It suits me. But what will you have ?" " Thank you. I went nothing here, unless you think it will be no robbery, to give another roll of your master 's tobacco, for a corporal's pay doesn't, I fad, teem with in- dulgences."
"-But wouldn't you like to taste. I expected a young !ellow like you would have been too glad to run riot a bit."
• "Then you, as an old fellow, ought to be ashamed to say so; or, at least, ought t') be asham,d to tempt me, a young fellow, if that was really your object, which, after all, I begin to doubt."
These last words were due to a strangely significant smile in the "old fellow's " face; who did not in the least appear offended by the reproof, but rather dwelt on it with enjoy- ment.

"We'll go back now," be said. And they returned to the hail; where, as Stephen went one way to regain his place, he found his companion had taken the other to meet a soldier servant who was advancing tows., ds him. There was an odd mixture of respect and awkward familiarity, Stephen thought, in this man's behaviour to the old fellow; which suggested for the first time the possibility of some awkward mistake as to ?he vocation and social rank of his acquaintance, who, after speaking to the soldier, left the hall.
Getting near to the soldier, Stephen said, " May I ask who that is you have just Wen talking to r " WI;o ? Why, don't you know ?" "No."

"Has he been lalking to you ?" "Yes, and so familiarly, that when he called me young fellow, I was not at all offended, but saluted him as ' Old fellow ' in return. I hope I haven't made a mess,ef it!"
" Ob, he likes that sort of thing when it conv.a fresh ani genuine."
"But who is he?"

"A retired Colonel of the Life Guards," replied the soldier, mentioning a well-known and highly-esteemed °nicer, on the staff of the Commander-in-Chief, aud•balieved to be use of his special favourites. _

Steptien could only .express his feelings irt a prolonged whistle—followed by a succession of short laughs, and broken elaculatiuns, which greatly amused the Colonel's servant, and who proceeded to reassure. Stephen by sayiwg, "Keep it up if he speaks to you again while here, but mind never.rentember it afterwards. He is not simply here as the brother of the Corntesse, but an possible business that makes him wish to be unknown—or if known unrecog- nised."

"Thanks, I understand. As to keeping it up, that's all very fine, but---" Here the soldier saw his master re-entering, and made a hurried movement to avoid being seen with Stephen. The "Old fellow" approached Stephen with the same mien and familiar manner as before, trisay to him— "Do you know wherelrou are going when you leave here —presently ?" "No," answered Stephen, trying to "keep it up" by tone and manner, but unable to control a growing sentiment of respect and deference which he felt, and which told the Colonel's quick eve—he was known. He spoke, however, and behaved exactly as before, and Stephen's instinct warned him to follow his guidance. "Well, the Comtesse has a friend a few miles off, the owner of some fine estates in this country as well as in England. Did you ever bear of the Barr of Harlax- ton ?" "Yes," said Stephen, after ieemingly thoughtful delibera- tion.

-" Well, the Earl has come here with his mother, and a' young relative, to spend his Christmas among the tenantry; and finds himself very much in the same straits as ourselves, with the exception that his robbing has yet to be done. And he doesn't at all incline to the idea of letting it be done."
"I don't wonder at that," said Stephen with a faint smile but scarcely trusting himself to speak, so great was the emotion the news had excited.

"He has sent for soldiers, but sending for them at this time doesn't exactly mean as a consequence their coming. So the Cemtesse has spoken to the Major, who has accepted the mission to go there; for, as he sagely remarked, if Fenians were expected, he should be delighted to have tke duty of properly welcoming them." Not one casual look, not oae doubtful tone, or a single peculiarity of expression on the 2olonei's filed intimated to Stephen that he also was known to the Colonel, as the Colonel was known to him.

Yet if the subject, and its being so directed at him, was all accidental and a mere recurrenca to the familiar confi- dences that had marked their brief intimacy, what an extra- ordinary accident! He, was confounded, knew not what to believe, and still pass was able to find anything appropri- ate to say. He was soon relieved on the latter score. The "old fel- low" did not wait for any kind of answer or comment, but went his way.
But only-to appear again presently at the hall do3r as the soldiers passed out to wish them "Good bye;" and to give to each man a rather formidable roll of tobacco from a basket on his arm.

When it Came to Stephen's turn, he too received the roll of tobacco. But instead of saying, " Good-bye, old fellow; I only wish I may come across you again some day, if I should be again as hard put to it, for something to eat, and drink, and smoke ;" as he pro- bably would have done if he could have "kept it up," in spite of his recent discovery, and still more recent fear ilia, he himself was known—he not only forgot the parting words he had shaped cut, but not knowing what he was doing, he put out his hand for the tobacco, his share of which he had already received, and dropped into a pocket. There was the slightest possible pause, then the Colonel took what he supposed to be the proffered hand, gave it a hearty squeeze, dropped it, and turned to the next comer, without one word; or any subsequent sign of interest in Stephen's departure. (To be continued.)
ACTION BY THE ST. HELENS
CORPORATION.

In the Quen's Bench Division, on Tuesday, the case of the Mayor, &c., of St. Helens v. St. Helens Colliery Corn- pany, Limited, came before Mr. Justice Day and Mr. Jus- tice A. L. Smith, sitting as a divisional court, in the shape of a special case. The point raised for the opinion of the court was whether the defendants were exempted from pay- ing a certain rate. According to the special case, on the sth of March, 1868, the inhabitants of the town of St. Helens and of the districts of Sutton and Parr, and all parts of the tranships of Windle, Eccleston, contiguous to St. Helens, were incorporated by the title of the mayor, alder- men, and burgesses of the town of St. Helens. By the 351st section of the St. Helens Improvement Act, 1869, it is provided that "the borough rate tql,:11 no: lit the aggregate exceed in any one year the sum of is. in the pound on the yearly rateable value of the property rateable thereto without the consent of the ratepayers as next hereinafter provided." Section 352 enacted that "if at any time the amount of the borough rate by this Act authorised be in- sufficient for the purposes thereof, the Corporation may, with the consent of a majority of the persons liable to be rated thereto present at a meeting convened for that purpose by the Corporation, increase such rate above the amount by this Act limited, such meeting to be held after foarteen days' notice given by the Corporation of their intention to propose an increase in such rate, and of the amount of the proposed increase, provided that no such increase shall be leviable upon the owner or occupier of any coal mine in respect thereof, or upon any person assessable in the pro- portion of one-fourth annually of any rate other than the highway rate in respect of his property or the premises oc- cupied by him. 'Die 227th section of the Public Health Act enacts that "any limit imposed on or in respect of any rate by any local Act of Par- liament shalt not apply to any rate required to be levied for the purpose of defraying any expenses incur- red by the urban authority in the execution of this act." The plaintiffs contended that a shilling rate was insufficient to defray the expenses charged on the borough fund, in- cluding the expenses incurred by the Corporation in the execution of the Public Health:Act; that the 227th section of the Public Health Act abolished the limit which had been inserted in the defendants' favour in the 352nd section of the local actS and that in order to meet the several expenses chargeable on the borough fund, the Corporation had been compelled to levy a rate of Is 6d. The defendants contended that under the 352nd section of the St. Helens Improvement Act they were exempted from paving a rate in excess of a shilling in the pound, and that they had paid £278 12s, being one shilling in the pound. The plaintiffs then brought an action to recover the balance—Ll39 6s— and it was agreed that the action should be tried in the shape of a special case.—Mr. Charles, Q.C., and Mr. Fitz- gerald appeared for the plaintiffs, while Mr. Bighorn, Q.C., and Mr. Swift represented the defendants.—Mr. Charles, in support of the plaintiffs' case, submitted that the 227th section of the Public Health Act abolished the exemption contained in the 352nd section of the local Act of 1869, and that therefore the defendants were liable to pay a rate in excess of a shilling in the pound, if the excess was necessary to carry cut the provisions of the Public Health Act.—Mr. Bingham, on behalf of the defen- dants, contended that the 227th section of the Public Health Act did not abolish the provision in the local Act of 1869, which exempted his clients from paying a rate in excess of Is. in the pound. The effect of the 352nd section of the Act of 1869 was that although it might be proper to exceed is. in the pound, yet collieries were all to be exempt from payment of any rate above that amount. The learned counsel cited several cases in favour of his argument.—Mr. Justice Day held that the 227th section of the Public Health Act abolished the exemption contained in the 352nd section of the local Act, so far as the provisions of the former Act were concerned. The defendants were ex- empted from paying a rate in excess of a shilling in the pound for borough purposes, but they were liable to pay an additional rate for carrying out the provisions of the Public Health Act. He therefore gave judgment for the plaintiffs with costs.—Mr. Justice A. L. Smith con- curred.

THE LOW FON MURDER, ACQUIPTAL OF GIBBONS. At the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday—before Mr. Justice Derma an—John Gibbons, 24; labourer, was charged with the wilfulemurder of his uncle, Joshua Rigby, 73 years of age, at Lowton, near Leigh, on the 13th September last.—The prisoner pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Shee and Mr. Lowther ap- peered to prosecute ; and the prisoner was defended by Mr. Addison, QC., and Mr. Wharton. Mr. Shee, in opening the case for the prosccution, said thug was no doubt the deceased had beeg murdered, wed the question the jury had to decide was whether the prisoner was the murderer. The evidence was all circumstantial, but the facts of the case clearly pointed out that the priso- ner was the man who had committed the crime. The de- ceased was, a farmer, and the tenant of Cheetharn Fold Farm, near Lorvton. At the time of his death he was worth about £6OO. He had several relatives—two sisters, Sarah Rigby and Martha Gibbons; a brother, named James Rigby e and two nephews, Joshua, the son of James Rigby, and !John Gibbons, the prisoner, son of Martha Gibbons. Up to 'the end of May last, Sarah Rigby acted a's the housekeeper to the deceased, and both the nephews worked on the farm but went home at night. Sarah Rigby gave up keeping her brother's house owing to some quarrel, and Joshua Rigby, who sided with her, left the farm. Prisoner took the part of the old man, and after Sarah Rigby left the house prisoner and his wife went to live there. On the 2nd June the deceased made a will in favour of the prisoner, and , made him sole executor. _ Some quarrel arose between the ptisoner's wife and the deceased, and she left the house and would not return. Prisoner on the night of the 17th Septem- ber slept with the deceased, and the prisoner, according to his own account, Went to bed at half-past ten. Nothing was heard during the night. Prisoner got up at as usual at five o'clock, and went to work. At eight o'clock, his uncle not turning up, he wept with some other men and found the old asan lying dead on the bedroom floor; The body was lying in the direction of the door; with the legs partly under the bed, and the. bedclothes were all over the .body.: There was a razor on the bed, and also a knife. The deceased's throat eree'cut, and the general impression at first was that the de- ceased had committed suicide. It was, however, found, upon the terudtal of the bedclothes and the nightcap; that the deceased had been struck with some heavy weapon, and upon the head were Marks ae of kicks by a boot, the nail marks being very distinct. There were also cuts on various parts of the body. A doctor was 'Celled in, and he gave it as his opinion that the deceased had not died from the wounds on the throlt, but from the other wounds. It was his opinion that the throat was cut after the deceased was dead. There should have been agreat quantity of blood; but, as a matter of fact, there was very little blood about. It would be proved that, though the prisoner said he did not get up until five o'clock, there was a light in one of the windows three-quarters of an hour before that time. Another fact which told against the prisoner was that the . trousers of the deceased were found in the prisoner's room, and not in the deceased's room, and they had -a blood stain upon them, and hadrevidently been recently washed. Blood spots were also found on a grey shirt, which it was supposed was the prisoner's, and on examining the boots a grey hair was found upon them which corres- ponded with the hair on the razor. Besides all these facts, which tended to the prisoner being the murderer, there was the fact that the will which the deceased made, and which he had told the prisoner might be altered any time, was mis- sing, and was found at the house of the prisoner's father-in- law. The house of the deceased showed no indications that it had been entered from the outside, though. it was evident that a struggle had taken-place in the bedroom. Plans of the farmhouse having been put in and proved, i Joshua Rigbyanephew of the deceased, was called, and spoke to the quarrel between the deceased and Saraleelligby, and the residence of the prisoner and his wife at the farm- house. He said it was not true that either he or his father ever meant to take out a warrant against the deceased for ill-usage, .although he had behaved in a cruel manner to- wards his sister. In cross-examination by Mr. Addison, witness said there was a tumour that the deceased had kicked another of his sisters to death. -He was not a niggardly man. The prisoner was his uncle's pet, and they were often like father-and son. The deceased was often spoken of by his neighbours as "newt," meaning that he was a" goad-far- nothing." John Bent, father-in-law of the prisoner, said he always thought the latter a quiet and well behaved man. On the night dello 17th September the prisoner came to witness's house and asked his wife to go back to the fermhouse, but she declined to do so. Edward Marsh, a cousin of the deceased, said the pri- soner was always an honest, industrious, and kind-hearted young man. He seemed to be in great grief at the death of his uncle. Police-Constable Naylor stated that when he was called to the farmhouse on the morning of the 18th of September, the prisoner was crying bitterly. He readily answered all questions put to him. Inspector Charnley deposed to the arrest of the prisoner, and the finding amongst his clothes of a grey shirt which had a spot of blood upon it. When he examined the house he found the back door fastened on the. inside ,by a bar. Only two windows in the house could be opened, and one of them was fastened by a screw. He found no marks of any force having been used to open either the doors or the windows. ' I Dr Campbell Brown, county analyst, said he had examined the grey shirt produced. There were two black stains on the front, and one on the back of the neck. He bad examined the boots and found on the right one, between tee sole aed the upper, a long grey hair, of the same ap- pearance and calibre as the grey hair taken from the decea- sed's nightcap. There were hayseeds attached all around the boot. The nightcap had stains and indentations, and one or two small punctures which might have been produced by the boots that he examined belonging to the prisoner. ICross-examined: He could not say that the blood stains were those of human blood. Mr. J. B. Perrin, surgeon, said he examined the deceased. The wound on the neck was superficial. The skull was fractured in several places, and the injuries were Such as might have been inflicted by boots such as those producsd, belonging to the prisoner. The cause of death was fracture of the skull. Several other witnesses having been examined, Mr. Addison addressed the jury for the defence. He con- tended that the prosecution had failed to bring the crime home to the prisoner. The murder was still wrapped in mystery, and the fallacy which always underlay the putting together of a case by means of circumstantial evidence char- acterised this case; and that was, that the prosecution first made up their minds that the prieoner committed the mur- der, and having done that, they brought into the case all the minute circumstances they possibly could to support their Presumption. The motive imputed to the prisouer that de- ceased had made a will in his favour, was altogether in- adequate. The prisoner's conduct throughout the whole of the period subsequent to the murder bad been such as to point conclusively to his innocence. With regard to the removal of the will, together with the bank books and schne silver teaspoons belonging to the deceased, nottdrag by the act of removal was established against the prisoner, he being the sole executor under the will, and in fact the person who would be, as the deceased was dead, responsible for their safe keeping. In summing up the case to the jury, his Lordship said this was certainly a very extraordinary case. If the pri- soner were guilty of the murder, he was guilty of one of the most brutal and barbarous murders he (Mr. Justice Denman) had ever tried. At the same time he did not think he had ever heard a case in which there was a more com- plete and cogent and satisfactory body of evidence to appeal to the jury that the prisoner was a man of humane, kind, quiet, gentle, and respectable character. There was another circumstance roost marvellous in this case. If the prisoner at the bar was the man who committed the crime with which be was coarged— 'At this stage of his Lordship's summing up one of the jurymen was taken suddenly ill with a fit. A doctor was called in, and the juryman was removed from the Court. Subsequently the doctor returned into Court, and, in answer to his Lordship, said the juror would not be able to take his place that night, and his Lordship thereupon adjourned the case until Tuesday morning at 10 o'clock, the jury Ewing taken charge of in the meantime by one of the Court bailiffs.

On Tuesday, Gibbons was again placed in the dock charged with the murder of his uncle. Dr. Phi!pot and Dr. Oross, who had been attending Mr. Dixon, the juryman who was taken ill in the jury box on the previous evening, stated that he was not sufficiently well to continue his duties, and had ben removed to his home.

The Judge said it was obvious that he must discharge the jury. A fresh jury was thereempanelled. At the invita- tion of his Lordship, a consultation took place between the counsel on both sides and the judge. in his private room. On returning into court, his Lordship said :—Gentlemen, be- fore Mr. Shea addresses you, I wish to inform you that he and his junior, and the counsel for the prisoner and his junior, have been in conference with me, and that, as I understand it, the result of that conference was that Mr. Shea does not feel it his duty to proceed further with this prosecution. _ _

Mr. Sbee : Of course I have only to lay the facts of the case before the eourt and the jury, and with the assistance of my friend Mr. Lowther we did that fully and carefully yesterday. I am aware now, and I was fully aware yester- day morning that the case against this man is one in which the evidence is purely circumstantial ; and I could not in any way alter the evidence by going through it again. The result of what passed between your lordship and my learned friends and myself in your lordship's room was this. Without saying more, it was apparent that there were in your lordship's mind difficulties in the way of the prosecution in arriving at conviction. If there were—f only say what I assume—but if there were such difficulties in your lorclsldip's mind, I cannot disguise from myself the fact that tbere would be such difficulties in the minds of the jury ; and not only that, but I go further, and sly that if such did exist in your lordship's mind they ought also to exist in the minds of the jury. The prosecution has no wish to obtain a conviction in a doubtful case, especially when the charge is one of murder. The Crown, of couroe, is desirous that crime should not go unpuniehtd ; at the same time they are desirous of seeing that the guilty cue should be conyieecl. I would, therefore, with your bold- ship's consent, not offer any evidence a second time to the jury. Hue Lordship.—Gentlemen of the jury, I am very strongly of opiaion that under the very peculiar circum- stances of this case the learned counsel is only doing that which, representing the Crown, he is warranted in doing,

and which is in accordance with the true, just, and merciful administration ot the cohninal law. l'ais man was charged with murder: ' For a whole day YesterdaY he stood his trial. Every fact that could tell against him was most ably commented upon in opera-lag the Case by the learned counsel for the prosecution ;- area with no bl,me to him at all—becaue.e no counsel for the prosecution ever can be quite away of theexact way inashich the case may present itself in the course of the evidencr—in some parts of the case he made observations which he himself, I am quite sure, feels now were not in the result clearly established by a good deal of tile evidence. fled that been so, the case would- have presented a more serious aspect against the prisener than it did. But the case was threshed ant to the very dregs. Every piece of evidence that could be given was given, and everything that could he said for and against the prisoner was said; so that but for the remainder of the sumraing'-up and the verdict of the jury the prisoner stood his trial from morning until night. ' I began to make certain observations to the jury, and I can ! assure you that when I began them I did so with some ! hesitation as to whether:l:had not done more than it was ,! safe and proper to do in not having at an earlier part of ! I the case put it to the ' learned 'counsel for the prosecution 1 1 whether he could expect a. conviction in such a case; and I Ido not hesitate to sly it was a case in which, having heard all that had to be said from the prosecution, and aal that was to be said for the prisoner, if there had been a cenvic- Lion it would have been one over which I should not: have slept. comfortably. . Without in the least infringing Upon the privileges of - the jury to decide according to their own - conviction, which I should have • ex- horted 'them to do, I should have felt upon the evidence that there was a serious and grave doubt as to whether the case had been really brought home to -the pri- soner; the law of this country being not who committed the murder—that is not the question—not whether it was hignly improbable that no one but the prisoner had com- mitted the murder, but whether it was absolutely and con- clusively brought home to the prisoner that that murderhad been committed by him. Upon the . facts r. should have 1 l•pointed out to the jury in my summing up many and :Many _a point in which there sem a failure to make out that which was supposed to be the damning evidence against the pri- soner, and in the result I felt certain that my opinion would not have been altered ; and I feel confident that the result, if they had listened ovith ! attention to what I - had- to say, would have seen an acquittal,' In such a case it did occur to me that there might be something _ like an undue prosecution if this man were put afresh on trial for murder. Under the circumstances I thought it right to communicate with the learned counsel on both sides to give them my view of the matter • and, that being so, Mr. Shee, =in the discharge of his duty, representing the _Crown, thinks it right not to offer any evidener, to you. I think that is a right_ thing to dorander the peculiar circumstances of the case; and inasmuch as no evidence is offered, your duty is a simple one. You are bound to give your verdict accord- ing to the evidence, and say "Not guilty." The jury then formally returned a verdict of acquittal, and the prisoner was discharged.
TITE REV. HENRY A. WOLSTENHOLME (Sr. Bee's Theo- logical College), senior curate of the Parish Church, Tan- k e rsl ey, Barnsley, has been appointed to the curacy of the Parish Church, St. Helens.

THE EARLESTOWN GOSPEL MISSION.—It is a pleasure to learn that the Gos;9el Temperance Mission, conducted in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, still continues to prosper. On Sunday last the morning preacher was Mr. John Jack- son, and in the evening the hall wa crowded, when the Rev. H. E. Smith, curate of St. John's -Church, Earlestown, preached an exeellent sermon. The usual weekly gospel temperance meeting was 'held in the hall on Tuesday even- ing, Mr. Soseph Cordingley Presiding. A programme of songs, recitations, &c., was nicely gone througb, and ens& dress was given by Mr. B. Walker. The attendancewas very fair and encouraging. THE EA REES rOWN LIBERAL CLUB: ELOCUTIONARY EEC ITAL.—In aid of the funds of the Earlestown and Dis- trict Liberal Club, Mr. Robert Hall, of Manchester, gave an elocutionary "recital "in thtz Co-operative Hall, Earle- street, on Saturday evening. Mr. Hall's abilities were clearly demonstrated, and the large audience considering the,short announcement of the event, heartily applauded his efforts. Those present were interested to the end by Mr. Hall's re- citals. The programme which occupied about two hours and a quarter, was as follows: " Hathlet "—Act 111., Scene IL—The instructions to the players, (Shakespeare) • "Life," (Barry 'Cornwall); "The Psalm of Life," (Longfellow) ; "Richard •Doubledick," from "The Seven Poor Travellers," (Dickens) ; Bob Ballad," Ferdinand° and Elvira," (W. S. Gilbert) ; The Dedication of "The Idylls of the King," (Tennyson); The Charity Dinner," (a Satire), (Litchfield Moseley); Speeches by the Earl of Mount-Stewert,-Chair- man ; A Duffer, Esq., Secretary; Alderman Gobbleton, Lord ---, and M. Hector de Longuebeau. " Hamlet"— Act V., Scene L—" A Churchyard." Mytnantis Personce— The Gravediggers, Hamlet, and Horatio; Lancashire Bal- lads, " Eawr Folk," and "Forgive one another," (Waugh) ; "Bridge of Sighs" (Hod); "The Subscription Lid," from "Handy Andy," (Lover). We understand that Mr. Hall's entertainment gave so much satisfaction, that it is likely he will again be invited to give a similar recital in a short period of time.

EXTRAORDINARY ADVENTURE OF A BOY.—At the Liver- pool Assizes this week, Francis Wells, aged 12, errand boy, pleaded guilty to a charge of having, on the 30th of last Imonth, forged a cheque for the payment of £7O, With intent to defraud his employer, Mr. Gardner, a solicitor in Man- chester. Mr. Gardner stated that up to We date of the ,offence he considered the prisoner a very clever, industrionS boy, who could be trusted with almost anything. On the 30th October, uuring his absence from the office, the pris- oner got his cheque book, filled it in for £7O, air!, having forged his signature to it, took it to the bank and got it cashed. He then went to Liverpool, where he purchased a watch and other jewellery and a new suit of clothes. He stayed that night at an hotel, and next morning, after driving about in a cab for some time, he told the driver to take him to the landing stage, as he was thinking of going to the Isle of Man. On arriving at the landing-stage, being under the impression that he was being watched, be gave a boatman 18s. to row him down the river. On the Manx steamer approaching. he told the boatman to pull alongside and, having scrambled on board, he obtained a ticket and proceeded with the vessel to Douglas. Here he stayed a few days, and then, having purchased a pistol and hired a horse, he went about the hills shooting at sheep. This arnueement soon got him into the hands of the Manx police, and the forgery having in the meantime been discovered,he was detained and handed over to an officer, who was sent for him from Manchester. It appeared that he had been in the habit of reading extensively pernicious literature. He was sentenced to a month's imprisonment and two years' de- tention in a reformatory. JUVENILE GOOD TEMPLARY : DISTRICT LODGE RUNCIL AT EARL So uth-West Lancashire quarterly council of the Lancashire District Juvenile Temples was held in the Good Templars lodge-room, Bridge-street, Earlestown, on Battu, day evening last. Bro. R. Anders. D.S.J.T., presided, and there was a fair attendance of .lodge representatives, includ- ing delegates from Liverpool, earston' Widnes, St. Helens, Lie. After the openirg ceremonies the roll of officers was called, and the minutes of the previous session, held at Run- corn, were read arid confirmed. The reports of the officers for the past quarter were next receivcd ; that of the district secretary showing that there were 2,008 juvenile members of the Good Templar Order in good standing on the books, being an inci'ease of over 100 during the quarter. The district treasurer's report showed a fair balance in hand, after the payment of all expenses. The reports of temple superintendents, dealing with the positions of the various temples, were to the effect that the majority of the temples were in a very good condition and making satisfactory prow gress. Several, however, were reported as being in need of assistance, and arrangements were made for the required as- sistance to be rendered. After the various reports had bee* adopted; the question of joining a National Prize Competi- tion in connection with the juvenile temples throughout the country was considered. It was ultimately decided that the matter should be left open for each temple to act as de- sired. It was resolved that the next meeting (which will be the annual meeting) should be held at Liverpool, on a date to be hereafter selected by the Executive; and the see& sion concluded. Those present afterwards partook of an excellent tea; the subsequent proceedings being of an en. joyable character. A kind of social gathering was held; several selections of music, Sic, being nicely rs ndered at intervals.

LECTURE AND CONCERT AT EARLESTOWN WESLEYAS Scnoor..—ln aid of funds being raised for the purchase of an organ for the Earlestown Wesleyan Chapel, a lecture on Ireland, interspersed with numerous selections of music, was given in the Wesleyan schoolroom, Cross-lane last even- ing (Thursday). . The well-known ability of the vocalists attracted a considerable number of persons, the large room being well filled. The lecture was -given by Mr. George Burgess, and consisted of an interesting description of a personal tour throughout the Sister Isle. The various points of interest in Dublin, Wicklow, Kilkenny, Waterford, Tipperary, Cork, Queenstown, Mb. larnev, &c., were lucidly explained; the lecture being illus- trated with a number of excellent and clear views, thrown upon a screen with the aid of a magic lantern, by M. J. H. Graham. In the course of the evening the chap:l choir, efficiently led, by Mr. Grundy, in the absence of Mr. Parr, effectively gave two glees. The duet 6' Huntingtower " received but a moderately well. rendering from Miss Swann and 51, P. Hastie. Miss C. Roberts was warmly applauded fo beautiful manner in which she gave the song "Kathleen Mavonrneen," and it wal evident that, though young, she possesses cofl. siderable ability. Mr. S. Swann's " Under the old:flag " was finely giv.n;.but the singer did not snm in his best form. -His efforts, however; were duly appreciated. " Ler- hoard Watch" was sung by Messrs. Gilmour and Gibson; after which Miss Sydes gave "Side by side to tie better land" in fair style. The greattst success of the eVening was undoubtedly scored by Mr. P. Hastie, ever inpular with an Earlestown at:dience. He gave "The yeoman's wedding song" in a mannPr which drew forth the hearty plaudits of his hearers, wl,ich were well des.rved. An encore was demanded, but it was an- nounced that oivirg to the length of the programme it was hoped the audience would kindly keep their enthusiasm within reas4qmlile bounds. The duett, " Hark, the good bells ringing," w,is nic,ly sung by Miss Swann and Miss Jones; and Mr. T. Gil rooni,,, song, "Under the stars." was impres- sively rewlet.(l. Messrs. Willis, Atkinson, and Hains effec• tively p.ave muleteer .s 2,,Lig ' • " and the prtnramme was brought t., a close with a capital glee by the choir. A , number of miscellaneous views and one or two comic scenes ! were afterwards depicted on the "canvas," the proceedingg : concluding with the singing of the National Anthem."

BY JOHN SAUNDERS, Author of " aiRELL ; cm, LOVE BORN OF STRIFE," " ABE DR's WIFE," " ISRAEL MORT, OVERMAN," &C., &C.
CHAPTER XLV.-THE - FLYING COLUMN AGAIN ON Till) WING.

The rails were soon replaced, though it was no easy ope- ration raider the extreme severity of the weather and the depth of snow on the ground, which removed one hour, would again cover the ground in the next as it drifted be- fo7e the wind. The order was given to go on slowly lest there might be fresh places prepared for the injury of the trains. But no- thing ;wore occurud till they reached Limerick Junction. , In any other part of the wcrld than Ireland, that name would naturally mean a place close to Limerick ; and where, thvefore, the weary, cold, and half-starved troops would be at once surtounded with the comforts of civilisation.

-As it happens, Litnerial: Junction is just twenty-two miles from Limerick. But, as if to add to the charming inconvenience of everything relating to it, instead of the distance from the city being a reason why there should be special accommodation provided, it seems to have been then thought that common sense dem,,nded exactly the reverse. A more desolate place in reality at the tune of our narra- tive there could searcely be icund in the three kingdoms. One or two houses oonstituted the place in addition to what was dignified as the Station. Arriving at this oasis in tha desert of snow in the morn- ing, all got out, anxious to stretch their limbs, and covetous of food. . .

-- --- What they got was a cup of,coffee, each costing sixpencl, which the Major took the risk of paying for from his own funk. This having been at tlrs.t made in the largest ves- sel atthe command of the purveyor, was then, perhaps, fairly good. But when, as fast as coffee was drawn out hot water was poured in, the character of the beverage rapidly deteriorated, and what it became for the last men, at the end, may be readily divined, . Stephen being in the front carriage was able to get his coffee good, and then, feeling -aztisfied himself, could jest good humouredly with those who followed on their ill- luck.

Whatever the poverty of the place, it was, at all events, better than r.o place at all. So they stayed there a couple of days, waiting for fresh supplies from the camp, picketing their horseu as they hest could amid the slough of mud and snow. _ .
%V ben the expected supplies come, on a special train sent after them, it was found to contain nothing but biscuits for

the troops, with oats and hay for the horzei. The distribution was as primitive as the food. The soldiers went to the train and held out their helmet or ether headgear as receptacles. Into these they received a handful of bis- cuits each—a ration of " six upon fours," as the men called it, meaning tint the proper quaatity for four men was por-

_ tioned out among six. _ But there was a hurried call to arms and to marching order. Sconts had come in with the news they had dis- covered the Fenians in a large body, drilling in a hollow below.the mountain, cs high hill, which was in eight, though I socie mile -distant. _
"Did they see you ?" asked Major Etheredge of the aeovts.

____ ...... Both the men were sure they had not. As they were ap- 1 proaehing the Fenians, they had heard words of command given and were warned ; to they only just allowed them- selves to reach the edge, crawling on the grass till they could look over, and then immediately withdrew. The cavalry went on in advance to try to find a way round, while the infantry were to mount the hill directly in their front. But when the latter arrived after a most rapid march, they found the cavalry waiting them. They had found no way round that could be of use in enabl ng them to get secretly behind the Fenians. [...0 all began th 3 ascent to- gether. Seldom has a more difficult job been imposed upon troops. The foot soldiers went otraight for the top, but were perpetually falling in the snow and on the bare icy slopes, where the snow had been driven off by the wind. As to the trskopers, direct assent being impossible, they went for their mark in a series of zig-zags, horses slipping and rolling down every few yards, many of their riders dis- mounted, and then having to lead the animals they could not ride. Strict orders for silence had been given and obeyed, so far as silence could be practicable nyder such circumstances. So the Major was in hope they would reach the top undis- covered, unsuspected, till they should be ready to plunge down upon the busy mass of men. A mist greatly aided the attempt at surprise. It seemed indeed probable it would make a veil for them during the 1 last eventful moments, when, having reached the top, they were getting their ranks in order, and advancing step by step within range of vision. When all were ready on the crown of the hill and most of the men breathless with their exertions, the Major gave them two or three minutes, and then in a low stern voice said, his words being repeated from rank to rank by the non-commissioned officers, Stephen among them, "Stop for nothing! Down upon them! March !" Over the hedge they went, down the slopes they plunged, Iscarcely able to see anything but the dusky forma in the hollow, when suddenly burst upon them a tremendous vol- ley which laid many of the soldiery low. -

But on they went, horse and foot. The descent was more dangerous than the ascent, and caused loss of time and division of the ranks. When they reached the bottom they could see nothing but the fast vanishing forms of the fugitives who, having waited to give tlern one deadly salute, had instantly taken to flight, aided by trees, drop water courses, and low spurs of the mountain which stopped all pcssibility of effcctivo purrmit. Many bullets followed the Fenians, and sortie were seen to fall, and to be snatched up and borne away bv their com- rades. . _ .

But that was the only solace afftirded to INlNjer Etheredge and his gallant troops in his bitter disappointment, for he had thought to capture the greater part of the body, a feat that would have told wonderfully all through Ireland at so 4iitical a time. However, there was nothing to be done but to bury their dead—three in number—besides two horses which had to be shot, and which were left to the tender mercies of the wild birds and the winter winds. Then having temporarily dressed the wounds of his five soldiers who had been hit, but noue very dangercusiy, they bore them away with as much care as was practicable, and then sadly they began their march along the lower lauds to find some town or village where they could rest and get food for which they were now in imminent need.

div.head: CHAPTER XLVI.-THE SCOVT'S FATE.
div.p: CHAPTER XLVI.-THE SCOVT'S FATE.

Prcsently another incident added to the tragical events of the day. The two men who had acted as scouts, and who had been reconamended as loyal peasants of the neighbourhood to Major Etheredge, accompanied the troops on the march for a short disanee ; but presently announced their inten- tion to return to their komes, by crossing the mountain, and demanded their pay. The Captain was about to satisfy their demand, having seen no reason to doubt their good faith; but finding that they wanted more than he had aiven authority to promise he p.tused, in the rear of the troops, to discuss the matter, wishing to satisfy them, but unwilling to submit to any kind of extortion. _ _

The troops were at this moment moving round a dense plantation that promiscd them speedily a sight of the vil- Istre or the mansion to which it belonged, and they moved all. the more rapidly when they did see a noble castle not far off, with many lov trectious round where they were likely to find all that they most needed. It thus happened that the whole of the troops, excepting the rear guard, had pa.sed out of view of the Major ; and even the rear guard, who waited, seeing their Captain pause, were at some distance when the incidents we have to speak of occurred, ami which were closely watched by one of the number, Stephen • who sinaply as a matter of precaution, but in no belief as to its necessity, said to his men, "Cover tho%e fellows with your pieces ! It's all right I dare say." Presently he saw the Captain make what seemed a final gesture of refusal and turn oway to rejoin the troops. Then the scouts also .noved as if to go back, but instead of going up the hill they turned towards a watercourse, lying deep b,:low its bauks, and lined with scrub. _ _

They had not got half-a-dozen yards away before Stephen sa.w them face round—revolver in hand and fire at the Captain. But Stephen had been equally prompt, and the moment after their fire was delivered it was answered by a volley, which caused one of the nen almost to leap into the air and then fall stiff on the sward. _ _ _

When the smoke passed off, and Stephen and a couple of poldiers reached the spot in a run, they saw one rnan dis- appear into the watercourse—the other lying dead. The Captain was happily safe, and deeply moved as he saw that in all probability I.e owed his life to that favourite young soldier, whose sudden vigour had prevented the treacherous rogues who had led them where they knew the Fenians were waiting to attack the unsuspicious soldiery— from completing their villainy by the murder of the corn- manUr. The revolver of the dead man was found with five shuts ready to follow the one that alone he had been able to fire before his career was summarily ended.
CIIAPTEIi XLVII. - STEPIIEN'g NEW ACQUAINTANCE. - - -

As the troops approached the castle they could not but notice how its size and architEctural magnificence seemed to contrast with the air of desolation all round. Not one s'ugle perswifirdlifey find in any of the out- buildings first reached. The lofty stables were empty ; and it was not till they came to the entrance gateway with its heraldic monsters high above, on piers at each side, that they saw any sign of life. Then faces began to appiar at tho windows, but only to hurry away as they beheld the troop. The hell was pulled with a rude vigour that would have commanded attention had that been necessary. But it was net. The inmates were all the while hastening as friends to the court yard, and presently the gates were unclosed, and the Comte de - :aid his wife, the Comtesse, ap- peared standing on the threshold of the hall door, with a few timid-looking setYants behind them, awaiting their ap- proach.

div.p: THE WIDNES POISONING MYStERY, A CHEMIST CENSURED: THE VERDICT. On Tueadey afternoon at the Angel Inn, Mersy-roa, Widnes, Mr. W. Hardy, barrister, Manchester, acting for the county coroner, resumed the inquest touching the death of William Williams, baker, of Davies-street, who died under mysterious circumstances on the 9th inst. Inspector Wood was lrtsent on behalf of the police authorities, and Mr. Faulkner was foreman of the jury.—Mrs. Catherine Mort, the daughter of the deCeased was recalled. She stated that about four or five months ago her father was taken seriously ill. He had had some drink and he said he wouli go to the druggist's to obtain some powder to "sober hint." He went from the house and on returning he asked for some tea, which was given to him, but he did not drink it. In a short time he cammenced to vomit, and witness sent for Mrs. Kinsley The former noticed a streak of white powder on a glass which he had used, and becoming very uneasy and sus- picious she called at the West Bank Pharmacy Company's shop when sne went down the street to market. The youth whe was in charge of the shop said he had supplied her father with some white precipitate. Her father recovered entirely 12 a few days. In answer to A question witness said that when her father came home from Rencoru on the Bth inst., he said that he took a bottle with him with some- thing in it to keep him warm. The Foreman: Have you heard it reported that he had been seen drinking from A small bottle while standing near his wife's grave at Runcorn ? Witniss : No. The Coroner said the statement now made by Mrs. Mort was very material evidence, and ought not to have been kept back. lie sympathised with her, but cmhl not help blaming her a little. She otherwise gave her evidence in a very satisfactory manner. He put her through a lengthy examination, whica WAS rather an ordeal, and she came out of that ordeal with very great credit, and now she had told everything she knew about this unfortunate affair, there was not the slightest blame to be attached to her. In his opinion she was a good daughter to her father when he was alive, and when tee took this poison she did everything that an honest and a humane wolaill could do. He desired to say, as far as hal position amongst her neighbours was concerned, that her character was not tainted in the slightest degree, but, on the contrary, ought to be enhanced. Alfred Jackson, manager of the Weat Bank I".larmacy Company's shop, Mersey-road, who reluctantly took the oath, produced his register ot the sale of poisons. In that book was an entry dated the 6th November, and related to a man named William Johnson, grocer, Thomas-street, as having bought half an ounce of arsenic for the purpose of p)isoning rats. It was signed by Johnson, who was introduced by Mr. Thomas Smith, grocer, 84, Mersey-road, Widnes. Smith was in the shop when Johnson entered and asked to be served with poison. Smith said he knew Johnson by sight, but not by name. Witness could not swear that William Johnson was identical with the deceased William Williams. He could tell if he saw a portrait. The Coroner said the actof Parliament contemplated that any person introducing a man who asked for poison should know his name and all about him. otherwise the very object of the Act was being defeated. He (the coroner) knew hundreds of persons by their features, but he did not know their name 3; but if they asked him tO certify that arsenic they wish, dto purchase was not for the purpose of taking human p -erne other illegal purpose, he should not do ' - •^ Jehnson that M. Smith,
(Wall • cLe, however, , Los person and dress of Johnson.—P.S. stated that Mr. Smith had accurately described the deceased.

Inspector Wood deposed to the steps he had taken with the viscera of the deceased, and produced the following cer- tificate from Dr. J. Campbell Brown, the county analyst :- 4'l have analysed the sample contained in the two jars received from P.C. Geo. Laing, on the 12th November inst., and I tind th et the stomach and part of the intestines said to be taken"frorn William Williams, deceased, contains a Comparatively large quantity of arsenic, more thansufficient to account for the inflammation of the stomach and death." The Coroner said this was the whole of the evidence be had to lay before them, and he thought the mystery had been unravelled. The coroner then reviewed the cir-

eurnstances of the case, and said Dr. McDonnell very pro- perly refused to give a certificate of the cause of death. By order of the coroner the doctor made a post-mortem examination, and the result of that examination confirmed him that this unfortunate man's death had been caused by some irritant poison. He could not say what, and he (the ar.....,er) quite understood why he ,nni,4 tie must commend Dr. McDonnell for the very rare judgment which be brought to bear upon the diagosis of hls assistant, and the symptoms which the de- ceased exhibited. The doctor had been perfectly correct throughout, and he only did his duty in refusing to give a certificate. He was sure be could not compliment him too highly for the rare skill and sagacity which he brought to bear upon this unfortunate man's death. After the certifi- cate of Dr. Campbell Brown the jury would he satisfied that death had resulted from poisoning by arsenic. How was that poison introduced into the deceasee's stomach ? Did he take it accidentally, or did he take it knowing what, effect it would have upon him—in order that he might deprive himself of life; or did some other person administer the poison. There was no evidence to show that he took arsenic accidentally. The hand that pur- chased the arsenic was William Williams, and there was no doubt it was his hand that administered it. There was no suspicion that anybody else administered it. What motive had he for such an act? We were not all constituted alike. Williams, who was 63 years of age, had the misfortune he lose his wife, to whom he was most tenderly attached, and his grief was so intense that he was anxieus to rejoin in the grave her whom he had loved in life. He had four or five months ago attempted to poison himself, but failed His motive, therefore, was death. if th jury were satisfied that the deceased administered the poison to himself, there was another point which they would have to consider. What was his state of mind when he took it, because the law said that a man who took his own life, knowing what he did at the time, was as much a murderer as if he took the life of another. The law attached a penalty to that act. Christian rights would not be performed at the burial of the body. Bat this penalty could not very well be carried out in this instance, because the poor unfortunate man's body had been interred under an order of the Coroner granted 10 days ago. But he thought the jery, on reviewing all the evidence, would come to the conclusion that the deceased administergd the poison himself, and that the bereavement under which Ise suffered bad so affected the balance of his mind that he was temporarily insane. It would take strong evidence to induce him to say that a man who deli- berately took his life away was sane at the time he did it. He trusted he should see the law relating to the burial of at:acid...1r.,...), it not for him to say how. It was a relic of a barbargus age. After again complimenting Dr. McDonnell on his skill, the Coroner said Sergeant Clarkson and the other police who had been engaged in the matter were deserving of his thanks. They had placed beyond a doubt that Wil- liam Johnson who bought the arsenic was William Williams the deceased. After a short consultation in private the jury returned a verdict to the effect that deceased committed suicide by poisoning himself with arsenic whilst temporarily insane.

div.head: SUNDAY SCHOLARS' LUFITER
div.p: SUNDAY SCHOLARS' LUFITER

COMMEMORATION AT RUNCORN. On Wednesday last a united Sunday scholars' demen- stration took place in the Public Hall, Runcorn, to hear and see an illustrated sketch of the life and work of the great reformer. We have been given to understand that the gathering was suggested by the superintendent of Bethesda Congregational Sunday School, Mr. William Handley, and that at a meeting of the superintendents of the various Sunday schools, both Episcopalian and Nonconformist, held the previous week, the suggestion was warmly approved,and active preparation determined upon to ensure cordial co- operation and a suceessful gathering. Mr. Frith, the super- intendent of Mill Brow Wesleyan School, promised his valuable assistance in providing and manipulating the oxy- hydrogen biunial lantern, and Mr. Charles Pounall, super- intendent of Newtown Mission Church Sunday School, un- dertook the secretarial duties, while all the superintendents and teachers gave active assistance. When we state that 3,000 tickets were issued to the various schoole and that these scarcely supplied the demand, it will be seen that the demonstration was no ordinary gathering The arrange- ments, included the delivery of a running descripticn of some 40 views, illustrative of the life of Luther, by the Rev. J. D Thomas. at 5-30, to children under ten year, ot age, the interest of the youthful audience being sustained by the singing of well-known hymns, the words of which were thrown at time 3 on the canvas by the aid of the lantern. At a quarter to eight the Rev. Sydney Mees delivered an admirable lecture to the scholars above ten, including also teachers and parents. This was also illustrated by the lime- light views, and in. addition to the singing of hymns, and excellent choir (nnder the direction of Mr. F. Fairhurst) sang selections from the historical cantata, "The Reforma- tion." The gathering was a complete success, and cannot fail to leave its impression on the memory of the young -respecting the noble life work of Martin Luther.
