div.p: AURING lON LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. THE 1-I.PRESENTATION OF THE PEOPLE. Tee above association inaugurated a seiies of public lec- tures on Tuesday evening, when Mr. William Clarke, M.A., lecturer of the National Reform Union, delivered an address in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on " The Repre- sentation of the people." There was a large attendance, and the meering was at times enthusia“ic. Mr. Councillor Crosfield, J.P., preside I, and was supported on the platform by the member for the borough (J.G. McMinnies, Esq.), Mr. Broadbent, Mr. J. LI. Goma'', Mr. F. A. Roberts, and Mr. ' H. Roberts (secretary of the Liberal Association). Amongst the audience we observed Councillors Monks, Greening, lied Dixon. Mr. H. ROBERTS first announced the subjects of the com- ing course of lectures, which have already appeared in thesa columns, and said in addition that they hoped to hear in January, or early in February, the annual address of the member for the borough in the Public Hall. (Applause.) The CIIIIRMAN, in his introductory remarks, said the ob- ject of these lectures was to give information to the Liberal party uponfthe different subjects they had heard mentioned —and information not only to the Liberal party, but to the opposite party, if they chose to listen and to read; because he took it that there was a want of instruction on the Tory side as much as there was on the Liberal side. (Laughter.) In fact, some of them thought, the Tories wanted a great deil more instruction than the Liberals did. (Renewed laughter.) "lhe subject which the lecturer had selected for that night was one of vast importance to the people, cud in fact, without exaggeration one might say that the safety of the kingdom almost depended upon the proper representation of the people. (Hear, hear.) If the people were not properly represented, it would tend very much to shake the stability of the throne, because the people who were not properly represented were generally in- clined to be restive, dissatisfied, and ia the end would rise in rebellion. They were thankful that in England they were a peaceable and, as a rule, a contented nation, and the reason of that was that they had had so many good measures passed, principally and almost entirely by the Liberal party, which had done so much to settle the minds of the people and to make them content. He supposed they might take it for granted as almost a certainty now, that the first great measure which would be in- troduced by Mr. Gladstone's Cabinet would be the extension of the franchise to the counties. (Hear, hear.) After that was passed, as it was pretty certain to be passed during the coming Session, there would have to be a Bill dealing with the redistribution of seats. That, as they were aware, was a very large and a very difficult question to deal with, because every member whose seat was taken away from him would be inclined to oppose the Bill which the Govern- ment might introduce. He was not one of those who were in favour of going the length of equal electoral districts, but he did think there was great room for improvement in the present representation of the people—(hear, hear)—becaus-e he thought there were numbers of electors who should be more equally represented by the members of the House of Commons, and he had no doubt their lecturer that night would give them some illustrations of he gross inequalities which at present existed. As regarded the extension of the fran- chise to the Counties, he fancied that there would not be much difficulty in carrying it through the House of Com- mons. He expected it would be carried by a very consider- able majority, so large that the House of Lords would not attempt to throw it out. It Was a monstrous thing that a man who happened live just outside the boundary of the borough of Warr; v•ould be disqualified from having that he lived outside the
-f —he thought It was ' •-•ted and well. ,1;r1 not

.„ ...enuaee are:, present time of making a comparison between the representative ~e .e._ ments which existed in different parts of the world and those which were founded either on the principles of absolu- tism or of aristocracy. On all hands the verdict was the same that representative government was superier both to aristocratic government and to the principles of absolutism. In former days it used to be thought, and he believed it was still thought by a number of old ladies of both sexes that representative government, the spread of what were called democratic opinions, threatened anarchy to society. It was thought that the foundations of society might be destroyed if they admitted the great multitudes of the peo- ple to a share of political power, but if they looked abroad and observed the actual facts in foreign countries, they would, he thought, came to the conclusion that that was by no means the case. In the greatest English speaking communities, in their own country, in the United States, in the various colonies which had been peopled by English— men, they found a representative system fully in force. He did not mean to say it was a necessary consequence, but at any rate it was a singular coincidence that those countries were now leading the van in the great march of civilisation, whereas those in which there was a Government founded upon the principles of absolutism, a government connected w;th the military system which was at present the curse of Europe, there they found disaster, anarchy, violence, and hetred amongst all classes of the people. (Applause.) If anyone wanted to make up his mind as to whether representative government was or was not a good thing, ell he would ask his to do was to compare the government which existed in England or the United States with the government they found in the great military empires of Europe—Russia, Ger- m any, or Austria. Therefore, he maintained that repre- sentative government was a good thing. (Hear, hear.) It was a good thing because it interested all persons and all parties in the government and institutions of the country, and because it set forth that great principle that people did not exist for institutions, but that institutions existed for the sake of the people. (Applause.) That was the great fundamen- tal modern principle of Uovernmsnt. This country bad been in times past the leader in the develonment of this great principle. England was a country which bad enjeyed for the greatest length of time Parliamentary institutions—re- presentative insWutions. There was no country in Europe which had a Parliament representing the people so old as their own Parliament; still less was there any country re- presenting institutions found,d on the principles of local self-government so long as their own country.. Their emi- nent contemporary historian, Mr. Freeman, said everywhere they found freedom to be older than slavery, liberty to be older than bondage, and that was especially true of the English speaking race. (Applause.) Although they had a representative Government, and although the nglish people were able to make their will expressed and known, yet owing to so many singular anomalies existing in the system, that will was not expressed so fully and so clearly as it ought to be expressed, and the great object of the Reform Union at the present time was to establish such a system expressed fully to the Government of the country. (Hear, hear.) The first great anomaly which struck them was that whilst people living in the towns could join in the suffrage, others residing in the country could not enjoy the suffrage, or, as Sir Wilfrid Lawson put it at the Leeds conference, the Par- liament and Government of this country appeared to think that the people who lived in the country were bigger fools than those living in the towns. (Laughter.) Regarding the arguments advanced by those opposed to the extension of the franchise, the lecturer remarked that it was said the people in agricultural districts were exceedingly ignorant and would not make goad use of the suffrage if entrusted with it. The same argument was given in 1831 and 1867, and in the previous year when the reform agitation took place under the lead of Mr. Bright. Such arguments bad been always brought forward when any pro- posal was madeto extend popular rights to all classes of the community. Mr. Lowe once said that the working classes of this country were drunken and venal, and that in all pro- bability they would degrade our political life. He (the lecturer) would appeal to anyone who was accueinted with English political life as it was in the days of Lord Palmers- ton, and compare it with the English political life as it existed at the present day, and ask him as a candid and honest man whether it was degraded or not. (Applause.) He would undertake that a candid man, whether Conserva- tive or Liberal, would admit that, so far from it being de- graded, it had improved since the time of Lord Palmerston. (Applause.) it was better and sounder, and more honest in its domestic policy and infinitely better in its foreign rela- tions. Another argument of those opposed to reform was that having reference to "their ancient and time-honoured institutions," and they went on to say that the particular measure of reform which wee advocated was not in harnionv with what they termed the English constitution. Now, if they imposed upon per- sons by using too long and fine words, it might mean any- thing or nothing. Strictly speaking, and as a matter of fact, they bad no constitution in this country. In France and in the United States they had ; but they had not a written constitution in England. True, their political system was altered from time to time, but it could not be said with truth that any proposal of reform which might be suggested was out of harmony with what was called the British Constitution, nor their "time-honoured institutions," when they were spoken of by Tory after-dinner orators. (Laughter.) However, perhaps it would surprise some of them to learn that universal household suffrage Was a time honoured institution. If they had lived in England 600 Years ago they would have found that practically universal shffrage existed at that time, and in addition they had annual parliaments and paid members of Parliament. Therefore, the arguments which he had I alluded to were not very- formidable after all. (Hear, hear.) Some people eb jetted to the extension of the franchise to Ireland on the ground that they would not mike good use of it. He wanted to put an end to dynamite in that coun- try. and that could only be done by giving equal ri,htg to the people of Ireland. Mr. Clarke next pointed out some ef the .inoinalies which he said existed in our electoral evs- I eni. At the last general eleFtion 27 boroughs returned' to Parliament 27 members, receiving in the aggregate 13 434 votes. The senior member for Bradford received at the i same time 14,242 voter; that was to say he received 800 more votes than those 27 gentlemen altogether. (Laughter.)
"." ;000, uei ttio b iraz

div.head: V: EXAMINER , SArITRDAY, NOVEMBER 24, 1883.
div.p: V: EXAMINER , SArITRDAY, NOVEMBER 24, 1883.

Mr. Chamberlain 'received at Birmingham 19,5441 votes, or nearly half as many votes again as those 27 gentle- men. Mr. John Slagg received at Mar.chester 24,951 votes, or nearly twice as many as those 27 gentlemen put together. Birmingham, at the general election of 1880 had 63,000 odd voters, and if she was represented w the same rate as those 27 boroughs she would. not have three, as she-had at present, but no fewer than 65 members. (Applause.) lie had a list of some other boroughs with the number of electors in each, which would be interesting. They were as follows :—Glase.'ow, 57,920; Birmingham, 63,398; Manchester, 61,234; Liverpool, 63,946; Leeds, 49,000; Finsbury, 44,934; Hackney, 43,733; Lambeth, 50,000; Sheffield, 42,797; Tower Hamlets, 41,042; M iry le- bone, 35,935; total, 554,142, or 19 times as mauy electors as in the previously-mentioned 27 boroughs. And yA the representation was the same in both cases, and if the latter were to be properly represented they would have no fewer than 520 members, or a whole House of Commons to them- selves. (Applause and laughter.) The Government of the country thought so much of the intelligence of Manchester men that a Manchester voter was estimated by them "as worth potitic illy one-nineteenth as much as a voto- in a large number of very small boroughs. Lord Randolph Churchill represented a mere village, whose inhabitants were compelled to vote at the will of the agent of the property, which was owned by the Duke of Marl- borough, and he had as much voting power as Sir Charles Mike, who represented 23,000 people, besides wasting a large amount of time in obstructing the business of Parlia- ment. Another obstructive was Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, the member for Eye, who surveyed mankind from China to Peru, and looked generally after foreign affairs, teaching experienced statesmen their duty in relation thereto. He , represented a place which had a population of 6,000 or 7,000, out of which 1,000 were voters, and he placed his vote against that of a member representing twenty-five or thirty times the number of electors to be found in Eye. Mr. Balfeur, the nephew of Lord Salisbury, and a very able and clever member of the obstructive party, represented a small borough of eight or nine thousand people, 600 of whomi only possessed votes. The remedy for this was reconstruc- tion. He thought the people of this country would demand a unitorm residential suffrage all over the country, and an equalization of political power amongst the electors. He had read of one man having 42 votes, and he wns very much exercised in his mind how to record all them. He was much troubled litcause at the last general election he was only able to record 26 out of 42 votes. He knew many who recorded eight or ten or a doz-m votes at the general election. This was practically one law for the , rich and another for the poor. (Applause.) These anomalies, they might depeud upon it, would not be tolerated much , longer, and in all probability the next Reform Bill would , put an end to everything of that character. As a matter of , fact a poor man had far more interest in the good govern- ment of the country than a rich man. No lets an authority than John Stuart Mill said that a poor mall had far greater interest in the good government and the permanence of the institutions of the country than a rich man. When a time of trouble came the rich man had resources to fall back upon, but the poor man had nothing but his labour. (Applause.) Therefore he was interested in all tho: a measures and institutions which would conduce to the permanence and well-being of the country, to the good trade of the country, and the general prosperity of the nation. The lecturer dealt with the arguments which some people put forward in favour of minority representation, observing that so long as the affairs of the country were con- ducted by party government, the majority, as was the case in all civilised countries, would rule. If the minority by means of the Press, the platform, and public meeting could , not convince the people of the truth of their principles, they , might rely upon it that Ws principles they advocated were not worth being converted to. He did not mean to say that majorities were always infallible, as sad experience had , taught them the contrary; all they said was that there was `iser method known to them by which representative go.esent could bo 'sr:.

Radicals said " You must go in for more than you can get because you never can get all you ask for ? ' (Laughter.) There was some reason in that. He might say for himself at present, although he was not favourable to the course leading on to electoral districts, still he could not say that he should vote for an absolute division of the population in- to electoral districts_ He hoped his frieLd the lecturer would not be discouraged by his expressing that opinion, because after all he was only what was called a moderate Liberal. (Laughter and applause.) He was ex'remely obliged to his friend Mr. Roberts for what he had said about him that night. They knew for the last twelve months he had been I locked up. (Laughter.) He had had to leave them all be- hind him. He dare not even come to look at them (laughter) —so anxious was he not to do anything which would appear to be partial or improper as Mayor of Warrington. (Applause.) He was anxious to be strictly impartial and not to show any favour to one party or other. He was sure his friends there and elsewhere would not imagine that bee tU:3O he stayed away it was from any want of interest in the Liberal Party. ("No, no.") His heart was just as much with the Liberal party, and had been during the last 12 months, as it ever had been during his life. ( Applause.) He hoped he might yet be able to do more service for the Liberal party in Warrington. He again thanked them very much for the kind way in which they had received the vote of thanks. (Applause.) 'rime meeting then terminated.

div.p: THE EMPLOYERS LIABILITY ACT.
APPLICATION FOR A NEW TRIAL IN THE WARRINGTON CASE.

At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before W. Wynne-Ffoulkes, Esq., Q.C., judge, the case of Burgess v. Naylor, which was before the Court a short time since. was again called on, tieing a claim under the Employers' Liability Act for £250 compensation for damages sustained by plaintiff whilst in defen4ant's employ as sawyer. The jury at the last hearing gave a verdict for plaintiff for £7O and costs.—An application was now made by Mr. Sutton, barrister, on the part of defendant, for a new trial.—Mr. Hamilton, however, for plaintiff, offered a preliminary ob- jection to the application on the ground that seven days' clear notice had not been given.—His Honour said intima- tion was given when the matter was previously before him that appeal would be male for a new trial. He would, there- fore, hear the application.—Mr. Sutton observed that the case being so recently before the Court the particulars would be fresh in his Honour's memory. It. WAS certainly a case of very great importance bon on account of the novelty of the law in which it dealt, and also the peculiar ciicuinstane,s of the case itself. Plaintiff was therefore well justified in coming before his Honour to:endeavour to show that the verdict of the jury was both contrary to the evidence and perverse. He would satisfy the court, he thought, that if the jury had attended to the direction laid down by his Honour, it was absolutely impossible for them to come to the decision they did. The case of the plaintiff was that he had been injured by the circular saw while acting in the employ of Naylor, the reason being that the fence attached to his bench was so constructed as to be dangerous, and in consequence of the bad construction the accident was occasioned. Mr. Sutton then referred to the question which his Honour had put to the jury as to whether plaintiff had shown by a consistent case that the accident happened by the canting over of the fence. The point he relied upon was, that Upon plaintiff's own showing, and by the evidence which be adduced, that the accident could not have possibly occurred by the defect in the fence. He also pointed out that the evidence of the skilled witnesses, Messrs. Jones and Dawson com- pletely upset the plaintiff's case, and if plaintiff's statement was correct then the testimony of his skilled witnesses was completely upset. If, he contended, plaintiff had dons his in screwing up the lug properly the accident Tlsaling with the lot

div.head: LATEST NEWS. SOCIALISM IN LONDON. PLOT TO BLOW UP THE GERMAN
div.p: LATEST NEWS. SOCIALISM IN LONDON. PLOT TO BLOW UP THE GERMAN
EMBASSY.

Considerable sensation was caused in London yesterday afternoon by the publication of reports which have been found to have a substantial foundation of a discovery of a Socialist plot to blow up the German Embassy. The credit of the discovery is due to chief Inspector Greenham, and Inspectors Von Tornow, and Conquest of Scotland Yard, who, acting promptly upon important information which they had obtained, made a raid on Thursday night upon a house in Vincent Square, Westminster: and therein arrested a German pole named William Wolff, who was formerly con- nected with a waxwork show at the Westminster Aquarium. Wolff, who is a good linguist, is, it is said, by profession an interpreter, but he is test known amongst the foreign colony as a leading member of the "Third," an advanced order of Socialists, in which body he holds office on the executive committee.

Wolff was charged, before Sir James Ingham, in the Ex- tradition Court, under the Explosives Act, with knowingly having in his possession an explosive substance for an un- lawful purpose. The prisoner is described as a chemist, and gave an address at 24, Vincent Square. He gave his age as 27. He is about rive feet ten inchea in height, very thin, and pale, with dark complexion, dark brown hair and whis- kers, with a slight moustache, and respectably dressed. When placed in the dock, shortly before Sir James Ingham took his seat on the bunch, the prisoner addressed Mr. Alexander, the chief clerk, and said, with a foreign ac- cent, that he should want an interpreter for such a serious charge, and on being asked in what language, replied, " Well, I don't care, say German." Mr. Supt. Williamson, of Scotland Yard, WAS sworn, and said : Ihe prisoner, Sir James, was last night in p Issession of a zinc pail, which contained about Sibs. of gunpowder and pieces of old iron. He was also in possession of a tin cooking pot, which also contained about 71bs. of gunpowder and pieces of old iron. This pet was perforated and a fuse inserted with the gunpowder, and the prisoner did not give a satisfactory explanation of his possession of the same. In reply to a question from the magistrate, prisoner said: The thing was found on the premises where I think lodger:, live, and not in the private room where I live. It was found in a room at the top of the house, which is only used by another person, named Boldovans, who was the informer in this matter.
Detective Towner here said the prisoner lived ln the house.

Wolf went on to say this was found in a cupboard, which was used by this person. He has the key, and I beg to ask yoti to take care of my goods now, and get care of this man. He will go away. You will see afterwards that it is a swindle altogether, and that those things were put there by himself. He was watched by a respectable witness whom you can trust, and this man is but an informer and is only an accomplice.

The prisoner spoke in a very excited, rapid manner, and could hardly be understood. He was understood, however, to say that he had given information to Inspector Marshall, at Rochester R,Av Police Station, concerning a plot to blow up the German Embassy. He asked that Inspector Marshall should be called.

Inspector Von Tornow said: After certain information a warrant was granted yesterday. I went to 24, Vincent- sqaare, and a watch was kept upon the house. Yesterday (Wednesday) evening, a little after 10, the prisoner left the house and went towards Vauxhall Bridge-road. When ap- proached by myself and Sergeant Corryurst he ran along the Vauxhall Bridge-road. He was stopped by Sergeant Corryurst, and when I came up I said, "Why de you run away." He said, .‘ I have important matter on which In- spector Marshall and lamin a great hurry." We then all went to search the prisoner's house. In going into the third floor front room we saw a cupboard which was locked. We theteupon requested the prisoner to give us the key be- longing to it, when he said, "I have not got the key. The Frenchman has got the key to whom the things belong in the cupboard." We then broke the door open, and found one tin pail, already described by Superinter,der.: Williamson. We also four,", it cooking pot containing con- tents gonilar to that of the pail, but a hole had been made ,in the side through which a fuse was inserted. We also found 14 empty tins, such as are used to put powder in. On searching further we found in a bedroom on the second floor, amongst some documents, a letter addressed to the German ambassador, written in red ink, and in the German language, the translation of which is as follows : "If you wish for freedom you must give an equality. Signed for Proteirier." The tins were examined by Colonel Majendie in my presence. The tin pail contained some white wadding alpacca and seven pounds of gunpowder, covered by pieces of cast-iron weigh- ing 16flbs. This tin pail was found to be perforated about three inches from the bottom, from which projected a fuse, •sn the inside of the perforating was a piece of German r and a match. The tin cooking pot contained s, a wadding and alpacca, together with fourteen ,nds of iron, seven pounds one ounce of gunpowder, d a fuse which passed through a hole from the gun- owder to the outside of the pot which was covered with Lead and wrapped up in another piece of alpacca. -^nlv to the usual question prisoner made a rambling 'k be was understood to say that the room . He repeated his re- nfl James Ing- oxce. was -aday

ay cue command oi Elhics ran.— • •- was tyrnu,,t,t to Khartoum by a Copt, disguised as a . : count it appears.`,hat Colonel Hicks divided his advance on ObeO from Meldas and Kasfel. As the '-srent divisions uniteithey were attacked by the overwlaelmi,..„ force of the MAW, estimated at some 300,000 men. This was on the 3ai of November. During that day and the two succeeding days a desperate tight against odds was maintained ending with the complete extinction of the Egyptian force. Coming from the battle field, he says he counted 150 survi- ving wounded, among whom was a European artist named Cower. All avatable troops, numbering about 5,000, will be at once concentrated at Khartoum, from Foa, Deum, and elsewhere. This terrible catastrophe seems for the moment to have wholly paralysed the Government, but probably by the ev..ing some practical measures will have been decided upon.—Evening ave, have DO further news as yet from Khartoum. This afterhoo.. gir Evelyn Baring, Sir Evelyn Wood, and Ahdel Kadir Paella, the Egyptian general who conducted the campaign against the Mandi in 1882, met at the house cf Cherif Pacha to di,Tass the situation, and are still (at 7 p.m.) sitting. The general impression here seeris to be ttat it would be wiser to aband al the commu:dcatioh with Khartoum by way of the Nile river, and to establish a strong line of communication between the town and Sou- akin, on the Red Sea, via Berber. Apart from the fact that between Khartoum and ASSAM there are 42 cataracts on the Nile, there is an obvious advantage in making Souakiin its base, as it is a defensible seaport, and could easily be supplied and covered by ships of war. But unless very speedy action is taken there is reason to fear that Souakim itself may fall into the hands of the revolted tribes, which lava been of late acting in concert with the Mandi. We are entirely without any intelligence of the movements of the Mandi since the sth of the month, but it is conjectured that he is now not far from Khartoum. Should he become master of that town, there is no good defensible position between him and the Egyptian capital until one comes to Minieh, which is only about six hours from Cairo. The longer the situation is looked at the more desper- ate does it appear. Even should it be possible without hitch or accident to concentrate at Khartoum all the troops now available in the Soudan, they would amount to no more than a meagre garrison of some four or five thou- sand troops of inferior quality, and certainly not to be re- lied upon to defend a forlorn hope. The small army which General Evelyn Wood has here in Lower Egypt, even if it were, which it is not, provided with transport and commis- sariat for a distant campaign, is much more needed and far more likely to be useful at home than in the south. In fact all the elements for a successful resistance to the swarms which the Mandi new has, and will hereafter have, at his disposal are entirely lacking. Little doubt is felt here that Tuikey will immediately insist upon reorganising her lost province' for the Mandi's spiritual pretensions touch very nearly those of the Sultan, and as Turkish interference might not possibly suit either English or French ideas, the prospect thus opened up bristles with serious political com- plications. Egypt alone is obviously incompetent to cope with the difficulty, and should the European Powers, or some of them, refuse to allow Turkish intervention, they would by' that refusal take the responsibility upon themselves. It will then remain to be seen whether the Powers would agree to joint action, with all its difficulties and dangers, or whether with their assent England would undertake the task and a definite protectorate. That the Mandi will be con- tent with the conquest of the Soudan no one imagines.

LATER DETAILS. Yesterday's telegrams state that orders have been sent to Rear-Admiral Sir William Hewitt, Cornmander-ia-chief on the East Indian station, to support the Egyptian interests in the Red Sea. The squadron under his command will be reinforced by gunboats from the Mediterranean squadron. The Egyptian Government has not yet come to any deci- sion as to the steps to b taken in consequence of the disaster in the Soudan. Sir Evelyn Baring opposed the adoption of histy measures under the inquence of panic. The prevalent opinion in Governmental circles favours the plan of for- tifying Khartoum and holding the chief points on the Blue Nile. An recognise the necessity of immediately re-open- ing the road between Suakirn and Baber, thus maintaining communication with Khartoum. The Government is stated to be in favour of despatching a strong force to Khartoum with this object.
The church of Stinchcomb, Gloucestershire, was struck by lightning on Thursday, and the spire destroyed. Other damage was done.

EXTRAORDINARY OCCURRENCE AT A WAICE.—While wake was proceeding in a cottage in Dublin on the bodies of a woman and child, the flooring gave way, and the assem- bled party were precipitated into a chamber of a disused well. The People and the bodies were extricated with con- siderable difficulty, but fortunately no person was seriously injured.
